News.title: Chancellor John Healey unveils £150m growth fund for North as he pledges to steer Britain through economic turmoil
News.content:
JOHN Healey will today gamble on growth to steer Britain through money market turmoil.

The Chancellor is betting on an economic boom in the wake of City jitters and Iran War fall-out.



He is under pressure to boost defence spending and faces putting up taxes in late October’s Budget.

Mr Healey will present Britain as “turning a corner” despite a slew of Labour taxes.



He will put more power in the hands of local leaders and say that growth can offset persistent inflation triggered by rising oil and gas prices.

He will say: “A new story about Britain. An optimistic story. One of resilience. Pride. Huge latent potential. A country turning a corner. A country whose people, businesses and communities are ready to seize the opportunity of new technologies and new ideas.”

The Chancellor will announce a £150million fund to help businesses in the North grow and create jobs.

Labour has already pledged to save small firms £450million by slashing form-filling.

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith branded Mr Healey’s announcement a “policy-light word salad”, adding: “It’ll do little to comfort hard-working families and businesses worried about more tax rises.”

Reform’s Robert Jenrick said: “Even Rachel Reeves had more vision than this guff.”



Meanwhile, the British Chambers of Commerce says Employer National Insurance should be axed for under-25s to make it cheaper fto hire youngsters.

It could be paid for by scrapping the triple lock, the group claimed.

And a consultancy says households would see a boost of £2,800 a year if the country emulates Greater Manchester’s growth since devolution.

Mandala Partners says £8.5billion handed to mayors could unlock 100,000 homes and support 70,000 jobs.

News.title: Chancellor finally sees the light on Labour’s war on business – now he must go even further
News.content:
Tape squirm

CHANCELLOR John Healey’s move to cut red tape is at least a glimmer of recognition Labour is throttling small businesses.

But what about the rest?



What about the disastrous hike in Employers’ National Insurance contributions — and the self-harming minimum wage rise — that continue to make jobs for youngsters too expensive?

What about Angela Rayner’s spiteful Employment Rights reforms hampering growth in order to appease Labour’s union paymasters?



What about the energy costs crippling industry and households because of Labour’s Net Zero obsession? What about the failure to get a grip on the unsustainable welfare bill bleeding Britain dry?

Labour MPs love to crow that Liz Truss’s infamous mini-Budget “crashed the economy” as the yield on long-term UK Government bonds soared to 4.99 per cent in 2022.

They’re not so noisy since the yield shot up to 5.89 per cent last week — the highest in 28 years — because investors doubt Labour’s ability to service the country’s debt and have been spooked by Andy Burnham’s determination to take Britain back to the 1970s.

The people-pleaser PM shows scant sign of saying “No” to further taxing and spending even with debt interest already costing more than £110billion a year.

If Labour can’t see all this is the problem preventing growth — rather than just some red tape — then they really have no clue.

Troubling time

AS the Government is urged to get on with the deeply flawed Troubles Bill, Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant insists he “has veterans’ backs”.



His words ring hollow, not least because former Armed Forces minister Al Carns resigned this summer, branding the Bill “unfit for purpose”.

While terrorists enjoy immunity from prosecution, old British soldiers face a hounding in decades-old witch-hunts.

Those who break the law should be held to account, but veterans who acted lawfully — under government authority, in accordance with rules of engagement — should not face repeated investigations and legal proceedings even when there is no new or compelling evidence.

This pernicious lawfare hits not only those who served, but also the recruitment of future soldiers who know they can’t trust the Government to “have their backs”.

Lose your Ed

NOT content with the harm he caused with his Net Zero obsession, Ed Miliband seems intent on destroying relationships with key allies now he is Foreign Secretary.



He has put the country on a collision course with both the US and Israel with his video attack on the treatment of Gazans, which the US Ambassador to Israel says is contrary to the facts.

He really is a Milistone around our necks.

News.title: Hero cop swims through Thames in full kit to save unconscious colleague after police boat crash
News.content:
AN armed police officer has been hailed a hero for saving a drowning colleague despite being seriously injured himself.

He fractured his pelvis and badly injured his spine when their Thames police boat crashed.



Weighed down by his uniform, sub-machine gun and kit, he swam to his unconscious pal, who was face down after they were thrown out of their rigid inflatable boat at Westminster Bridge.

He flipped him over and kept him afloat until help arrived.



One source said: “The guy saved his colleague’s life even though he had terrible injuries himself. It was an extraordinary thing to do.’’

The hero officer is still in a wheelchair facing months of recuperation before being able to walk properly again.

In July, he was part of an anti-terror patrol called to help a lifeboat save a person in the water by Battersea Bridge, three miles up river.

But their boat hit an arch under Westminster Bridge at high speed.

Tourists watching above feared there had been an explosion on board.

The lifeboat turned round and plucked the officers from the river.



They were taken to hospital with three other colleagues, including the seriously injured driver.

An investigation is under way.

News.title: Two Border Force officers arrested at Heathrow over alleged drug trafficking
News.content:
TWO Border Force officers based at the UK’s biggest airport were nicked on suspicion of drug trafficking, The Sun can reveal.

A woman was arrested at Heathrow Airport and her male colleague detained at home on the same day because he was off sick.



The joint August 26 raids have stunned aviation colleagues and baffled irate bosses.

National Crime Agency officers were involved as the woman staff suspect was handcuffed as she went about her duties in Terminal 3.



The arrested duo were part of the law enforcement command within the Home Office responsible for immigration, passport control, and customs security across all four operating Heathrow terminals.

Both have been suspended from Border Force while investigations continue.



A source told The Sun yesterday: “These arrests have sent shockwaves through the Heathrow community.

“Border Force staff perform important duties including detecting and stamping out drug use and importation into the UK.

“The fact that two officers have been nicked on suspicion of drug trafficking is frankly astonishing.

“This has been a complex and forensic investigation, which is ongoing. It has left colleagues open-mouthed and in disbelief at what has happened.”



A Home Office spokesperson told The Sun yesterday: “We expect the highest standards from our Border Force officers in their vital role to protect our borders.

“We are unequivocal that where unacceptable behaviour is found, it will be subject to robust disciplinary proceedings.”

News.title: BA flight hit by £100k blunder after senior cabin crew member accidentally fires emergency slide sparking chaos
News.content:
A SENIOR cabin crew member cost British Airways £100,000 by accidentally activating the emergency slide, sparking an agonising flight delay.

The embarrassing bungle by the inflight lead came ahead of take-off from Montreal in Canada to London Heathrow.



A snap shared with The Sun shows Flight BA94 stranded on the tarmac on Saturday morning, with the rubber chute deployed from the rear doors.

An emergency slide deploys automatically when an aircraft door is opened while the slide system is set to the “armed”, or automatic, position.



Bosses were baffled by the expensive gaffe due to the hours of training given to BA crew to prevent such disasters.

The accident sparked a 3 hour, 15 minute delay before the passengers take-off for the UK on a Boeing 787 Dreamliner, arriving on Saturday at 12.30pm.



In January, another bungling crew member activated the emergency slide by mistake.

Travellers waiting to board a British Airways jet from London Heathrow to Brussels had their flight cancelled by the error.

Last year, The Sun told how a BA Captain was dramatically grounded seconds before take-off from Heathrow to Bucharest after he activated his jet’s emergency slide – costing the airline another £100,000 and sparking long delays.

The experienced £160,000-a-year pilot was taken off flying duties after leaving colleagues and passengers stunned with his “inexplicable blunder”.



It was one of multiple flights recently delayed or cancelled due to hapless crew wrongly deploying the emergency slide.

We told how a crew boss activated the rubber tube in error.

The inflight manager bungled in front of startled passengers after Flight BA199 from London arrived in Mumbai.

He was showing a new starter the procedure for deploying the chute in an emergency – but accidentally sent the inflatable slide careering to the ground.

He was flown home as a passenger and banned from operating on further flights.



A similar mishap occurred when a British Airways cabin crew member accidentally activated an emergency slide as her plane was pushing back from the stand at Heathrow, delaying passengers for more than five hours.

The flight attendant, who was on her debut flight aboard an Airbus A350, mistakenly opened an emergency door while the aircraft was preparing to taxi for its scheduled flight to Austin, Texas.

And a year ago a bungling steward had a first day to forget when he activated the emergency slide as his plane taxied to the runway.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He was on his debut flight on a Boeing 777 and accidentally opened an emergency door after push-back from the stand at Heathrow before take-off to Nigeria.

Last night, BA told The Sun of the Montreal error: “We have apologised to customers for the delay to their journey. Our teams worked hard to get them on their way as quickly as possible.”

News.title: Ex-BBC journalist & author Stephen Walker, 61, dies as ‘we’re all heartbroken’ tributes paid to ‘outstanding’ reporter
News.content:
SAD LOSS Ex-BBC journalist & author Stephen Walker, 61, dies as ‘we’re all heartbroken’ tributes paid to ‘outstanding’ reporter

FORMER BBC journalist and author Stephen Walker has died aged 61 as tributes pour in from “heartbroken” friends.

Walker was best known for his work documenting Northern Ireland’s political history, including biographies of former SDLP leader John Hume and ex-Ulster Unionist Party leader David Trimble – both central figures in the North’s peace process and negotiations that ultimately led to the 1998 Belfast Agreement.

He began his career at Radio Leeds before joining the BBC in 1991, where he would spend the next three decades.

Walker went on to become the BBC’s Northern Ireland political correspondent and later served as its London correspondent during the final years of the Troubles, the peace process and the period surrounding Brexit.





He also worked as an investigative reporter on the BBC’s Spotlight programme, covering a wide range of major stories.

News of his death was shared by his friend and former colleague Mark Carruthers.

Carruthers wrote that he was “sorry to be the bearer of such sad news” as he paid tribute to Walker.

He said: “The Walker family – Katrin, Grace, Jack and Gabriel – have asked me to let people know that Stephen passed away at home this morning surrounded by the people he loved and who loved him.



“He was a wonderful husband, father, brother and son, a fine journalist and author, and the very best of friends.

“We are all heartbroken, but grateful for his life so well and fully lived.”

Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill and deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly also expressed their sadness, describing him as a “hugely respected and dedicated professional”.

SDLP leader Claire Hanna remembered Walker as an “outstanding journalist and writer” who recorded important moments in recent history with “intelligence, curiosity and great humanity”.



She said: “He brought warmth and good humour to his work and to those around him, and his contribution to how we understand and tell the story of this place will endure for years to come.

“My deepest sympathies are with his family and friends, and with his many colleagues at the BBC and across journalism.”

He is survived by his wife Katrin, daughter Grace and sons Gabriel and Jack.

News.title: Shock as more than 60,000 Brits are arrested over ‘speech offences’ in five years – including for social media posts
News.content:
COPS have arrested more than 60,000 Brits for speech offences in just five years with people even being collared for TikTok posts.

Free-speech campaigners branded the crackdown “Orwellian” amid fears police are clamping down too much on everyday conversations.



A bombshell report by Big Brother Watch found 62,199 people were arrested over the past half-decade, with 18,510 charged and 12,292 convicted, the Mail on Sunday revealed.

Activists accept many cases are legitimate including those linked to domestic violence but they argue broadly drawn laws have unleashed a wave of over-zealous policing.



West Midlands Police in one case visited the home of a vulnerable teenage girl over a TikTok post featuring an image of a teacher alongside negative comments.

The investigation later concluded with the child formally told that no further action was taken.

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “Freedom of speech is a cornerstone of British democracy. People should not be arrested for a tweet or Facebook post, no matter how much you may disagree with it.

“Police shouldn’t be wasting time on the internet. They should be catching real criminals.”

Free Speech Union director Toby Young said: “Free speech in Britain has been on life support since Labour came to power.

“Unless we come to its defence, I fear Andy Burnham is going to pull the plug.”

News.title: Wimpish Burnham faces his Thatcher moment over the Falklands — but he’d rather launch a focus group than a task force
News.content:
CABINET ministers are ­gathered around the table when an official bursts through the door shouting: “They’ve invaded.”

Phones start ringing. The generals are furious.



The Defence Secretary is demanding answers.

Andy Burnham is staring helplessly at his Spotify playlist.



Britain is engulfed in a new Falklands crisis.

Only this time the Armed Forces are threadbare and the Royal Navy is a shadow of the fleet that sailed 8,000 miles to reclaim the islands in 1982.

And at the centre of it all stands our new PM, confronted with the one thing he has spent his political career trying desperately to avoid.

A decision that might make him unpopular.

It’s not a task force he wants to launch but a consultation.

“Could we perhaps have a national conversation?” he asks.



“Could we put it to a public vote? A review or at least a pause? Has anyone asked what the focus groups think?”

His aides point out that it’s not about a bus route or public service reform. It’s British territory.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting produces a map of the South Atlantic.

Burnham studies it. “It’s a long way from Manchester,” the PM gulps.

The scenario may seem far-fetched but sabre-rattling Buenos Aires is about to test the Prime Minister’s diplomatic mettle for the first time.



Having spent his entire political life denouncing Margaret Thatcher, he now finds himself trapped in her shadow, forced to channel the iron resolve he once vilified as he navigates the unfolding Falklands row.

Argentina President Javier Milei has turned up the heat after detecting a weakness at the heart of the Labour Government.

The Austin Powers lookalike plans a new naval base in Tierra del Fuego and has threatened legal sanctions to halt drilling for oil 140 miles off the islands.



It’s unlikely that he will turn into his alter ego, Dr Evil, and mount a second attempt to seize them by force.

But that is almost beside the point. Silly Milei is probing Britain’s resolve through diplomacy, sanctions and military posturing.

And the uncomfortable question for Downing Street is not whether Argentina will send troops storming ashore tomorrow.

It is what Britain could realistically do if the rhetoric became something more dangerous.

Forty-four years ago, Margaret Thatcher sent a task force of 127 ships, 43 of them Royal Navy vessels, across the Atlantic to fight a war.



Today, the Navy is a much smaller force and has just 13 operationally available warships.

That matters because deterrence depends on what you are actually able to do — as well as what you say.

And so far, the words from No10 have been nothing short of wimpish.

Burnham, who has pontificated on everything from GCSE results to his favourite pub snacks, has kept a Sphinx-like silence on the Falklands.

The lily-livered reaction from his spokesman was: “We continue to have a diplomatic relationship with Argentina, and . . . want to continue to strengthen that.”

But there’s worse. Former Foreign Office chief Lord McDonald questions whether the 3,600 islanders, who voted 99.8 per cent in favour of remaining a British Overseas Territory in 2013, should have the right to self-determination when British taxpayers fork out £500million a year to defend them.



His stance is an insult not only to democracy but to the 255 British military personnel who died liberating the islanders from Argentinian invaders.

Lord McDonald may have left the Foreign Office in 2020, but his views give an alarming insight into Whitehall group-think — the same mentality which last year surrendered sovereignty of the Chagos Island and tried to block Brexit after the biggest democratic vote in our history.

Will our new PM have the clout to stand up not only to Argentina but to the civil service too?



Margaret Thatcher famously charmed a reluctant US President Ronald Reagan to back Britain in 1982.

Burnham faces a tougher task persuading Donald Trump, furious over his decision to press on with the Chagos deal and Labour’s refusal to join the Iran war.

Massive oil reserves off the islands — enough to fund defence of the islands for the next two centuries — could drive him to rethink the USA’s traditional neutral stance.

Which makes it an even bigger headache for Burnham.

He has spent the past few years arguing about redistribution of power in Britain. Now the world has presented him with a rather different question, he is silent.



In a bizarre twist, while he snubs the Thatcher legacy, President Milei is a great admirer.

The Argentine leader imported her policies successfully to tame inflation and drag the country out of debt for the first time in years.

He even brandished a chainsaw to illustrate his determination to cut out waste and slash the benefits bill.

But the cuts have dented his own popularity, which is why he’s now banging the Falklands drum.

Milei may have just handed Britain’s most reluctant Thatcherite the one thing he never wanted: a Thatcher moment.



Will he rise to the challenge — or retreat to his favourite soundtrack by The Smiths?

I was looking for a job and then I found a job. And Heaven knows I’m miserable now.

MORE than 60,000 people have been arrested over the past five years for things they posted online, according to a report by campaign group Big Brother Watch.

That’s 33 every day.

With so much police time taken up, is it any surprise that shoplifters and burglars are ­having a field day?



A HIGHLIGHT of Andy Burnham’s first week in the Commons as PM was his “love in” with Lib Dem leader Ed Davey.

The PM nodded as he was asked about forging closer links with the EU.

To Davey’s delight, Burnham confirmed he would use an upcoming summit with Brussels chiefs to continue pushing us back into the EU’s orbit.

Predictably, he also blamed Brexit for a “decade of low growth” in Britain.

Have these two Remainers forgotten that their parties voted down THREE TIMES Theresa May’s withdrawal agreement, which would have left considerable room for the closer ties they now crave?



They threw it away in their enthusiasm to block the biggest democratic vote in UK history.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It’s also worth noting that Burnham’s first act as PM – saving households £45 a year by cutting VAT on energy bills – would not have been possible had we still been EU members.

Just saying.

News.title: Chancellor to say UK economy 'turning a corner' despite debt concerns
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey is set to unveil a Â£150m fund for companies in the north of England as part of a wider plan to generate more economic growth around the UK.

In a speech on Monday, he is expected to outline his proposal to boost development by using public investment to attract private capital.

The speech comes against a challenging backdrop as the chancellor faces pressures ahead of his first Budget on 28 October, including concerns about a jump in government borrowing costs and the inflationary impact of the Iran war.

In response to Healey's plan, the Conservatives said that what was being proposed would "do little to comfort hard-working families and businesses".

Healey is set to announce a new Â£150m allocation from the British Business Bank which would offer support to the "most innovative and fast-growing firms".

He will detail plans to use public investment to "unlock private investment, to support our innovation economy, and to create the new jobs their areas need".

The fund, from money already allocated to the British Business Bank, will provide investments of between Â£5m and Â£15m.

It is expected to back university spin-outs and other "ambitious businesses" across the north.

The chancellor is expected to say: "The prime minister laid out a clear diagnosis of what has gone wrong in the past. The solution is a fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places.

"The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places."

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Economic growth in every postcode sounds great and is something we would all love. I think it'll actually be much harder to achieve in practice."

She said it would be easier to see how the government could make stronger second and third cities than to see "how it would drive growth in literally every postcode".

During his first Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, Andy Burnham faced scrutiny over rising UK borrowing costs.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged him to say how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high.

Burnham blamed the previous Tory administration, and said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility".

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Healey's plan would do "little to comfort hard-working families and businesses across the country who are worried about more tax rises or the fact that government borrowing rates are near a 28-year high".

He added: "We are facing serious threats from Russia and Iran on our doorstep, as well as threats to the Falkland Islands.

"Yet the chancellor, the man who resigned over defence spending, seemingly does not want to mention our armed forces or how we will reach 3% of GDP on defence."

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "Re-announcing Â£150m across the entire north of England will barely shift the dial on growth."

Robert Jenrick, Reform UK's economic spokesman, said: "Days after a market meltdown, when grip and direction are required, John Healey has revealed himself to be an empty vessel with no idea about how to rescue our economy."

News.title: BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri reveals she has blood cancer
News.content:
BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has revealed she is living with blood cancer.

Moshiri, who joined the BBC in 2003 and is one of the news channel's best-known anchors, told the BBC she wanted to share her diagnosis to raise awareness about the disease.

"It's been two years since my diagnosis and I've felt that I've started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I've got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness," the 49-year-old said.

"I'm going to have to spend the rest of my life being treated for this," she added.

Moshiri was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.

In PV, your body makes too many red blood cells, which makes the blood thicker than normal.

It leads to a higher risk of developing blood clots, which can cause a stroke, heart attack or deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Symptoms can include headaches, confusion, dizziness and blurred vision.

"I was told by my consultant that I have this incurable blood cancer," she said.

"Mostly I had no symptoms and that's one of the problems with this disease.

"The only reason mine was caught was because my GP was so fastidious in the way she did my routine blood tests and immediately sent them for further diagnosis."

As part of her initial treatment, the BBC News chief presenter underwent several "debilitating" hour-long sessions of venesections.

Venesection is a procedure where a needle is put into a vein in the arm to slowly draw the blood out.

This blood letting can be an effective way to reduce the thickness of the blood.

"In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted," she said.

"After a while I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue."

Later, Moshiri was able to get on an immunotherapy treatment called interferon through the NHS, and after some tweaks, she says she is in a better place.

"I've only needed one venosection in about 15 months, so that's been really good. The last couple of months have been better than the last two years," she said.

"I think it's really important people understand that this blood cancer is incurable but it's manageable with the right treatment and you can lead a relatively healthy life.

"It's just a question of finding the right treatment and making sure it works for you."

She admits she is "not the person I was two years ago" but says she feels "much better".

News.title: 140 migrants in single dinghy rescued in English Channel
News.content:
Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy have been rescued in the English Channel.

The people on the inflatable vessel, which launched from the Normandy coast on Saturday night, requested help in UK waters and were picked up by two RNLI boats, the French coastguard said, before being taken to shore in the UK.

It comes days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

On Sunday night protesters were involved in a stand-off with police near the Eastney Landing ferry port in Portsmouth, where small boat occupants had been brought to shore.

The protest came a day after a large group of masked men held a demonstration over the small-boat crossings at the Port of Dover, causing major disruption.

In August a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.

The latest dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water.

It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth.

French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles away from the usual launches around Calais making the crossing to the UK significantly longer.

News.title: Minister to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected
News.content:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expected job cuts at the car maker.

JLR confirmed to the BBC it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The company did not confirm the numbers but the Times reported as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

Reynolds told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the meeting early next week will focus on ways to "mitigate any job losses" but ruled out a bailout for the company.

Asked about the cuts, which are believed to impact mainly white collar workers, Reynolds said: "A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change.

"If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have."

He said there would be no support "if it's to bail people out", but opened the door to a "long-term investment in the future" of the company.

The cuts come as Chancellor John Healey is preparing to deliver a speech in the Midlands on Monday promising to boost economic growth by changing how the government values investment in infrastructure such as transport and housing. JLR is based in Coventry, in the West Midlands.

The Liberal Democrats said the news would be "devastating" for JLR staff and called for Healey to use his speech to offer "support for those jobs at risk".

"This development lays bare that the government's growth mission is falling far short," the party's business spokesperson Sarah Olney said.

News.title: Jamaica to bring slavery reparations petition to King Charles
News.content:
The Jamaican government will highlight to King Charles a petition over slavery reparations on Monday, the country's culture minister Olivia Grange has said.

It will ask the King, who serves as Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the country's highest court, over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

Grange said it could pave the way for a "long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured".

She will also meet with British Museum officials to discuss the repatriation of artefacts taken during the colonial era.

The three questions which the Jamaican government is asking the King to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) are: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law, whether it broke international law, and whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress.

The petition, which is not a demand for payment, goes to the King who then refers it to the JCPC.

King Charles has no personal discretion in deciding whether to make a referral.

Grange said: "Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined."

Buckingham Palace has been working closely with the Governor General of Jamaica to ensure the petition is correctly lodged.

A Palace spokesperson said: "His Majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today."

News.title: The £70 refund letter that isn't a scam
News.content:
You may be among the one million people, mostly women, who will receive letters explaining how you are eligible for top-up pension payments - and it's not a scam.

Those entitled are low earners who have missed out on the money because of the way their pension is administered.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) will write to people over the next few months, explaining how to receive the payment. Typically they will be due Â£70, but that may vary considerably depending on their circumstances.

Anyone eligible will be contacted automatically but, if you receive a letter, there are various checks you can do to ensure the letter is genuine so you don't get hoodwinked.

News.title: Rapist serving life may face more assault charges
News.content:
A convicted serial rapist described by police as "one of the most prolific predators" in the UK could face further charges after fresh allegations involving seven more women were passed to prosecutors.

Chinese national Zhenhao Zou is serving a life sentence with a minimum term of 24 years after he was found guilty of drugging and raping 10 women in London and China between September 2019 and May 2023.

Believing Zou had committed further crimes, police appealed for more potential victim-survivors to come forward.

The Metropolitan Police has sent a file containing the new allegations of sexual crimes to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which will decide whether to bring further charges.

According to the Met Police, the file contains evidence relating to several alleged offences, including rape and administering a substance with intent to commit a sexual offence.

It relates to reports made by five women who contacted police following the appeal, as well as the alleged rape of two women who remain unidentified, the force said.

A total of 23 women contacted police following the appeal, but most of them did not want to pursue criminal charges, the force added.

The Met said separate inquiries were ongoing into allegations involving women who were allegedly assaulted by Zou in China, with officers working to obtain evidence from the Chinese authorities.

News.title: Iran warns of 'faster, heavier, more painful response' to US attacks
News.content:
Iranian state media also reported on Sunday that the country's Navy had attacked an American remote-controlled vessel that was trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz.

The US military has denied the claim.

"The report came from Iranian state media and it's a total lie," said Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, according to the Associated Press.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has issued his own threats back at Iran, writing on social media on Saturday, "It's simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers."

A 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, and that period of relative calm was shattered when the US resumed attacks last Sunday.

Fighting has continued throughout the week, with the US launching multiple strikes on Iranian targets and Iran retaliating against US targets in the region, including in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan.

US President Donald Trump said this week that the renewed fighting would not last "too long", echoing comments both he and his administration have frequently made since the now six-month-long war began in February.

Months of negotiations between the US and Iran have not amounted to lasting peace, and there's little sign of a further diplomatic settlement on the horizon.

The Strait of Hormuz, which is crucial to the world's oil and gas industry, has been effectively closed since the war began, and has become a major source of leverage for Iran.

Tehran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway.

But Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route.

The conflict in the strait has led to an increase in gas prices globally, and ahead of the US midterm elections in November, Trump is facing pressure over how much the war is costing American consumers.

The average price for one gallon of diesel in the US hit $5.85 on Friday, compared to an average of $3.71 a year ago.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that an average of 9 million barrels of oil a day were passing through the strait, which could help ease pressure on energy prices.

Wright told CNN with oil also moving through pipelines in the region, "we're probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows".

In an interview with ABC This Week on Sunday, Wright added that gas prices should start to come down for Americans as summer demand begins to wane after Labor Day.

News.title: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
News.content:
Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.

Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.

Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port.

Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".

Mills said the force "appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing".

"The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen," he told the BBC.

"But then I accept that the police resource is stretched."

The Labour councillor said "no-one actually knew" what was happening on Saturday morning and there "needs to be a wash-up over that".

"All in all it was a pretty traumatic day for a lot of people travelling, trying to get around their business," he said.

Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests and described it as a "spontaneous protest".

Mills added that the council later received complaints from villagers in Preston, where "protesters appear to have parked their vehicles before they came in".

Chris Vinson, leader of the council's Conservative group, previously said the men had "loaded into rental vans" and then travelled to the town.

News.title: Baby girl dies while camping with family in woods
News.content:
A three-month-old girl has died while camping in woodland with her family, police have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to land off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at 08:45 BST on Saturday, to a report of a child in cardiac arrest.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

"While the investigation remains at an early stage, this is an isolated incident," Det Insp Katie Gregory said. "The death is being treated as unexplained at this time."

People living in the close-knit community, a village of around 7,000 people, have been left shocked by the child's death.

News.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
News.content:
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

News.title: Raise the Colours founder charged with 14 offences
News.content:
The founder of an activist group which has been putting Union Jack and St George's Cross flags on lampposts has been charged with a string of offences including racially aggravated harassment, threatening behaviour and assault.

Ryan Bridge, 45, of Blackwell, Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, has been erecting flags in the Midlands and the south of England since last summer as part of Raise the Colours.

Thames Valley Police said Bridge had been charged with 14 offences from a two-month period in Oxfordshire earlier this year.

He is due to appear at Oxford Magistrates' Court on 3 November.

The offences are:

Seven counts of using threatening words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm or distress

Three counts of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause fear of, or provoke, unlawful violence

Two counts of racially aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distress

One count of racially aggravated fear of violence

One count of common assault

In July, Oxfordshire County Council was granted a High Court injunction to stop people placing flags near highways because of safety concerns, trespass and obstruction.

Birmingham City Council has applied for a similar injunction which will be heard at the High Court on Tuesday.

News.title: Three charged with attempted murder after shooting
News.content:
Two adults and a teenager have been charged with attempted murder after a shotgun was fired in a town centre.

Police were called to Market Place in Braintree, Essex, at about 22:10 BST on Monday following what officers described as a "targeted attack".

Two teenagers sustained serious injuries to their face and upper body, while a third person was also injured.

Destiny Ema, 23, of Meadgate Avenue, Chelmsford, Kayden Brown, 18, of Noaks Avenue, Chelmsford, and a 17-year-old from Braintree who cannot be named for legal reasons are due to appear at Chelmsford Magistrates' Court on Monday.

A 16-year-old boy previously arrested in connection with the incident has been released on police bail until 30 November.

Ema was also charged with numerous other offences connected to separate investigations including:

Attempted grievous bodily harm with intent

Possession of a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence

Possession of a firearm while committing an indictable offence

Possession of a firearm while prohibited for life

Harassment

Malicious communications

Possession of a shotgun with intent to cause fear of violence

News.title: Two killed as car hits group of cyclists
News.content:
Three people have been arrested after a car crashed into a group of cyclists, killing two riders.

Kent Police said a white Ford Focus was travelling along Sole Street in Cobham near Gravesend just before 07:50 BST on Sunday when it was involved in a collision with three cyclists.

Two of the cyclists - a man in his 60s and woman in her 50s - were confirmed dead by emergency services on the scene, the force added.

Their next of kin have been informed.

A third cyclist was taken to a local hospital for treatment with minor injuries, according to officers.

Two men aged 20 and 21 were arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

A 19-year-old woman was also detained on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Kent Police said the road was closed while an investigation took place.

The force is now appealing for anyone who witnessed the incident or saw the car or cyclists before the crash to contact them.

News.title: Swinney suggests Scots will not travel further for health care under reforms
News.content:
Scots should not have to travel further for health care under the government's plans to cut the number of health boards from 14 to two, John Swinney has suggested.

The BBC asked the first minister about the impact of such changes for people who are already travelling long distances - such as women living in the far north who have to travel 100 miles down the A9 to give birth in Inverness.

Swinney said it would "not be my intention" for people to travel further, with initial modelling showing the country divided into two east and west health boards.

He also said he could not put a "specific figure" on NHS job losses, but he had been "open about the fact that public sector employment will fall".

News.title: Body-worn cameras given to school crossing wardens
News.content:
Lollipop men and women in Sheffield have been given body-worn cameras in an effort to combat abuse and aggressive behaviour from drivers.

Sheffield City Council said school crossing wardens at several unspecified locations across the city would be given the cameras, which will record interactions, as part of a new initiative.

The local authority said the measure would create a safer environment for families walking to school in the new academic year and provide reassurance to staff working alone.

Wardens have been subjected to "unacceptable behaviour" and dangerous driving by a "small" number of motorists, the council added.

Jefferson Nwokeoma, the authority's assistant director of city transport said: "These body-worn cameras will help protect our staff, provide valuable evidence when incidents occur and encourage motorists to follow the rules of the road.

"Ultimately, this is about making the journey to school safer for everyone."

Drivers who fail to stop for a school crossing warden can be fined up to Â£1,000 and have three penalty points added to their licence.

Clinical Carlos Alcaraz moved a step closer to making more tennis history after cruising into the US Open quarter-finals.

The Spaniard, still showing no signs of the wrist injury which sidelined him for more than four months before the tournament, dismantled American Tommy Paul in straight sets.

Alcaraz is already the youngest man to complete career grand slam and should he go on to win back-to-back Flushing Meadows crowns he would become the only man in the open era to successfully defend major titles on all three surfaces.

Having won on the grass of Wimbledon in 2023 and 2024 and on the French Open clay in 2024 and last year, the 23-year-old can complete the set on hard courts if he triumphs next Sunday.

Paul, the 20th seed, had talked up his chances before the match, saying “I like to think of myself as somebody who always thinks I can beat those (top) players”.

But a 6-4 6-3 6-4 defeat means Alcaraz has now beaten the 29-year-old six times in a row, winning the last 14 sets they have contested.

He actually faced two set points at the end of the third, but swatted them away with two contemptuous forehand winners on his way to victory in two hours and 21 minutes.

“I played my game, tried to play my style,” he said. “Tommy is such a talented player, his shots are dangerous so I tried to be ready for the battle, to be ready to run and be aggressive.

“I think I did it pretty well. Really happy with the performance today. Am I back to full power? I mean I think so.”

open image in gallery Ben Shelton returns against Stefanos Tsitsipas (Adam Hunger/AP) ( AP )

Alcaraz will face Ben Shelton, who beat Stefanos Tsitsipas, in what will be the first genuine blockbuster match in the men’s draw.

The American eighth seed’s 140mph-plus serves will provide the sternest test yet for Alcaraz’s wrist.

Alcaraz has a better grasp of a tennis racket than he does of how to read the draw, as he initially thought he was playing the winner of Frances Tiafoe’s match with Daniil Medvedev.

After being pointed in the right direction, he said: “Shelton’s a really powerful player. I think he’ll use the crowd, get the people behind him, especially when he’s playing here at home.”

Tiafoe beat 2021 champion Medvedev to ensure at least one American will reach the semis as he will face Alex Michelsen, who downed Argentina’s Tomas Martin Etcheverry to reach his first grand slam quarter-final.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un commissioned his second naval destroyer and called for building a more reliable nuclear deterrent, state media reported Monday, as the U.S., South Korea and Japan began a trilateral military exercise he views as a security threat.

The development comes as North Korea is dialing up pressure on the U.S. after rebuffing President Donald Trump's decision to scale back a major military drill with South Korea in a conciliatory step toward Kim. Observers say North Korea wants to wrest bigger U.S. concessions.

The destroyer Kang Kon was commissioned into North Korea's navy in the eastern port city of Wonsan on Sunday at a ceremony attended by Kim and his teenage daughter whom South Korea’s spy service calls his likely heir. North Korean state media photos showed the girl dressed in a white dress and blazer walking alongside her father on a red carpet, touring the warship and posing with sailors together.

The ship and the Choe Hyon, commissioned in June, are both 5,000-ton destroyers equipped with nuclear-capable missiles, making them North Korea's most advanced warships.

In a speech at the ceremony, Kim said the destroyers' back-to-back commissionings instilled fear in the enemies as the nuclear armament of North Korea's navy made it possible to exercise its nuclear deterrent in a more diversified, practical manner.

“Concerns of the enemies will be surely deepened,” Kim said. "We must establish more clearly a powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent, to put into practice the diverse and effective operation of our nuclear combat systems and further strengthen our military activities for maritime defense and war deterrence.”

On Monday, the U.S., South Korea and Japan were set to kick off their five-day Freedom Edge exercise in the waters off South Korea's southern Jeju island. South Korea's military recently said the exercise is defensive in nature is meant to respond to North Korea's nuclear threats.

Last week, North Korea's Foreign Ministry accused the U.S. of more clearly expressing its confrontational posture against the North. It cited the Freedom Edge exercise and U.S. officials' reported comments that the U.S. remains committed to the complete denuclearization of North Korea.

On Aug. 21, the U.S. and South Korean militaries ended their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise six days earlier than originally planned, after Trump said he had ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the drill. Trump cited what he described as a good relationship with Kim, who views the drill as an invasion rehearsal.

But Kim's sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, shrugged off Trump's outreach, saying just shortening the drill won’t change its “provocative, aggressive nature.” North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea, apparently delivering on its previous threat to respond to the U.S.-South Korean drill.

Kim Jong Un has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its “hostile policy” against North Korea and respects what he calls North Korea's status as a nuclear state.

Kim and Trump's earlier diplomacy collapsed in 2019 due to disputes on how much economic benefits North Korea should get in return for a limited denuclearization step. Now with his advancing nuclear program and deepened ties with Russia and China, experts say Kim has greater leverage than before.

At least five people have been killed and five more injured after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway at Miami International Airport, according to authorities.

The plane hit multiple vehicles and burst into flames, sending thick, dark clouds of smoke into the air Sunday afternoon.

The Federal Aviation Administration said the aircraft overran the runway and crashed while landing at around 2 p.m. The flight had been heading to Florida from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

“Five people lost their lives and five others were injured,” Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a press conference later Sunday. “My heart is with all of the families who were affected and to everyone who is grieving tonight, and we’re also praying for the injured and for their families.”

open image in gallery At least five people have been killed and five more injured after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway at Miami International Airport, according to authorities ( Reuters )

open image in gallery The Federal Aviation Administration said the aircraft, which was heading to Florida from Puerto Rico, crashed while landing at around 2 p.m. ( Getty Images )

Photos and videos shared online appeared to show the Prime Air plane had come to a rest beside a roadway. More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the airport to extinguish the blaze, officials said.

Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement Sunday, “We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport. Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.

“The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA was sending investigators and issued a full ground stop at Miami International as emergency crews responded to the crash.

open image in gallery Airline passengers can expect average delays of more than six hours until Monday at around 4 a.m. ( Reuters )

During a ground stop, all flights are put on hold and the airport is essentially shut down.

The ground stop will end at 9 p.m., but travelers will continue to experience flight disruptions into early Monday as the FAA has also issued a ground delay.

Airline passengers can expect average delays of more than six hours until Monday at around 4 a.m.

The National Transportation Safety Board said it was “gathering information” about the crash.

Donald Trump has been mocked over his new design for Space Force uniforms, with social media users comparing them to the costumes worn by sci-fi villains – and even Nazis.

The president raised eyebrows Sunday after posting a graphic of a “next generation” design for Space Force uniforms that includes a sleek, charcoal-colored collared jacket and pants with a black belt, black boots and a matching cap. There’s also the Space Force Delta symbol on the collar, sleeve patch, belt buckle and the front of the cap.

The graphic says the design is “inspired by the discipline and functionality of the Starship Trooper uniform. Modernized for the guardians of the space domain.”

Starship Troopers is a 1997 space epic — directed by Paul Verhoeven, who grew up in Nazi-occupied Netherlands — about a future Earth governed by a fascist regime that wages war against giant alien bugs. Some social media users picked up on the inspiration behind the uniforms, while others compared them to other space films.

“Designing the Space Force uniforms to look like the evil bad guys from Star Wars, who are led by an elderly, power hungry tyrant, who lose, repeatedly, is a bit too on brand, no?” healthcare advocate Melanie D'Arrigo wrote on X.

open image in gallery Donald Trump has been mocked over his new design for Space Force uniforms, with social media users comparing them to the costumes worn by sci-fi villains – and even Nazis ( Donald Trump via Truth Social )

An independent military history author who goes by ChrisO_wiki shared a GIF of a scene from the 1987 Star Wars parody film Spaceballs, and wrote, “Ah yes, I see the source of inspiration for this uniform.”

“This is the kind of design costume designers make to tell you who are the bad guys in a space movie,” menswear writer Derek Guy posted.

Speaking on Starship Troopers, Jonah Goldberg, the editor-in-chief at The Dispatch, a digital media company focused on politics and culture, said, “My concern is whether these guys understand the point Verhoeven intended in Starship Troopers.

“The thing is I don’t know what would be worse: whether they got it or didn’t.”

A political X account that goes by Wu Tang is for the Children sarcastically wrote, “No Nazi vibes here.”

open image in gallery The new design includes a sleek, charcoal-colored collared jacket and pants compared to the current Navy blue uniforms ( AFP via Getty Images )

Several conservative voices also chimed in, noting the similarity to Star Wars uniforms.

Christian broadcaster Erick Erickson called the uniforms, “A cross between Star Trek in the symbols and Imperial Forces from Star Wars.”

Jennifer Zilla, who identifies as a “conservative critic,” said she was “entirely on board with Space Force and the new Space Academy coming and everything we’re doing in space and President Trump.”

But she admitted that the new design was “the uniform of the Imperial Army from Star Wars.”

“Aka the people Darth Vader works for. Emperor Palpatine’s people. I’m not saying don’t use it I’m just pointing out that’s what it is,” she wrote.

It’s unclear if Trump will actually push to change the design of Space Force uniforms or if the graphic was just part of one of his regular social media sprees.

The Independent has reached out to the Space Force and White House for comment.

Just one week after a Republican senator pleaded with him publicly to turn on the faucet and save Republicans in key races, Donald Trump appears to be listening.

FEC filings from the president’s MAGA Inc. PAC over the weekend detailed a $10m spending surge in favor of controversial Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton as he battles in a surprisingly tough race to hold on to a GOP Senate seat currently occupied by Sen. John Cornyn. Paxton defeated Cornyn earlier this year in a primary, with Trump’s backing.

However, he is now facing a fierce battle for the crucial U.S. Senate seat from his Democratic Party rival, Texas state representative James Talarico. The close polling in the traditionally red state has spooked Republican leaders and prompted them to press the president to start spending from the giant warchest he has been accumulating – money that Trump traditionally considers his own.

Talarico himself has already raised more than $50m since his primary concluded weeks before Paxton's.

The expenditure is the first of its size and kind for the 2026 cycle coming from MAGA Inc., the president’s primary vehicle for political spending. It came almost exactly a week after a Republican senator from Louisiana, John Kennedy, begged Trump to get involved in the Texas race.

open image in gallery Ken Paxton with Donald Trump in Dallas, Texas, in June 2020. Paxton won his primary despite facing a major cash disadvantage ( AFP via Getty Images )

"We in the Senate don’t have the money budgeted for Texas. We need help from the president,” Kennedy told Fox’s The Sunday Briefing.

Kennedy wasn’t the only one ringing the alarm bells about Texas. As Paxton continues to run neck-and-neck with Talarico, the Republican’s onetime rival is also painting a frank picture about the state of the race.

open image in gallery Paxton’s former opponent, John Cornyn, has vowed not to support or raise money for him ( Getty )

“Paxton’s a poor campaigner,” Cornyn told The Texas Tribune last week. “He’s lazy and doesn’t raise money. And he basically is not offering a very compelling case for his election.”

Paxton’s reputation may not be helping: His vulnerabilities, highlighted by Cornyn and his allies during their bitter primary, stem from an ugly divorce from his wife, Angela, as well as an impeachment effort in the Texas state legislature headed up by his fellow Republicans.

He's accused of misusing state resources and corruption, and even using his office to conduct affairs. He has denied the allegations as politically-motivated attacks.

Now, the strategy seems clear: Make up for issues of candidate quality with a massive surge of national money, the same strategy that saw Republicans make gains but ultimately fall short of taking a Senate majority during the 2022 midterm cycle. But how much can money buy in Texas?

For Paxton, a $10m gift may seem like quite a lot. But it’s a drop in the bucket compared to the total size of Trump’s war chest, which according to FEC data is sitting north of $400m. And it’s also relatively small compared to the amount that Republicans have already spent against Paxton, back during a divisive primary and runoff that concluded in May that topped more than $130m in spending — the vast majority of it in favor of Cornyn, not Paxton, and a sizable amount spent on negative ads against the man now running with the GOP’s flag.

Paxton, it should be noted, won that runoff handily, leading Cornyn by nearly 30 points in the final voting. He spent less than that $10m sum throughout the entire primary season, focusing on an expansive ground game across the vast stretches of Texas while being bombarded on the airwaves. His victory spoke to both Cornyn’s unpopularity and the ineffectiveness of that media-focused strategy practiced by Cornyn and his D.C. allies.

open image in gallery Democratic candidate James Talarico is running neck-and-neck with Paxton in a recent poll ( Getty )

Polling of the GOP primary showed large numbers of undecideds leading up to election day with Paxton carrying a comfortable lead in every poll, only dropping to the single digits in some Cornyn internals.

A very different dynamic is pictured in the latest polling of the general election, with Paxton consistently trailing his opponent in surveys dating back to April and the two candidates dead even, 50% to 50%, in a recent Overton Insights poll with undecideds asked to pick one candidate or the other.

Surveys have been less than reliable this cycle but the existence of a consistent lead for Talarico suggests that Paxton really is in trouble — especially combined with the worried sentiments of his would-be Senate colleagues.

And there’s no sign of any GOP unity emerging in Texas: Cornyn has said that he will not campaign or raise money for Paxton in the general election, and one of his former aides jumped ship to join Talarico’s campaign last month.

All eyes will be on Paxton and Trump this week for an abbreviated GOP convention set to be held in Dallas, where Trump will make his first campaign appearance in the Lone Star State since Paxton won his runoff.

The closeness with which Paxton ties himself to Trump could either win the attorney general the financial backing he’ll need to win in November, or chain him irreversibly to a president with failing approval ratings and a diminished pull at the ballot box among Republicans and independents especially.

Demonstrators have descended on Portsmouth after migrants heading towards the Hampshire coast on a small boat were intercepted and brought ashore.

Around 140 migrants are believed to have disembarked near Eastney in Portsmouth, and will be taken to Manston immigration centre in Kent for processing.

Video footage showed protesters facing up to police and shouting “stop the boats” on Sunday evening. Far-right agitator Daniel Thomas, an associate of Tommy Robinson, was live-streaming from a beach in Eastney and encouraged his supporters: “Roads are all blocked, they are never going to be able to leave here.”

He added: “It was only yesterday (at the protests in Dover) when we warned them that we will not accept this any more, and that this is no longer an option to tell us that the boat numbers are down.”

Police asked people to avoid the area and said a dispersal order was in place until Monday evening. A government spokesperson condemned the “intimidating and thuggish behaviour” of the demonstrators, saying: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.

“We thank the emergency services who are working to safely manage the situation”.

Emergency services rushed to intercept the small boat on Sunday evening, with two RNLI lifeboats called out and a HM coastguard helicopter and plane also deployed.

A Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesperson said: “In response to a report on 6 September of a small boat heading towards the Hampshire coast, HM Coastguard sent lifeboats, an HM Coastguard helicopter, an HM Coastguard aeroplane and HM Coastguard Rescue Teams.

“Border Force, Border Security Command, Hampshire Police and South Central Ambulance Service were also sent.”

open image in gallery Police officers at the scene near Eastney Beach, Portsmouth, where protesters have gathered, after a small boat thought to be containing asylum seekers and heading towards the coast sparked a major response with a helicopter, aeroplane and lifeboats sent to the scene. ( PA )

Reform leader Nigel Farage claimed that the boat had launched from Baie de Seine, near Caen, saying: “Today a boat launched from Baie de Seine, 170 miles from Calais, arriving on the beaches of Hampshire for the very first time. This is a joke”.

The French maritime prefecture of the Channel and the North Sea said on Sunday that around 140 migrants had set out on a small boat from the west of the Baie de Seine overnight on Saturday. The departure was “unusual for the area”, with small boats usually launched from further up the French coast near Dunkirk.

The French maritime prefecture said on Sunday that the “migrant boat is currently continuing its journey towards the United Kingdom”, after people on board refused assistance.

Footage taken from the scene near Eastney showed a large emergency presence, and men wrapped in blankets were seen being taken ashore on RNLI boats.

Christine Martin, who was on a boat on the Eastney Cruising Association pontoon, told Portsmouth’s The News that she was unable to leave due to the incident. She said: “Being on my own in the boat, I am a little bit worried. The coastguard has been here sometime not letting anyone in or out. I just don’t know what to do.

“There have been lots of ambulances turning up. There is maybe 50 or 60 police and ambulance officers down near the Hayling Ferry pontoon.”

Conservative MP for MP for Isle of Wight East, Joe Robertson, posted on social media on Sunday: “Extremely concerning to see an illegal migrant crossing this far west.

“We don’t know if this migrant boat was headed for the Isle of Wight but I’ll be contacting the Home Office first thing. We need to know exactly what happened and if new routes are being used for mega-dinghies by people smugglers.”

A spokesperson for Hampshire Police added: “We have been working alongside and assisting our partners from Border Force, Maritime & Coastguard Agency and Portsmouth City Council at Eastney Marina following the arrival of a boat crossing the channel.

“We have officers in the area to ensure the prevention of any disorder. We ask that people please avoid the area. A dispersal order is in place until tomorrow evening (Monday 7 September). Anyone who refuses to comply with the direction to leave the area is liable for arrest.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.

“We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.

“But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40 per cent more boots on the ground on French beaches.”

News.title: ‘I want to see wealth creation’ John Healey to say as he tries to reassure nervous markets over economy
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. Britain is turning a corner but must back wealth creation and ensure prosperity reaches every region if it is to solve its woes, John Healey will say in his first major speech as chancellor.

As he seeks to reassure nervous markets over Labour's stewardship of the economy, he will also argue fiscal credibility is “indivisible” from growth.

Laying out his vision on Monday just weeks before what is expected to be a painful Budget, he will say: “I want to see wealth creation in this country. I want to see businesses make a profit… (and) we need an active, accountable state at all levels to remove blockages and create the conditions for more investment.”

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first Budget at a time of turmoil in the bond markets (PA) ( Getty )

New PM Andy Burnham has set out a “clear diagnosis” of the problem and the “solution” is a “fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places”, he will say.

That starts with strong city regions that bring government, local leaders and businesses together to chase investment and jobs instead of “getting in the way with complexity and red tape”.

Growth will tell a new story about Britain, he will say in his address in the Midlands, “an optimistic story. One of resilience. Pride. Huge latent potential. A country turning a corner. A country whose people, businesses and communities are ready to seize the opportunity of new technologies and new ideas."

Despite the upbeat tone, he will come under pressure to rule out tax rises, after the PM failed to do so, and to reassure jittery markets.

UK government borrowing costs reached their highest level since the 2008 global financial crisis last week, in part thanks to continued instability caused by the Iran war.

On Saturday, ministers published plans to slash outdated reporting rules, saving businesses more than £450 million a year in total.

Mr Healey will also announce £150m from the British Business Bank for northern scale-ups "to get behind the most innovative and fast-growing firms”, a move which he will insist is not “sentimentality” based on the PM’s birthplace, but instead is “supply side economics".

open image in gallery Andy Burnham failed to rule out tax rises last week (Leon Neal/PA) ( PA Wire )

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith accused him of a “policy-light word salad from a chancellor who seemingly does not understand how growth is created. It will do little to comfort hard-working families and businesses across the country who are worried about more tax rises or the fact that government borrowing rates are near a 28 year high.

“Commitments to reduce red tape are welcome but given this Government’s track record with its Employment Rights Act and other anti-business measures, people will rightly question their sincerity.

“We are facing serious threats from Russia and Iran on our doorstep, as well as threats to the Falkland Islands. Yet the chancellor, the man who resigned over defence spending, seemingly does not want to mention our Armed Forces or how we will reach 3 per cent of GDP on defence.

Reform’s Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said: “Even Rachel Reeves had more vision than this guff. Days after a market meltdown, when grip and direction are required, John Healey has revealed himself to be an empty vessel with no idea about how to rescue our economy.

"He won’t cut the ballooning benefits bill, foreign aid, or net zero subsidies so taxes on working people will inevitably rise at the budget. Reform is the only party that will cut wasteful spending so we can raise the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 in our first budget.”

News.content:
