World.title: IG Kanja orders probe into abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Standard Group PLC Associate Editor Alex Kiprotich. [Stafford Ondego, Standard]

The Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja has ordered immediate and transparent investigations into the alleged abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor Alex Kiprotich in Gilgil.

The National Police Service (NPS) said it had taken note of reports that Kiprotich was allegedly kidnapped on Tuesday and had moved swiftly to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

NPS spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga said the police service treats kidnapping and abduction with the utmost seriousness, describing the offences as a threat to the lives, liberty and security of Kenyans.

“The Inspector General of Police has accordingly ordered immediate investigations to determine what transpired, including the identity of the heavily armed individuals reportedly seen ordering occupants out of their vehicle,” Nyaga said in a statement.

The NPS said its Anti-Abduction Unit, established to investigate abductions and disappearances, had taken up the matter and would work to ensure that those responsible are brought to justice.

“We unequivocally condemn any act of kidnapping, abduction, or intimidation intended to interfere with press freedom or any other constitutional right,” Nyaga said.

The police service assured the public that the investigation into the Gilgil incident would be conducted transparently, stressing that no one was above the law.

The development comes amid growing condemnation of Kiprotich’s alleged abduction, with the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also calling for an immediate investigation.

CPJ Africa Director Angela Quintal described the incident as a “shameful indictment” of the Kenya Kwanza administration, raising concerns over the safety of journalists and press freedom in the country.

“The attempt to forcibly disappear Alex Kiprotich, three days after President William Ruto railed against The Standard Group, reflects the growing dangers that journalists face in Kenya, despite the president’s earlier promise to allow the press to work freely,” Quintal said.

The New York-based press freedom organisation further expressed concern over what it described as an escalation in cases of abductions and enforced disappearances in Kenya.

World.title: Trumpets of reforms blow louder as Kenya marks 16 years under 2010 Constitution
World.content:
The Constitution, Kenyan flag and the National anthem. [PCS]

On Thursday, August 27, a group of people largely composed of the youth gathered under some trees at Jeevanjee Gardens in Nairobi, carrying Kenyans flag, and banners and placards inscribed with "implement the constitution. Kenyans first" words.

These were in protests against what they believed is deliberate failure of those in authority to fully implement the 2010 Constitution.

World.title: Ruto allies hit back at Gachagua over IEBC tender concerns
World.content:
The Kenya Integrated Elections Management System (KIEMS) kit. [File, Standard]

President William Ruto’s allies led by National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula have launched a scathing attack on former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua and the Opposition over their criticism of the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), citing blackmail by the Opposition.

The leaders warned that attempts by politicians to dictate how the electoral agency procures technology and other election materials could undermine public confidence in the 2027 General Election.

World.title: Without Charlie Kirk, Turning Point is building a future for his movement — and for JD Vance
World.content:
Charlie Kirk sat before a Salt Lake City audience of restaurateurs last September 10, dispensing business advice drawn from his own unlikely rise.

The conservative activist argued that a company needed a deep connection to the founder’s “energy and vision” to endure, but he also warned that “separating the brand from the founder” was among the greatest challenges an entrepreneur could face.

“We have not done this successfully yet,” Kirk acknowledged of Turning Point USA, the organization he built to influence and mobilize young people.

Hours later, a gunman fatally shot Kirk on a Utah college campus. He was 31.

In the year since his death, Turning Point’s leaders — including Kirk’s widow, Erika, and some of his closest friends and lieutenants — have confronted the very challenge he described that tragic morning: preserving and expanding a political movement that had been built, to an extraordinary degree, around the energy, instincts and celebrity of its charismatic leader.

They have done so amid remarkable circumstances, including the criminal case against Kirk’s alleged killer; conservative influencers warring over his legacy; and far-right figures, led by former Turning Point employee Candace Owens, spreading baseless conspiracy theories about his death.

The 2026 midterm elections present the biggest test yet of the question hanging over the organization: What is Turning Point without Charlie Kirk?

“There is a void, and lots of people are trying to fill it,” Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters told CNN, “but no one will be able to do what he did.”

By some measures, the answer is a larger organization than the one Kirk left behind. About 1,500 colleges have Turning Point chapters on campus, up 64% over the past year, according to an internal document obtained by CNN, and affiliated high school clubs have nearly tripled. Turning Point now says it has over 1 million donors and more than 1,200 employees.

Its political operation is expanding, too. Turning Point staff and volunteers are embedded in more states with contests critical to Republican power in 2026 — and the presidential race two years later.

The stakes extend to the political ambitions of Vice President JD Vance, a close Kirk friend whom the organization has already endorsed for president in 2028. Whether the organization can sustain Kirk’s movement — and mobilize the voters he spent years courting — could help determine whether the vice president can inherit the political coalition Donald Trump assembled.

“If you believe in JD that much, that’s even more motivation to work our butts off and throw the kitchen sink at this thing,” said Tyler Bowyer, the chief operating officer for Turning Point Action. “We’re going to do everything we possibly can to win (in 2026) because so much is at stake — in this case, getting JD to run.”

Turning Point’s own effectiveness, though, has come under scrutiny in its home state, Arizona, where some Republicans fault the polarizing organization for the party’s recent electoral defeats. This year, the group has put its muscle behind Rep. Andy Biggs, a conservative Trump ally whose candidacy for governor has revived anxieties about hard-right nominees who narrowly lost statewide races.

Meanwhile, the political coalition Turning Point helped build faces new strains largely beyond the organization’s control. Polls show that young voters, whose sharp shift toward Trump in 2024 further elevated Kirk’s stature within the party, have soured on the president.

Turning Point spokesman Andrew Kolvet acknowledged the movement is facing headwinds, “and that’s especially true among young voters.”

“They are telling us they are worried about housing, affordability, foreign policy, etc.,” Kolvet said. “But if anyone has the political talent and ability to address their needs, wants and concerns directly ahead of the midterms, it’s President Trump and JD Vance.”

Finding Kirk’s voice

Charlie Kirk throws hats into the crowd during his American Comeback tour stop in Northridge, California, on March 6, 2025. Benjamin Hanson/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images

Kirk founded Turning Point USA in 2012 at age 18. What began as a nonprofit for young conservatives eventually grew into a sprawling, multimillion-dollar network that touched all aspects of American politics, including faith, culture, schools, voter registration, candidate endorsements and campaign fundraising.

But Turning Point also served as a massive platform for Kirk himself. His podcast and viral confrontations with liberals on college campuses made him one of the right’s most visible personalities, while his relationships across the movement bridged some of the divides within Trump’s MAGA coalition.

That part of Turning Point has proved difficult to replace.

Clips from Kirk’s podcast, now hosted by Kolvet, rarely draw the YouTube audiences they once did. Others have tried, with mixed success, to re-create the virality of his campus debates. And the right-wing online ecosystem where Kirk served as connective tissue between competing factions has frayed during Trump’s second term.

Turning Point’s leaders privately acknowledge there is no replacing Kirk, who will be honored one year after his death at Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday. Instead, they have focused on what they can preserve and expand: the organization he built around himself.

“Yes, we don’t have Charlie’s social media anymore, which is a big loss. And we don’t have his voice — huge deal,” a person involved in the organization told CNN. “But the actual machinery of Turning Point has never been bigger.”

As evidence, they pointed to a recent training for 150 new staffers. Online job boards show dozens of openings to work for Turning Point in battleground states.

“We’re going to be even bigger this election than we were in 2024,” Bowyer said.

Turning Point’s Super Bowl

Attendees observe the National Anthem during AmericaFest, the first Turning Point USA summit since the death of Charlie Kirk on December 20, 2025, in Phoenix. Cheney Orr/Reuters

Political memorabilia adorns the shelves of Bowyer’s office — a Calvin Coolidge pendant, a bust of Teddy Roosevelt, and a framed print of Newsweek’s never-published 2016 “Madam President” cover of Hillary Clinton next to Time’s cover featuring Trump as Person of the Year.

Among them is a painting of Kirk, whose face is inescapable throughout Turning Point’s Arizona campus.

There, Bowyer oversees the organization’s voter turnout machine — the “pinnacle” of Kirk’s legacy, as he described it.

“It’s kind of like the Super Bowl,” Bowyer said. “It’s pointless to educate hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of young people, for them just to go, ‘Oh, you know, don’t use that.’ Right?”

He added, “Charlie really believes in that,” slipping into present tense to describe his deceased friend and former leader — not for the only time during a 90-minute interview with CNN.

Bowyer is now expanding a program piloted in the 2024 election. Then, the group embedded staff and volunteers in neighborhoods throughout Arizona to mobilize potential Republican voters. Rather than send canvassers to knock on as many doors as possible, Turning Point instructed its organizers to make genuine connections, build relationships, show up at local events and, at least initially, avoid talking politics.

It’s a strategy built around quality, not quantity, Bowyer argues.

By Election Day, organizers are expected to have a plan for getting their assigned households — about 600 to 1,000 people — to the polls or to vote by mail. “Ballot chasers” are tasked with ensuring they follow through. Each organizer’s goal is to turn out about half their designated voters — a much higher threshold than traditional canvassers.

The effectiveness of the operation is difficult to measure, and there are Republican skeptics, including within Trump’s own political operation. But Turning Point emerged from 2024 with a compelling result to point to: Trump won Arizona by 5.5 percentage points, his largest victory of all the battleground states.

President Donald Trump waves as he leaves the stage after addressing a Turning Point USA event in Phoenix on April 17, 2026. Jim Watson/AFP/Getty Images

The victory emboldened Turning Point to double down in 2026. Even before the midterm map had fully taken shape, the organization was deploying staff and hiring in key battleground states. Maps of those states line the walls inside Turning Point Action’s headquarters with heat maps of voters and detailed breakdowns on “chaseable votes.”

This spring, the operation had a dry run when it joined the White House’s retribution campaign against Republican lawmakers in Indiana who resisted Trump’s calls to redraw the state’s congressional boundaries. Trump-backed challengers defeated seven of the eight GOP holdouts.

Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith, a Trump ally, said Turning Point mobilized quickly despite little history in his state and noted the group left behind manpower for future political battles.

“The proof is in the pudding. Critics could say, ‘This is the first year. What good are they going to do?’” Beckwith said. “I don’t know how you break down the pie chart of who deserves credit, but we won and won in a big way.”

Republican operatives in key states say Turning Point is already making its presence felt. Former New Hampshire GOP Chairman Chris Ager said the group arrived on the ground far earlier than usual for a grassroots organization, hired experienced local activists and their visibility has been “extremely high.”

Jason Roe, a veteran Michigan strategist, said Turning Point’s organizers have been more “engaged and impactful” than the college-age men and women he typically encounters in groups for young Republican.

“Turning Point is made up of true believers,” Roe said. “They’re griding because they care, not because it’s the first step on a journey to getting involved in politics.”

In Iowa, Turning Point’s growing influence has already been tested against the most powerful endorsement in Republican politics.

The organization supported businessman and farmer Zach Lahn in the state’s closely watched Republican primary for governor. Trump backed Rep. Randy Feenstra.

Lahn won.

“We were so busy talking about the Trump endorsement,” said Jeff Angelo, a prominent conservative radio host in Iowa, “that we missed the most important endorsement: Turning Point Action.”

Trouble in the desert

Tyler Bowyer speaks during the public memorial service for Charlie Kirk in Glendale, Arizona, on September 21, 2025. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images

No one needs less convincing of Turning Point’s sway with GOP voters than Julie Spilsbury.

Last year, Bowyer made it his stated mission to oust Spilsbury, a registered Republican who supported Kamala Harris for president over Trump, from the City Council in Mesa, where he resides. Turning Point helped lead an effort to recall her, and in December 2025, Spilsbury lost the seat she had held for five years by about 700 votes.

“It was devastating and heartbreaking and made a lot of people mad,” she said.

Spilsbury considers herself a casualty of Turning Point’s growing clout in the Arizona GOP — and what she and others described as its vindictive approach to intraparty politics. The organization has aggressively intervened in primaries and endorsed dozens of candidates, stacking up wins and bruising fellow Republicans along the way.

The clashes have become increasingly public. Bowyer faced blowback in July after he questioned on X whether Arizona state Rep. Quang Nguyen, a Republican who escaped communist Vietnam as a child, can speak English. When Republican state Rep. Nick Kupper came to Nguyen’s defense, Bowyer threatened to back a challenger against Kupper in 2028 and later announced Turning Point was withdrawing its endorsement.

Reached by CNN via email, Kupper declined to revisit the episode. Attempts to reach Nguyen through his office were unsuccessful.

Such tactics might go overlooked by Republicans in the Trump era if Turning Point was consistently turning its primary success into general election wins. In Arizona, it has not.

The organization played a key role in the unsuccessful 2022 campaigns of Republican gubernatorial nominee Kari Lake and GOP Senate candidate Blake Masters. Lake lost a Senate race two years later.

A Turning Point official noted the organization didn’t endorse Lake in her primaries but jumped in to help after she became the GOP nominee. Still, Bowyer contended they were “on the path for Kari to win” in 2022. The lesson from the loss, he argued, was that the organization needed more manpower.

“If we would have kept going and chased more votes, I think we could have won,” he said. Lake lost the governor’s race by roughly 17,000 votes.

The defeats have spread to far smaller Arizona contests. Earlier this year, Turning Point jumped into races for the Salt River Project, a local utility board whose elections typically draw little public attention. The group’s involvement drove a surge in turnout from both sides, but clean-energy candidates ultimately won a majority of seats for the first time in recent memory.

The Turning Point official argued that the group secured the two most critical positions leading the board “amid national headwinds that have impacted local races.” But progressives claimed victory after the election, and even local Republicans have acknowledged the board’s leftward turn was a significant setback.

“I think (Turning Point) is bombing hard, and it’s excellent for everyone else. I hesitate to say too much because we don’t want them to stop,” said Autumn Johnson, executive director of the Arizona Solar Energy Industries Association. “They have absolutely no idea what they’re doing, and they don’t know they don’t know what they’re doing. And it turns out a lot of people hate them.”

Their presence is causing divisions within the GOP at a time when the party is losing power across the state, argued Nick Myers, a member of the Arizona Corporation Commission, a state utility board. A Turning Point-backed challenger defeated Myers in a primary earlier this year. He said he lost the organization’s support after a back-and-forth on X with Bowyer a few years ago.

“As soon as they started getting involved, Republicans started losing,” Myers said. “It’s not because we’re becoming a purple state. Voters can’t stand the candidates Turning Point is nominating. Their days are limited if they don’t start putting up candidates who can win.”

The organization is betting on Biggs, the gubernatorial nominee, to reverse the party’s recent fortunes. The Turning Point official noted that Biggs was one of Kirk’s final and most passionate endorsements, viewing him as “a transformational and generational leader for Arizona — somebody who could turn Arizona into the Florida of the West.”

Bowyer said Biggs is a more seasoned politician than his predecessors and is better positioned to take on Katie Hobbs, the nation’s most vulnerable Democratic governor this year. Turning Point is now more experienced in campaign work, too, he added.

Some Republicans in Arizona view the race as a referendum on Turning Point as much as Biggs. Barrett Marson, a longtime GOP operative in Arizona, said if Biggs wins, many Republicans expect Turning Point to effectively take over the state GOP. A loss, though, would have its own consequences.

“Turning Point is all in on two people: Andy Biggs and JD Vance,” Marson said. “If both of those guys lose their upcoming elections, I predict they won’t be around much after 2028.”

Vance-Turning Point 2028?

Erika Kirk greets Vice President JD Vance during Turning Point USA’s AmericaFest in Phoenix on December 21, 2025. Jon Cherry/AP

Turning Point recently doubled its staff in Iowa and is rapidly deploying organizers in New Hampshire ahead of key midterm races in both states. When the elections are over, the teams will remain — and wait for Vance to make a decision.

Erika Kirk sent one of the first shockwaves through the 2028 presidential race in December when she endorsed Vance — getting ahead not only of the vice president, but of Trump, who is widely expected to play a decisive role in choosing his successor. Since then, Turning Point has set out to demonstrate that a turnkey organization will be waiting for Vance if he launches a White House bid.

Ager, the former New Hampshire party chairman, said Turning Point could present a “significant organizational advantage out of the gate” for Vance in 2028 when Republicans there vote in the GOP’s first presidential primary. Iowa, meanwhile, will hold the party’s first nominating contest.

“It’s still up to the candidate to convince voters,” he said. “But a good organization absolutely helps.”

Vance has remained close to Turning Point, appearing at several events and guest-hosting Kirk’s podcast.

The mutual loyalty is “downstream of the genuine close friendship that JD had with Charlie,” a source close to the vice president told CNN. Kirk helped propel Vance within the party and into his current role.

Though he remains reticent to publicly discuss his political future, Vance privately views Turning Point’s support as a key to his future ambitions, the source said. The organization offers Vance a connection to “America First” stalwarts in Trump’s coalition and a well-funded political infrastructure separate from the president’s political operation.

“They are specifically a MAGA power center, versus a traditional power center,” the source said. “They are distinctly different from the old guard establishment that wouldn’t necessarily support JD, and that serves as a true home for the MAGA voters.”

Bowyer said he expects Vance to closely watch the midterm results before he finalizes his plans. But he added, “If people want you to run, and you decide not to run, you usually don’t ever get a chance to run again.”

For Turning Point, delivering Republican victories this fall, particularly in Arizona, would give Vance reason to trust the organization Kirk left behind could help carry him to the White House.

Failure would bring its own reckoning, and Bowyer said Turning Point would judge itself more harshly than any outside critic if the group fell short.

Said Bowyer: “Charlie felt that way.”

World.title: Parents of San Diego mosque gunman say a mental health facility failed to heed FBI warning
World.content:
LOS ANGELES AP —

Just days before two teenagers carried out a mass shooting at a San Diego mosque, federal law enforcement officials warned the parents of one of the shooters that their son was making concerning comments about school shootings on the dark web, according to new details included in a recently filed lawsuit.

The mother of Caleb Vazquez alleges in her lawsuit that Park Mental Health Treatment of San Diego failed to intervene despite signs that her 18-year-old son posed an imminent threat to himself and others. Vazquez was living there and receiving treatment for a range of mental health conditions, including depression and psychotic episodes, the lawsuit says. The court filings follow a number of high-profile convictions of guardians who provided teenagers with weapons that were later used in mass shootings.

The FBI called Vazquez’s mother on the evening of May 14, and she said she immediately left a message with the treatment facility to notify its staff, according to the lawsuit, filed in a San Diego court on Aug. 31. Vazquez’s mother again shared the FBI’s warnings with her son’s therapist on May 15 and with a program director later that night.

On May 18, the morning of the shooting, employees at the facility contacted Vazquez’s mother to tell her that he was missing. Video surveillance footage subsequently showed Vazquez leaving the property at 8 p.m. the night before.

Vazquez’s parents were driving around looking for him on the morning of the shooting. Vazquez and another teenager killed three people at the San Diego mosque that day before taking their own lives.

It is unclear whether Vazquez was allowed to leave the previous evening or whether he broke facility rules by doing so. Park Mental Health offers a range of treatment options, some of which advertise 24-hour surveillance, while others provide more limited counseling.

The center did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment Saturday afternoon. In a previous statement to radio station KPBS, Park Mental Health disputed the assertions in the lawsuit.

“While it is understandable that his parents might seek to blame someone in their time of loss, this lawsuit is misguided in that neither Park nor its employees are responsible for Mr. Vazquez’s actions,” the statement to KPBS read. “Only he and his coconspirator bear responsibility for their conduct and, ultimately, his death.”

Three people were killed in the attack. Nelvin C. Cepeda/The San Diego Union-Tribune/MediaNews Group RM/Getty Images

An FBI spokesperson declined to comment Saturday, citing agency policy.

The FBI’s alleged contact with Vazquez’s parents was not the first sign of his mental deterioration.

Vazquez had been hospitalized for roughly three days in January 2026 after telling a classmate that he wanted to carry out a school shooting.

Almost exactly a year earlier, Vazquez was flagged to law enforcement for exhibiting alarming behavior and idolizing Nazis, prompting police to confiscate 26 guns from his father under a 2014 California law allowing firearms to be taken from people considered dangerous.

Authorities have said Vazquez met the other shooter, Cain Clark, 17, online and that both were radicalized there. Police have not shared more details about how they knew each other or specified whose weapons were used in the shooting.

The lawsuit was filed on the same day that North Carolina authorities announced the indictment of a 17-year-old in connection with the shooting.

World.title: Witkoff and Kushner arrive in Kyiv for second leg of US diplomacy push
World.content:
US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner travelled to Kyiv on Sunday after concluding intensive talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as Washington renews its push to end the war in Ukraine.

It marks their first visit to the Ukrainian capital since the war began and comes amid near-constant Russian missile and drone strikes on the Ukrainian capital.

After greeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the US envoy was taken on a tour of a cathedral in central Kyiv damaged in Russian attacks. St. Sophia’s Cathedral, which is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, has had its windows and window frames damaged. On Friday, CNN reported on a Russian strike hitting Ukraine’s Security Service headquarters in Kyiv, which also affected the cathedral.

Ahead of their meeting, the Ukrainian president thanked US President Donald Trump for allowing the trip to happen “from a security standpoint,” adding that Ukraine had been “waiting a long time” for Witkoff and Kushner’s visit.

Earlier, Zelensky wrote on Telegram, “We are ready for talks. Ukraine has always been and will continue to be constructive.” He added, “We are committed to bringing the war to an end. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A dignified post-war peace is needed. Our proposals are ready.”

Zelensky has previously stressed said that an acute shortage of air defense interceptors has left Ukraine vulnerable to ballistic missile attacks.

Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the Ukrainian Presidency, said that representatives from France, the UK and Germany were also in Kyiv. “We have a busy day ahead of us, filled with important talks,” he said.

The delegation was taken for a tour to St. Sophia Cathedral, which has been damaged by a Russian strike. Ukrainian Presidency

Witkoff and Kushner made a stop in the Polish city of Rzeszow en route from Moscow to Kyiv, Russian state media outlet TASS reported. The plane landed at 1:31 a.m. local time. The US envoys most likely continued their journey by rail, it reported.

Russia and Ukraine have enacted a 72-hour temporary truce for the duration of the US envoys’ visits, specifically halting airstrikes on each other’s capitals, Kyiv and Moscow. The halt in strikes began at midnight on Friday into Saturday and will last for the duration of the weekend of diplomacy.

The truce applies only to the two capital cities, and overnight attacks into Sunday saw Russia continue its bombardment of Ukraine while avoiding Kyiv city. According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russian forces launched 108 Shahed-type drones fired from Russia, while at least three people were killed in the latest strikes and infrastructure was hit in Kyiv region.

Russian airstrikes were recorded in 11 locations across Ukraine, while a large-scale fire has been extinguished at an infrastructure facility in Kyiv region as a result of a Russian strike.

In total, 10 Ukrainian civilians have been killed over the past 24 hours, and a further 65 injured.

Witkoff and Kushner began their whirlwind weekend of diplomacy with a three-hour meeting with Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday afternoon. The negotiations were followed by dinner with the Russian leader, according to a Kremlin press briefing.

Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov later described the talks as “useful” and said the American representatives had “prepared seriously for this trip.” He said the US team expressed interest in ending hostilities as quickly as possible and offered “a whole series of considerations regarding possible paths to a settlement.”

A White House official said both sides “discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks.”

World.title: The world is about to meet Apple’s new CEO. Here are his biggest challenges
World.content:
When Apple holds its annual iPhone event on September 9, it’ll be the first time in more than a decade that Tim Cook won’t introduce the company’s latest products.

Instead, John Ternus will debut as Apple’s new chief executive during the company’s most important event of the year.

Expectations are high. Ternus takes over as Apple faces pressure to evolve its products for the AI era. In July, the iPhone maker became the second company in history to reach a $5 trillion market capitalization, raising the bar for what analysts and investors expect from product advancements and financial performance.

Ternus’ background in hardware engineering led many to believe his tenure is likely to usher in a new age of innovation for Apple. Many will be watching for signals of Ternus’ vision this week, especially as the company is expected to follow rivals into a new product category with a foldable iPhone.

Ternus will need to quickly cement his direction for Apple beyond the fanfare of this week’s event. The company faces a string of pressing challenges, including regulatory obstacles in Europe and a memory shortage.

Apple’s AI troubles

Ternus’s engineering experience could be a big advantage for Apple, which has suffered criticism over its approach for the last two years.

Last year, the company delayed a new version of Siri that is now set to launch this fall.

“It was a huge miss,” Gene Munster, managing partner for tech investment firm Deepwater Asset Management. “Thankfully, they’re on the right path, but it could have been so much bigger of a win for them.”

The Apple Siri prompt bubble on an iPhone arranged in February. The iPhone marker delayed a new version of Siri until this fall. Jason Henry/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Apple often tailors its devices and chips for its own services and software, and Ternus’ deep background in hardware could be critical in designing new devices that are optimized for AI.

In the near term, Apple is banking on Siri to help gain ground in the AI race. The revamped AI assistant will leverage data – like text messages and photos – from a user’s iPhone to answer questions in a personalized way. For example, you could ask Siri to reference your text messages to find your upcoming doctor’s appointment or dinner reservation.

Apple says the new Siri will be able to complete tasks in certain apps and answer questions about what’s shown on screen, a feature that could help it catch up to Google’s Gemini.

Nabila Popal, a senior director for tech market research firm International Data Corporation, told CNN that two things could give Apple an edge: its traditional focus on user privacy as well as the way it incorporates AI directly into iOS tools like the camera and messages apps.

“(Consumers) just want a device that makes their life easier and takes it to the next level, and I think that’s what Apple will do,” Popal said.

Then-Apple CEO Tim Cook on March 21, 2016, in Cupertino, California. Apple reached a larger-than-live valuation of $5 trillion in the Cook era. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Pressure to deliver hit products

More than anything else, all eyes will be on Ternus to deliver a new blockbuster hit.

Cook will be remembered for scaling the iPhone to a business that rakes in hundreds of billions of dollars every year. By launching a web of services and accessories, such as Apple Music, the Apple Card, the Apple Watch and AirPods, Cook made the iPhone feel essential to everyday life.

Yet investors and analysts are hopeful that Ternus’ will bring a fresh push into new products, such as the foldable iPhone. The IDC projects that Apple will capture 40% of the market for foldable phones by 2027, despite being years behind rivals Samsung and Chinese smartphone giant Huawei.

“Apple’s entry into the foldable market has done more than reignite growth in a category that was losing momentum,” Popal wrote in a recent IDC report, ahead of the foldable iPhone’s release. “It has fundamentally altered the market’s trajectory.”

Memory shortage

The tech industry has been rattled by an ongoing shortage of memory, critical hardware that devices need to quickly retrieve stored information. Data centers have led to a surge in demand for these components, making them significantly more expensive.

That’s caused tech companies like Apple, Nintendo and Microsoft to raise prices of their products. Apple in July increased prices for iPads, Macs and other devices but left iPhone price tags unchanged.

“We’re in what I would characterize as a 100-year flood on memory pricing, with exponential increases in memory prices,” Cook said during his last earnings call as CEO in July.

The iPhone 17 series is displayed at an Apple Store in New York City on September 19, 2025. Shannon Stapleton/Reuters

Consumers should brace for higher iPhone prices, some analysts say.

Mike Howard, vice president of memory coverage at research firm TechInsights. estimates Apple would likely have to increase its smartphone prices by about $250 to $300 to maintain margins.

“We should start thinking about a $1,500 iPhone instead of a $1,000 (or) $1,200 iPhone,” he told CNN in July.

European regulation

Apple likely has more obstacles ahead in the European Union’s crackdown on Big Tech.

The company recently announced changes to its App Store’s business terms to comply with EU regulations. And it won’t launch the new version of Siri on iPhones and iPads in the European Union because of the European Commission’s rules. Europe is Apple’s second-largest market after the United States.

The EC wants Apple and Google to give third-party AI assistants more access to iOS and Android systems. But Apple and Google have both argued that doing so would raise privacy concerns.

An Apple Store in Madrid, Spain, on October 30, 2025. Mateusz Wlodarczyk/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

And experts agree that consumers should be careful about giving AI agents broad access to content stored on their phones and computers.

An AI agent “could exercise the user’s delegated authority to do other things that maybe the user might not have wanted it to happen,” Michael Stokes, senior vice president of emerging technologies at Veilant, a company that sells secure infrastructure and communications products, previously told CNN.

But the EC allows companies like Apple to “implement appropriate privacy, security and integrity safeguards,” a spokesperson previously told CNN.

Ultimately, Ternus will have to navigate these challenges while living up to the larger-than-life valuation Apple reached in the Cook era.

“Apple is already so large, profitable, and deeply embedded in its customers’ lives that incremental excellence may no longer be enough to redefine the company,” Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan wrote in an August research note. “Ternus’s challenge will be to preserve the profitable machine Cook built while restoring a stronger sense of technological surprise.”

World.title: Egypt and seven key allies condemn Israeli ministers’ Gaza displacement proposals
World.content:
Foreign ministers from Egypt, Qatar, Jordan, the UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia issued a joint statement condemning comments made by Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Defense Minister Israel Katz regarding the displacement of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip.

The ministers denounced proposed plans and mechanisms aimed at forcibly removing Palestinians from their land, characterizing the provocative statements as a blatant violation of international humanitarian law, and a direct threat to the legitimate, inalienable rights of the Palestinian people.

In their unified declaration, the diplomats emphasized their absolute rejection and condemnation of any attempts or plans targeting the displacement of Palestinians—whether within or outside the occupied Palestinian territory—under any pretext.

Foreign ministers from eight nations warned of severe consequences if calls for forced displacement are translated into declared policies or actionable measures aimed at uprooting Palestinians from their land.

The ministers stated that such actions present a direct challenge to international peace efforts—most notably President Donald Trump’s comprehensive plan to end the conflict in Gaza, which includes an absolute rejection of forced displacement.

They added that these measures carry grave risks capable of undermining regional stability.

World.title: Sisi follows up on efforts to revive Cairo’s Islamic and historical landmarks
World.content:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi urged the relevant state agencies to continue their efforts to revitalize Cairo’s various historical and heritage landmarks and develop the surrounding areas to attract more tourists.

Sisi emphasized the importance of adopting the “greening Cairo” project, which aims to transform any vacated land into green spaces.

This came during a meeting between Sisi and Minister of Religious Endowments Osama al-Azhari, Cairo Governor Ibrahim Saber, Advisor to the President for Urban Planning, Amir Sayed Ahmed,and the Head of the Armed Forces Engineering Authority, Walid Aref.

Presidential Spokesperson Mohamed al-Shenawy said that the President followed up during the meeting on efforts to revitalize Cairo’s Islamic and historical landmarks.

The official spokesperson added that the Governor of Cairo highlighted the efforts to revitalize numerous Khedival, historical, and Islamic landmarks in Cairo, as well as the ongoing rehabilitation and development of infrastructure in and around historical areas.

The Minister of Religious Endowments reviewed the progress of the restoration and revitalization of several historical mosques and shrines, noting that these efforts extend to the development of more integrated tourist routes connecting various historical and heritage sites.

He continued that upon completion of all the ongoing work related to the revitalization of historical landmarks, the “heart of Cairo” will become an open-air tourist destination, attracting even more visitors.

World.title: The downfall of Sarah Khalifa – from TV host to death row
World.content:
She used to grace TV screens across Egypt – now she’s been sentenced to death.

Sarah Khalifa’s journey spanned many years, beginning with media appearances and program hosting, progressing through production, event organization, and private projects.

But a catastrophic downfall led to her conviction in one of the largest drug manufacturing and trafficking cases Cairo’s courts had ever witnessed.

Cairo Criminal Court, convened at the Fifth Settlement Court Complex, concluded the “Grand Drug Case” on Saturday September 5.

The court sentenced Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging, fining each of them LE500,000, and confiscating the seized drugs, cars, equipment, gold jewelry, and mobile phones.

The verdict was unanimous after the defendant case files were referred to the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion.

TV Presenter

Khalifa was born in Cairo on March 29, 1994, and began her career in the media by presenting programs on the “ART” channel, before moving to work on the Iraqi Al-Sharqiya channel for a long period.

Over time, she moved into production and event planning, launching her own company, “Sarah Production,” specializing in organizing parties.

She also participated in numerous events and artistic performances, expanding her presence on social media.

In 2024, she returned to the spotlight with the program “Sarah and Beka,” which she co-hosted with the popular singer Hamo Beka.

She also performed in Dubai and opened a beauty clinic in Agouza district, Giza, becoming a well-known figure on social media and among celebrities.

Downfall

In April 2025, Khalifa’s life took a shocking turn when security forces arrested her.

The New Cairo Public Prosecution began investigating her on charges related to possession of narcotics with intent to distribute.

At the start of the investigation, the prosecution ordered the summoning of witnesses and the review of surveillance camera footage from the vicinity of her residence to determine the movements of those frequenting the area, before expanding the investigation into the case.

Security services had been monitoring the group’s activities for approximately 40 days before obtaining an arrest warrant for the defendants on April 17, 2025.

The investigation revealed that Khalifa was leading the group, with the assistance of her brother and others, and that raw materials were being brought in from abroad before being smuggled into Egypt to manufacture and distribute narcotics.

The Trial

The case grew to become one of the largest drug cases in the nation, with the Public Prosecution referring 28 defendants to the Criminal Court.

The prosecution charged the defendants with forming an organized criminal group specializing in importing, manufacturing, packaging, trafficking, and distributing materials used in the production of synthetic narcotics, as well as possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition.

Investigations revealed the seizure of more than 750 kilograms of synthetic narcotics and raw materials used in their production, along with weapons and ammunition.

The referral order was based on the testimonies of 20 witnesses and technical and digital evidence, including conversations, photos, and videos.

The trial of Khalifa and 27 other defendants began before the Cairo Criminal Court.

The case continued for months, with legal arguments from the defense focusing on the arrest and search procedures, the evidence presented, and the extent to which the elements of the crimes attributed to each defendant were met.

During the trial sessions, some defense lawyers maintained their clients’ innocence, arguing the invalidity of the arrest and detention procedures, the lack of connection between some of the defendants and the seized items, and the admissibility of the forensic evidence and investigations.

Referral to Grand Mufti

On August 4, The Cairo Criminal Court referred the case files of Sarah Khalifa and 12 other defendants to the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion on the death penalty.

Death Sentence

The Cairo Criminal Court ultimately sentenced Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging.

The court also sentenced nine defendants to life imprisonment and a fine of LE 100,000 each, while acquitting seven others, bringing the total number of defendants in the case to 28.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Mohamed Salah in court over former lawyer’s fees
World.content:
The New Cairo Court will hold its first hearing on Sunday in the lawsuit filed by Amr Faragallah, Mohamed Salah’s former lawyer, demanding payment for legal and administrative services he claims to have provided to the player.

Salah in Court

The court scheduled Sunday’s hearing for Salah to appear in person and take the oath, the wording of which was determined.

The oath includes a denial that the former lawyer performed the services in question or that the player owes him any money.

Effect of Absence

The court clarified that Salah’s failure to appear, or his refusal to take the oath without a valid excuse, constitutes a breach of oath and entails the legal consequences stipulated by law.

Official Proxy

The details of the lawsuit date back to September 2015, where the former lawyer bases his claim on an official power of attorney issued to him by Mohamed Salah in 2012.

He is demanding financial compensation for legal and administrative work he claims to have performed on behalf of the player.

World.title: Liberia: Opposition Roundtable Sets Steering Committee for 2029 Collaboration
World.content:
Monrovia — Liberia’s opposition political leaders have agreed to establish a steering committee to develop a framework for sustained political collaboration, following a high-level roundtable hosted and presided over by former President George Weah of the Congress for Democratic Change on Sunday.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The meeting, held at the Jamaica Resort in Thinker’s Village, Paynesville, brought together leaders and representatives of several opposition parties to explore greater cooperation and collective engagement on national political issues ahead of the 2029 elections.

Under the agreement, the steering committee will comprise two representatives from each participating political party.

The committee is expected to develop a framework document outlining the nature, structure and guiding principles of the proposed collaboration, including how the participating parties will coordinate their positions and engage collectively on issues of national importance.

Participants emphasized that the framework is not an electoral alliance or an agreement on a 2029 presidential ticket. Instead, it is intended to provide a foundation for political cooperation and establish how the parties will work together going forward.

Among the prominent political leaders in attendance were Alexander Cummings of the Alternative National Congress; Musa Hassan Bility, Citizens Movement for Change (CMC), Simeon Freeman of the Movement for Progressive Change (MPC), D. Maxwell Kemayah, Movement for Economic Empowerment (MOVEE).

The All Liberian Party led by businessman Benoni Urey, was represented at the gathering.

Several senior CDC officials also attended, including former Speaker of the House of Representatives J. Alex Tyler, former Speaker of the 54th National Legislature Bhofal Chambers, and other party officials.

Addressing journalists after the meeting, former President Weah described the gathering as the beginning of a series of engagements intended to promote greater unity among opposition political forces.

MPC Political Leader Simeon Freeman said the participating leaders are expected to reconvene within the next two weeks at another venue to continue discussions and advance the process.

Lessons From Past Alliances

Sunday’s agreement represents the latest attempt by Liberia’s opposition to overcome political divisions and establish a common platform for collective action.

In 2016, opposition leaders gathered in Ganta, Nimba County, where they reached an agreement aimed at coordinating their efforts ahead of the 2017 presidential and legislative elections. However, the initiative failed to produce a lasting political alliance.

Another major effort came three years later with the formation of the Collaborating Political Parties (CPP), which brought together the Unity Party, ANC, ALP and Liberty Party.

Although the CPP established a common political platform, internal disagreements and competing political interests eventually weakened the coalition, leading to its collapse.

For ANC Political Leader Alexander Cummings, however, the latest initiative offers reason for optimism.

Cummings, a key figure in the former CPP arrangement, said the current process is still in its early stages but expressed confidence that it can succeed if the parties remain focused on their broader objective.

He said the initiative is not about elevating any individual but about opposition parties coming together to hold the government accountable.

“They are in power, and they are managing our resources. We will unite and be the voice of the Liberian people in holding the government accountable,” Cummings said.

Bility Joins Opposition Push

CMC Political Leader Musa Hassan Bility, who initially declined the invitation to the roundtable, later accepted and attended the meeting.

Speaking at the press conference, Bility welcomed the gathering and said the focus should remain on the interests of ordinary Liberians.

“We are happy that we are able to come together. It is about the Liberian people, united under one voice to advocate for them and to rescue them from the so-called rescuers,” Bility said.

The formation of the steering committee now places the opposition parties at the next stage of the process, with its proposed framework expected to determine whether the latest effort can overcome the divisions that undermined previous attempts at opposition unity.

World.title: Liberia: CDC Debunks NPP Chairman Mulbah, Says NPP Was Never Invited to Opposition Roundtable
World.content:
Monrovia — The opposition Congress for Democratic Change has rejected claims by National Patriotic Party Chairman George Mulbah that his party declined an invitation to participate in a proposed opposition roundtable, insisting that no such invitation was extended to the NPP as an institution.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

CDC Secretary-General Jefferson Koijee said the record must be set straight, arguing that the NPP and its national leadership were never formally invited to the planned engagement.

“At no time and at no point did the Congress for Democratic Change extend an invitation to the National Patriotic Party or its national leadership to participate in the proposed opposition roundtable discussion,” Koijee said.

His comments followed an announcement by Mulbah that the NPP would not participate in the planned opposition meeting.

Koijee said while a number of “outstanding, uncompromising” members of the NPP were invited, they were invited in their individual capacities and not as representatives of the party.

“Neither the NPP as an institution nor its National Chairman, Mr. George Mulbah, was invited,” he said.

He accused Mulbah of creating the impression that the CDC had sought the institutional participation of the NPP and was subsequently rejected.

“The National Chairman should therefore immediately cease and desist from creating the impression that the CDC sought the institutional participation of the NPP and was subsequently rejected,” Koijee added.

The dispute comes against the backdrop of the two parties’ political history. The NPP was a key component of the Coalition for Democratic Change during the 2017 presidential and legislative elections. The coalition brought together the CDC, which produced then-presidential candidate George Manneh Weah, and the NPP, which produced then-Vice Standard Bearer Jewel Howard-Taylor.

The CDC-led coalition won the 2017 presidential election and subsequently governed Liberia from 2018 to 2024.

Koijee also questioned the political circumstances surrounding Mulbah’s statement, particularly his reported employment within the Office of Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung.

He said the relationship raises questions about the “independence, timing and motivation” of statements directed at opposition cooperation.

Koijee further criticized what he described as the NPP leadership’s weak response when its standard bearer and former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor faced criminal allegations and incarceration.

“At that defining moment, the statement attributed to the party leadership was, in our view, one of the weakest responses in the history of a party once renowned for its fighting spirit, political potency and revolutionary character,” he said.

The CDC Secretary-General maintained that his party would not allow what he described as political distractions and manufactured controversies to undermine cooperation among opposition forces.

“The mighty Congress for Democratic Change has no room for political distractions, manufactured controversies or attempts to fracture genuine opposition solidarity,” Koijee said.

He pledged that the CDC would remain “vigilant” and respond to what it considers efforts to undermine democratic cooperation among opposition groups.

Koijee concluded by thanking individuals and institutions that were formally invited to the roundtable and accepted the invitation, saying their participation demonstrated that the broader democratic conversation would continue.

“The democratic conversation continues, and no political grandstanding will derail it,” he said.

World.title: Co-Defendant Challenges Judge’s Ruling Granting Ex-VP Taylor House Arrest, Calls It Unlawful
World.content:
MONROVIA — A day after Criminal Court “C” ordered former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor moved from Monrovia Central Prison to guarded house detention on medical grounds, a co-defendant in the same narcotics case has formally challenged the ruling, arguing that Judge Ousman F. Feika had no legal authority to grant it and asking him to reverse himself.



In a filing captio ned “Exceptions to His Honor Ousman F. Feika’s Ruling in Granting Co-Defendant Jewel Howard Taylor Compassionate Release,” Garpue K. Wonlue takes issue with the September 4 order on six separate grounds, most of them turning on a single argument: that the law Judge Feika relied on does not apply to someone in Taylor’s position.



The Case So Far



Taylor, Liberia’s vice president from 2018 to 2024, was arrested at Roberts International Airport on August 19 in connection with what officials have described as a transnational narcotics trafficking investigation tied to a record cocaine seizure earlier this year.

She was formally charged over eight counts, including unlicensed importation, unlicensed sale and trading, and illicit trafficking of drugs, along with money laundering and abuse-of-office allegations.



Her lawyers spent the following weeks trying, without success, to keep her out of the general prison population.

A Monrovia City Court magistrate denied an initial request for compassionate detention, ruling that granting it fell within the authority of the Ministry of Justice rather than the judiciary the defense’s follow-up appeal to the Supreme Court challenging that denial did not stop Taylor from being remanded to Monrovia Central Prison. She entered custody on September 2.



The case then moved to Criminal Court “C,” the circuit with jurisdiction over major drug offenses, where Judge Feika ordered Taylor’s immediate transfer from prison to 24-hour guarded house detention at her residence, converting her pre-trial custody into house arrest pending the outcome of the criminal proceedings.

Feika was explicit that the order rested solely on medical grounds and carried no bearing on guilt, writing that the release “shall therefore not constitute dismissal, acquittal, pardon, immunity, or termination of the criminal proceedings.

The judge also noted that the State itself had not opposed the request.



The Challenge



Wonlue’s filing does not dispute that Taylor has a medical condition. Instead, it argues that the court used the wrong statute to address it — and in doing so, exceeded its authority. The exceptions raise six points:



1. Jurisdiction: The filing argues that Chapter 34, Section 34.20 of the Criminal Procedure Law — the provision Judge Feika relied on — applies only to people who have already been indicted, tried, convicted, sentenced and committed to prison. Taylor, still awaiting trial, doesn’t fit that description, the filing contends, and Wonlue asks the court to rescind the ruling and have her returned to custody at Monrovia Central Prison.



2. No such remedy exists: The Criminal Procedure Law provides for bail under Chapter 13 for the accused, and for commitment under Chapter 34 for the convicted, the filing says — but nothing in between for a pre-trial detainee seeking release on medical grounds. Granting “compassionate leave” from pre-trial detention, it argues, is a remedy the court created rather than one the statute authorizes.



3. Consent doesn’t create jurisdiction: The fact that the State did not oppose Taylor’s request doesn’t change the analysis, the filing argues — parties cannot agree to give a court power the statute doesn’t grant it.



4. Equal treatment. This is the filing’s broadest argument: that granting one high-profile, pre-trial detainee a form of release unavailable to others sets up a two-tier system, at odds with the fairness-in-administration standard in Section 1.2 of the Criminal Procedure Law and Article 11 of the 1986 Constitution. The filing points out that many pre-trial detainees at Monrovia Central Prison have untreated medical conditions of their own, and argues the proper remedy was to order the Bureau of Corrections to provide adequate care in custody — not to release one defendant from it.



5. The nature of the charges and the cost of enforcement: Given that Taylor faces serious felony charges — importation of controlled drugs, money laundering and abuse of office, as the filing describes them — Wonlue argues the release conditions impose an unfunded, unauthorized burden on the State, which must now provide round-the-clock security at her residence. Surrendering travel documents, the filing adds, doesn’t eliminate flight risk on its own.



6. The inquiry should have ended sooner: Once the court determined that Section 34.20 doesn’t apply to pre-trial detainees, the filing argues, that finding should have ended the motion rather than being followed by relief anyway. It maintains the appropriate avenue for a detainee with medical concerns is a bail motion under Chapter 13 — with bond, sureties and monitoring conditions — not compassionate leave.



What’s Being Asked



The filing asks Judge Feika to reverse course: to rule that Section 34.20 doesn’t apply to pre-trial detainees, to direct the Bureau of Corrections and Ministry of Health to provide Taylor medical treatment at JFK Medical Center or another approved facility while she remains in custody, and — if release is warranted at all — to take it up as a bail application under Chapter 13, with a substantial bond and formal sureties, rather than as compassionate leave.



Judge Feika has not yet ruled on the exceptions. Taylor remains under house arrest at her residence pending the outcome. All defendants in the case, including Taylor, are presumed innocent, and the charges against them remain allegations that have not been tested at trial.

World.title: Liberia Champions Key Discussions on Preventive Diplomacy and a Robust E10 Voice at the 9th E10 & I5 Annual Dialogue in Panama
World.content:
Panama – Liberia’s Political Coordinator to the United Nations Security Council, Cllr. Aloysius Jappah assumed an active role in the 9th E10 & I5 Annual Dialogue, hosted by the Republic of Panama in Panama City from 1 to 2 September 2026, delivering substantive interventions on preventive diplomacy, Council effectiveness, and the responsibilities that come with elected membership of the UN Security Council.

Since 2019, the Dialogue has convened annually to unite the ten elected members of the Council (the E10) with the five incoming members (the I5) to enhance institutional memory, coordinate priorities, and bolster the Council’s ability to uphold international peace and security.

This year’s event was inaugurated and concluded by Panama’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, H.E. Javier Eduardo Martínez-Acha Vásquez, and honored at its closing by former President H.E. Mireya Moscoso.

The current E10 for 2026 includes Bahrain, Colombia, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Liberia, Pakistan, Panama, and Somalia.

Starting on 1 January 2027, the newly elected I5 will consist of Austria, Kyrgyzstan, Portugal, Trinidad and Tobago, and Zimbabwe, replacing Denmark, Greece, Pakistan, Panama, and Somalia as their mandates end on 31 December 2026.

Speaking during the session on “Preventive Diplomacy in Action,” moderated with the support of the Dag Hammarskjöld Foundation and its presenters Sigrid and Henrik, Cllr. Jappah anchored Liberia’s contribution in the letter of the United Nations Charter — Chapter VI (Articles 33–38) on the pacific settlement of disputes, Chapter VIII (Article 52) on regional arrangements, and Article 99 on the Secretary-General’s early-warning authority.

“The best Council intervention is a crisis that diplomacy prevents,” Cllr. Jappah affirmed, adding that “the Charter calls on us to extinguish the spark of conflict before it becomes a blaze. When we subscribed to this organization, we pledged to fulfill that obligation.”

Commenting on the operational challenge of moving from early warning to early action, the Political Coordinator emphasized what he called the prevention paradox — that when preventive diplomacy succeeds, the crisis does not occur, and success is therefore less visible than failure.

He cautioned that sovereignty concerns and geopolitical divisions frequently delay Council action, resulting in inaction until violence erupts. He warned that “Early warning without early action,” he warned, “is only a forecast of failure.”

Drawing on Liberia’s own post-conflict experience, Cllr. Jappah stressed that peace agreements close a chapter but do not, by themselves, remove the grievances, institutional weaknesses, or local tensions that can reignite conflict.

He called for the sustained deployment of good offices, mediation support, regional engagement, inclusive dialogue, confidence-building measures, early-warning capacity, and local peace infrastructures — with the consent and ownership of the country concerned.

“Peace agreements close a chapter; preventive diplomacy helps keep the next chapter from reopening the war,” he said, noting that sustained international, regional, and national engagement has been decisive in consolidating and protecting Liberia’s hard-won peace.

Contributing to Session V on reinvigorating the Council’s role in preventive diplomacy, Cllr. Jappah observed that the Dialogue offered members a valuable opportunity to internalize how a hasty drawdown of peacekeeping operations can leave a country vulnerable.

He was speaking in response to interventions on how transnational organized crime — including transcontinental drug trafficking — can undermine governance in states just emerging from conflict, where institutions remain fragile.

On the question of how the E10 should engage the incoming Secretary-General, Cllr. Jappah urged elected members to first conduct an honest internal assessment and to invest deliberately in strengthening themselves as a caucus.

He proposed that the E10 build the discipline and coordination required to create what he described as a collective “veto,” together with the guardrails to use that leverage responsibly. He observed that, over a two-year tenure, “before an elected member really gets to understand the Council and its dynamics, it is time to exit,” and he called on the E10 to systematically leverage the institutional memory of what he termed the “Farewell Five” — the five outgoing members concluding their terms each year — so that hard-earned experience is transferred rather than lost.

He further cautioned that the Council too frequently holds briefings and open meetings at which statements are made that contain useful antidotes but are followed by no concrete action.

He urged that the traditional E10 luncheons move beyond merely setting the agenda for the Secretary-General’s luncheon with Permanent Representatives, and instead become a forum in which elected members act with one voice on decisive issues before the Council.

Cllr. Jappah welcomed the newly elected members—Austria, Kyrgyzstan, Portugal, Trinidad and Tobago, and Zimbabwe—emphasizing the importance of continuity in preventive practice, disciplined coordination among members, and adherence to the Charter as the Council’s composition changes.

“Prevention is not an abstract ideal,” he concluded. “It is the disciplined practice of acting before choices disappear.”

The E10 & I5 Annual Dialogue, established in 2019, gathers incoming, serving, and outgoing UN Security Council members to enhance institutional memory and align objectives. Panama, holding a non-permanent seat, hosted the 9th edition during its term, ending on December 31, 2026.

World.title: Liberia Elevates Diplomatic Standing as August E10 UN Security Council Coordinator
World.content:
NEW YORK — Liberia has successfully concluded its leadership as Coordinator of the Ten Elected Members (E10) of the United Nations Security Council for August 2026, marking a historic milestone in its global diplomatic resurgence.

Stepping into the helm of the E10 alongside Bahrain, Colombia, DRC, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Panama, Somalia, and Pakistan, Liberia strategically projected African leadership, unified non-permanent members, and shaped critical debate on pressing global peace and security files.

Key Achievements and Diplomatic Interventions

High-Level Security Council Diplomacy: Hosted UN Secretary-General António Guterres and E10 Ambassadors for a strategic luncheon centered on accelerating humanitarian interventions in Gaza and the West Bank.

Regional & Crisis Resolution:

Chaired the Political Coordinators’ Meeting to align consensus on the Libyan political process, security dynamics across West Africa and the Sahel, and the E10 Joint Statement on Security Council Working Methods.

International Judicial Oversight: Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary Lewis G. Brown II convened high-level negotiations with International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT) President Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, driving resolution terms on judicial archives, institutional downsizing, and UN oversight sensitivities involving Rwanda and Tanzania.

🇹🇿 Humanitarian Advocacy & International Law: Spearheaded expert briefings on the Ukraine humanitarian crisis and led targeted press interventions demanding the immediate release of illegally detained UN and aid personnel in Yemen.

Council Reform & Strategic Alignment: Championed reform of Security Council Subsidiary Bodies to streamline operations and ensure unified diplomatic alignment between the E10 and the Permanent Five (P5).

A Lasting Legacy on the World Stage

Liberia’s month-long tenure as Coordinator demonstrated strategic leadership, robust policy alignment, and an elevated ability to forge consensus among diverse international partners. Upon concluding its leadership, the E10 alliance formally commended Liberia for its decisive steering of the Council’s thematic priorities throughout August.

Meanwhile, Pakistan has assumed the E10 Coordination role for September, while Liberia remains positioned as an influential, principled voice on the Security Council, committed to driving international peace, stability, and multilateral cooperation.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor to Receive Medical Care at Residence Under Restrictions as Drug Case Continues
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor is set to receive medical attention outside detention under strict conditions imposed by Criminal Court “C” Judge Ousman F. Feika amid ongoing concerns about her health.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The court’s decision comes after Howard-Taylor’s lawyers raised medical concerns and sought her release from detention to allow her to receive treatment.

Under the court’s directive, Howard-Taylor is required to surrender all travel documents, effectively restricting her ability to leave the country while the case remains pending.

The former vice president will also be subject to limitations on visitors at her residence, with access restricted to a family member and her physician or physician’s assistant.

Howard-Taylor remains entangled in an ongoing investigation and prosecution involving allegations connected to an alleged transnational cocaine-trafficking operation.

Her legal team has maintained that her medical condition requires appropriate care, while the case continues to attract public attention because of the seriousness of the allegations.

The court’s latest action provides for medical considerations while maintaining judicial controls over Howard-Taylor as proceedings continue.

World.title: Liberia: Judge Feika Grants Jewel Howard-Taylor Compassionate Release
World.content:
Monrovia — Criminal Court “C” Judge Ousman F. Feika has granted former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor’s request for compassionate release from detention on medical grounds.

The ruling follows concerns raised by Howard-Taylor’s legal team about her medical condition and their request that she be permitted to receive medical care outside detention.

Under the court’s ruling, Howard-Taylor is required to surrender all travel documents to the court as part of the conditions of her release.

The court also ordered that visits to her residence be limited to a family member and her physician or physician’s assistant.

Howard-Taylor is facing criminal charges in connection with an ongoing narcotics investigation. She has denied the allegations.

The court’s decision allows her to leave detention while the legal proceedings continue.

This is a developing story.

World.title: Liberia: LIS Officer Thomas Kesselly Reportedly Shot in Foya
World.content:
MONROVIA — Thomas Kesselly, a member of the Liberia Immigration Service (LIS), was reportedly shot on Thursday, September 3, 2026, with conflicting accounts emerging over the incident.

Kesselley was reportedly shot at the LIS Academy in Foya.

While initial reports said Kesselly was shot, another account claims he shot himself.

However, family sources have expressed doubts about the self-inflicted shooting claim and are seeking clarity on what happened.

Kesselly’s condition and the circumstances surrounding the incident remain unclear as authorities have yet to provide a definitive account.

World.title: Mukandila challenges cancellation of NRC, passport as M’membe condemns move
World.content:
Opposition politician and lawyer Celestine Mukandila has challenged the cancellation of his National Registration Card and passport, maintaining that he is a Zambian citizen by descent and calling on authorities to disclose the legal and evidentiary basis for invalidating his national documents.

Mukandila said in a statement that he was born in 1990 in Lubumbashi, Democratic Republic of Congo, to a Zambian mother and a Congolese father. He said his mother is Ushi, from Matanda Village in Mansa, and that his maternal family has roots in Luapula Province.

His statement followed what opposition leader Fred M’membe described as a Government Gazette notice issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security invalidating Mukandila’s NRC and passport on grounds that the documents had been obtained through “fraud, false declaration, and misrepresentation.”

Mukandila rejected any suggestion that being born outside Zambia made him a foreign national.

He said his claim to Zambian nationality was based on citizenship by descent through his mother and cited Article 36 of the Constitution, which he said provides for citizenship by descent for a person born outside Zambia when at least one parent was a citizen by birth or descent at the time of the person’s birth.

“My position is therefore straightforward: I acquired Zambian citizenship by descent at birth through my Zambian mother,” Mukandila said.

He said he had neither applied for Zambian citizenship as an adult nor obtained it through naturalization.

Mukandila also questioned allegations surrounding the circumstances under which he obtained his NRC, saying he was about 16 years old when he became eligible for national registration.

He argued that if authorities allege fraud in the acquisition of the NRC, they should identify the alleged false representation, establish who made it and explain the legal basis for holding him responsible for events that occurred while he was a minor.

“I was a child,” Mukandila said. “I did not independently create my family history, determine my nationality, or manufacture the circumstances of my birth.”

Mukandila said his family returned to Zambia in 1999, although his mother continued spending periods in the Democratic Republic of Congo because of her employment.

He said his mother’s residence or employment outside Zambia did not change her Zambian citizenship.

Mukandila also pointed to his previous service in Zambia’s civil service, saying he underwent vetting and verification processes before entering public service and that his nationality had not previously prevented the state from employing him.

He said national registration authorities had also previously recognized him and issued him national documents.

Mukandila questioned why concerns about his status were being raised now if authorities believed there had always been a fundamental problem with his nationality or national registration.

“If there was genuinely a fundamental defect in my nationality or national registration, why was this not raised during the various occasions when the Zambian State had the opportunity and responsibility to verify my status?” he said.

Mukandila expressed particular concern about what he described as the apparent involvement of a permanent secretary in the process that resulted in the Gazette notice.

He argued that public officials could exercise only powers granted to them by law and that decisions affecting citizenship or national documents had to comply with procedural fairness and due process.

“A Gazette notice cannot itself become a substitute for the law,” he said.

Mukandila drew a distinction between citizenship and possession of an NRC or passport, arguing that cancellation of national identification documents would not by itself determine whether he remained a citizen under the Constitution.

He said an NRC served as evidence of identity and registration but was not the source of his citizenship by descent.

Mukandila called on authorities to explain which constitutional or statutory provision was being used to challenge his citizenship, what specific fraud was alleged, who was accused of committing it and what evidence supported the allegation.

He also demanded disclosure of which authority made the decision concerning his NRC and passport, the statutory power relied upon, whether he had been given notice and an opportunity to respond, and what procedure had been followed before the decision was published.

Mukandila linked the dispute to his political activities, saying he had participated in public affairs and expressed views different from those of the government.

He said political disagreement and criticism were legitimate elements of constitutional democracy and should not result in arbitrary treatment by the state.

“Citizenship cannot become a political weapon against citizens because they hold views that are unpopular with those in power,” Mukandila said.

He said he was prepared to have any genuine dispute over his nationality determined through legal and judicial processes.

“What I cannot accept is a situation in which my nationality is effectively determined administratively, without transparent due process,” he said.

Mukandila said he remained confident that Zambia’s Constitution and courts would uphold the principle that public authorities were subject to the law.

“Let the law be followed. Let the evidence be produced. Let due process be respected. And let the rule of law prevail over political expediency,” he said.

M’membe, meanwhile, condemned the cancellation of Mukandila’s documents and described the action as the “foreignising of political opponents.”

“From whatever angle one looks at it, this is unacceptable,” M’membe said. “The foreignising of political opponents must stop.”

M’membe compared Mukandila’s situation with the cases of John Chinula and William Banda in the 1990s after the United National Independence Party lost power to President Frederick Chiluba and the Movement for Multiparty Democracy.

According to M’membe, Chinula and Banda were deported to Malawi. He said he and others supported the two financially and in other ways, and that Chinula later died in Malawi.

M’membe said they subsequently persuaded President Levy Mwanawasa to allow Banda to return to Zambia.

He also placed the dispute within what he described as a broader African pattern in which citizenship cancellation has sometimes been used for political exclusion, national security enforcement or in response to alleged fraudulent documentation.

M’membe said arbitrary deprivation of nationality was prohibited under international human rights principles and frameworks such as the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights.

He cited examples from elsewhere on the continent, including a claim that Chadian President Mahamat Idriss Déby revoked the nationality of two France-based activists in late 2025 after accusing them of conduct incompatible with citizenship because of their criticism of the government.

M’membe also referred to historical controversies involving Zambia’s founding president, Kenneth Kaunda, under Chiluba’s government and former Ivorian Prime Minister Alassane Ouattara in Côte d’Ivoire.

At the same time, M’membe acknowledged that governments can cancel national registration documents or passports where authorities determine they were acquired through false declarations, misrepresentation or administrative corruption.

But he rejected such treatment in Mukandila’s case.

“Mukandila doesn’t deserve this unfair, unjust, and inhuman treatment,” M’membe said.

Mukandila’s statement did not deny that authorities have powers to investigate allegations concerning national documentation. His central argument was that any such action must distinguish between citizenship itself and the validity of particular documents and must be carried out under clearly identified legal authority and through due process.

The two statements frame the dispute as extending beyond the status of one politician, with Mukandila casting it as a test of administrative legality and constitutional citizenship protections and M’membe portraying it as part of a wider concern about the use of nationality disputes against political opponents.
