World.title: Kabimba is on point, President Hichilema must appoint Action-Oriented Cabinet!
World.content:
Economic Front President Wynter Kabimba has appealed to President Hakainde Hichilema to consider assembling a more action-oriented cabinet as he begins his second term in office.

Speaking to Phoenix News ahead of President Hichilema’s official announcement of his cabinet, Kabimba said he expected the President to appoint a team of ministers who would perform better than those in his previous administration.

The Economic Front strongman is definitely on point. As a matter of fact, this measure shouldn’t just stop at Cabinet level. It should be extended Permanent Secretaries and District Commissioners.

In his previous administration, we had a number of officials who either priotised private jobs or had a laissez faire approach towards work. They never bothered venturing into the field to investigate whether government policies were being implemented accordingly.

As Kabimba has rightly observed, the President deserves a stronger team to help him fulfil the commitments he made to the Zambian people during his campaigns.

The President needs to assemble a team of the likes of ZNS commander Lt. Gen. Maliti Solochi. The man is action-oriented…..he has hands on approach towards work. Whenever there’s an assignment to be undertaken within his jurisdiction, he doesn’t leave the responsibility at the mercy of his juniors. You’ll find him ‘pa ground’ supervising the work himself or getting soiled.

Some PSs and DCs are not even known by the masses as they are always closed-up in their deluxe offices enjoying tea with cookies! Only a few such as the likes of Elvis Nkandu and Thabo Kawana easily stand out as their work speak for themselves.

With more challenges expected in the years to come such as youth unemployment, the El Nino factor or food shortages, we expect the President to take his time to identify individuals who are easily going to align themselves with his vision for the country. As for you job seekers, a little patience would definitely do😊

We submit…..

Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

Political/Social Analyst

Zambezi

World.title: SADC Troika Considers Zambia’s Post-Electoral Crisis
World.content:
SADC Troika Considers Zambia’s Post-Electoral Crisis

The Southern African Development Community’s security organ is preparing to take up Zambia’s post-election crisis, after receiving a preliminary report from its election observer mission.

King Mswati III of Eswatini, who took over the chairmanship of the SADC Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation Troika last month, is expected to convene member states to consider the situation. Zambia’s main opposition leader remains in jail, and a former Cabinet minister is dead following a military raid conducted during the vote count.

Zambia held its general election on August 13. Voting passed off peacefully, but the aftermath brought allegations of vote manipulation and result tampering, including claims that the Zambia Army was deployed inside counting centres and that results were altered under military supervision.

On August 14, a military raid on the Lusaka home of opposition leader Brian Mundubile left former Minister of Transport and Communications Mutotwe Kafwaya dead. Several of Mundubile’s colleagues were arrested in the same operation, among them UNIP president and former Botswana bishop Trevor Mwamba, and former Law Association of Zambia president George Chisanga.

Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, took refuge inside the United Nations building in Lusaka after the raid. UN Secretary-General António Guterres sent a Special Envoy from New York to negotiate a resolution.

The UN sought safe passage for the two men, or their transfer to a third-party embassy in Lusaka. President Hakainde Hichilema rejected both options, demanding they surrender to police, who were investigating alleged security breaches and claims that the opposition had formed a militia.

Five days after the raid, Secretary to Cabinet Patrick Kangwa confirmed Kafwaya’s death. He said Mundubile had formed a militia intending to seize power illegally.

Mundubile and Zulu were handed over on August 27 to the Eight Church Mother Bodies at the Anglican Cathedral of the Holy Cross in Lusaka, who surrendered them to police. Both now face treason charges and are held at Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility in Kabwe, roughly 200km from Lusaka, awaiting trial.

Soldiers sealed Zambia’s courts during the constitutional window for filing election challenges, blocking Mundubile and civil society groups from lodging a petition through normal channels.

Chief Justice Mumba Malila later disclosed that a petition had reached him regardless, filed by private mail. He named former Law Association of Zambia president Linda Kasonde and civil society leader Brebner Changala as the petitioners. Malila said the filing method was unusual but that he would use his constitutional powers to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court.

The Constitution requires election challenges to be resolved before a new president is inaugurated. Government proceeded with the inauguration regardless. Hichilema was sworn in for a second term on September 1 at National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka, with the Kasonde-Changala petition still before the Constitutional Court.

World.title: From Civil Servant to Stateless: Mukandila’s Citizenship Ordeal
World.content:
A man does not need to lose his freedom and his nationality on the same day, yet that is precisely the position in which incarcerated Lusaka lawyer Celestine Mukandila now finds himself, after the state moved to cancel his National Registration Card and passport while he remains in custody, effectively declaring him stateless at the very moment he is least able to contest it in the ordinary course of civic life.

Mukandila, secretary general of the Tonse Pamodzi Alliance, says he is a Zambian citizen by descent and has challenged the cancellation of his documents, arguing that citizenship cannot be revoked through administrative action without following the law.

His position rests on a specific constitutional provision. Mukandila says he acquired Zambian citizenship at birth through his mother, who was a Zambian citizen at the time of his birth in 1990 in Lubumbashi, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. He explained that his mother was Ushi by origin, from Matanda Village in Mansa, Luapula Province, and that his maternal family had deep roots in the province.

Being born outside Zambia did not, in his account, make him a foreigner, because Article 36 of the Constitution provides for citizenship by descent where, at the time of birth, at least one parent was a Zambian citizen by birth or descent.

“My position is therefore straightforward: I acquired Zambian citizenship by descent at birth through my Zambian mother. I did not apply to become Zambian as an adult, nor did I obtain my citizenship through naturalisation,” Mukandila said.

He said he was approximately 16 years old when he became eligible for national registration, and therefore could not be personally held responsible for any alleged irregularities surrounding the acquisition of his NRC, since he was still a minor navigating a process his family, not he alone, would have managed.

“If the State alleges that fraud was committed in the acquisition of my NRC, then it must identify the alleged fraudulent representation, identify who made it, and establish who had the legal responsibility for making the relevant declarations at the time,” Mukandila said.

He said his family returned to Zambia in 1999, although his mother continued spending periods in the DRC because of her employment. Mukandila also questioned why his nationality was only being challenged now, when he had previously served as a civil servant and had undergone State verification processes without issue.

“The National Registration authorities themselves have previously recognised me and issued me with national documentation,” he said.

He has also demanded that authorities explain the legal basis for cancelling his NRC and passport, including identifying the alleged fraud, the authority that made the decision, and the procedure followed before the cancellation was carried out.

Mukandila said a Gazette notice could not substitute the law, arguing that public officers must exercise statutory power within the limits prescribed by law.

He said the matter was bigger than him personally, because citizenship should not be used as a political weapon against citizens holding views different from those in government.

“I demand only what every citizen is entitled to demand. Let the law be followed. Let the evidence be produced. Let due process be respected. And let the rule of law prevail over political expediency,” Mukandila said.

The case adds to a growing list of disputes in which opposition-aligned figures have found their legal standing, whether through citizenship, bail, or access to counsel, challenged through administrative or security channels rather than tested first through ordinary judicial process, a pattern that has drawn concern from legal commentators and civil society figures in the weeks following the general election.

World.title: UPND Alliance Spars UN Human Rights Report
World.content:
A government publicly disputing the findings of a United Nations human rights mandate holder is not, in ordinary circumstances, a routine political exchange. It is a moment in which a state stakes its own credibility against that of an international system built specifically to scrutinise governments during periods of political stress. That is precisely the position Zambia now occupies.

United Party for National Development Alliance spokesperson Edmond Miti has rejected a statement issued by UN Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and association, Gina Romero, calling it hasty, inaccurate and one-sided. Romero had called on Zambian authorities to release political detainees and restore democratic accountability, a statement made against the backdrop of events that have already claimed one life and placed a former presidential candidate and his running mate in detention on treason-related charges.

What is actually being disputed

Miti’s rebuttal is not a minor clarification. He accused Romero of presenting unverified allegations as settled fact, and of containing significant errors of law. His central argument rests on a distinction he insists must hold regardless of political rank: “Being an opposition leader or a political figure does not place anyone above the law, nor does it transform a criminal suspect into a political detainee,” he said.

That distinction, however, sits at the heart of why UN Special Procedures exist in the first place. Special Rapporteurs are appointed precisely because national governments, when accused of political persecution, are not considered neutral arbiters of whether their own conduct amounts to persecution or legitimate law enforcement. Miti’s insistence that allegations of treason must be tested by independent courts is, in the abstract, unremarkable. What makes it significant here is the context in which it is being asserted: a former Cabinet minister and sitting MP is dead following a raid conducted during live vote counting, his death denied by the state for five days until a habeas corpus filing forced disclosure, and the two men now facing treason charges were present at that raid.

The government’s defence

Miti sought to reframe the UPND administration’s record affirmatively, describing it as a law-abiding government that has elevated respect for human rights to unprecedented levels. He pointed to the abolition of the death penalty and changes to public order practices as evidence that reform in Zambia is substantive rather than rhetorical, and cautioned the international community against confusing legitimate criminal investigations with political witch-hunts.

He drew a deliberate contrast between Romero’s approach and that of a separate UN figure, the Secretary-General’s own Special Envoy, who Miti said engaged constructively on the ground in Zambia rather than issuing judgment from a distance. According to Miti, it was this envoy who facilitated the handover of opposition leaders to security agencies, operating on explicit assurances that their fundamental rights would be respected, a commitment he said the Zambian government continues to honour.

That claim of continued protection sits uneasily alongside separate, corroborated reporting that the detained opposition figures have faced severe restrictions on legal and family access at Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility, and reports that they have twice refused prison-supplied food amid unresolved concerns over their safety. Whether those restrictions are consistent with the assurances Miti describes is a question his statement does not address.

Sovereignty versus scrutiny

Miti’s legal argument leans heavily on the principle of non-interference. “Under international law, the mandate of UN Special Procedures requires strict adherence to objectivity, impartiality and non-interference in the internal affairs of sovereign states,” he said, arguing that Romero failed to meet this standard by operating from a distance without thorough local verification and without adequately incorporating input from Zambian authorities.

This is a genuine and long-standing tension within international human rights law: sovereign states retain the right to conduct their own criminal justice processes, while UN mandate holders retain the right, indeed the obligation, to scrutinise those processes when credible concerns arise about politically motivated detention. Neither principle automatically overrides the other, and disputes of exactly this kind, a state insisting on non-interference, a rapporteur insisting on independent scrutiny, have historically been resolved only through sustained international pressure, further investigation or, in some cases, neither, leaving the underlying facts contested indefinitely.

Why this matters beyond the statement itself

Miti closed by describing Zambia as a committed constitutional democracy, open to fair scrutiny but grounded in mutual respect and national sovereignty. That description will now be tested against events that are, for the most part, no longer in serious factual dispute: a sitting MP died from gunshot wounds during a state security operation; his death was not acknowledged for five days; two senior opposition figures remain detained on charges connected to that same raid; and questions about their access to legal counsel, family visits and safe food remain unresolved more than a week into their detention.

The dispute between the UPND Alliance and the UN Special Rapporteur is, in that sense, not merely a disagreement over wording or diplomatic tone. It is a contest over which account of these events, the government’s or the international community’s, will shape how Zambia’s post-election period is remembered and how accountable its institutions are ultimately held to be.

World.title: Death of Constitutionalism — How August 13 Marked a Turning Point for Zambia’s Democracy
World.content:
Death of Constitutionalism — How August 13 Marked a Turning Point for Zambia’s Democracy

By Oscar Mike Chops

For five days, the Zambian state told the public, implicitly and explicitly, that former Cabinet minister and sitting Member of Parliament Mutotwe Kafwaya could not be found. For five days, his family did not know whether he was alive. When the truth finally emerged, it came not from a government statement volunteered in good faith, but because a court had been asked to compel one.

The sequence of events, now established through official confirmation, opposition accounts and a court filing, has been described by commentators as marking a decisive rupture in Zambia’s constitutional order rather than a gradual decline. What happened in the 48 hours after polls closed on August 13, and in the five days of silence that followed, has become the defining controversy of President Hakainde Hichilema’s second-term inauguration.

The raid

On the evening of August 14, as live vote tabulation was still under way across the country, a heavily armed Joint Task Force entered the private Kabulonga residence of Tonse Pact presidential candidate Brian Mundubile. The unit was made up of elite personnel drawn from the Zambia Army, the Drug Enforcement Commission and the Zambia Police Service.

During the operation, state security personnel opened fire inside the residence. Among those present was Mutotwe Kafwaya, former transport minister and Member of Parliament for Lunte, who sustained multiple gunshot wounds. Eleven other individuals, including opposition political staff, were forcibly apprehended and detained at the scene.

Kafwaya did not survive his injuries.

Five days of silence

What followed was not an immediate acknowledgement of a death in state custody, but an extended period in which senior government representatives explicitly rejected reports of Kafwaya’s death or critical condition.

When Mundubile’s running mate, Makebi Zulu, publicly stated that Kafwaya had been taken to a military health facility with severe chest wounds, officials at the Ministry of Defence dismissed the claim outright, insisting that no record of Kafwaya existed at their facilities.

The blackout held for nearly five days. It was broken only when Kafwaya’s wife, Dinis Ng’andu Kafwaya, filed an urgent habeas corpus application in the High Court of Zambia, a legal instrument that compels the state to produce a detained person before a judge or account for their whereabouts. It is a measure of how completely ordinary channels of accountability had broken down that it took a widow’s court filing, rather than a government press briefing, to force disclosure.

Faced with mandatory judicial scrutiny, Inspector General of Police Graphel Musamba issued an official statement on August 19, finally confirming that Kafwaya had died from gunshot wounds inflicted during the August 14 operation.

Competing narratives

To justify the use of lethal force during a raid conducted while votes were still being counted, state security organs have pointed to an alleged “insurgency plot,” citing the recovery of cash and weapons at the scene.

Mundubile and Zulu have firmly rejected this characterisation. They argue the narrative was constructed to achieve three specific outcomes: to rebrand what they describe as an extrajudicial killing as a response to armed confrontation; to justify non-bailable charges of treason, sedition and espionage against senior opposition figures; and to force principal opposition contenders into hiding or legal detention during the narrow statutory window in which election petitions must be filed.

Whichever account proves accurate through further judicial process, the underlying facts are no longer in dispute. A sitting Member of Parliament died from gunshot wounds during a state security operation conducted at a presidential candidate’s private residence while the country’s votes were still being tallied. His death was denied by the state for five days. It was confirmed only after his widow sought judicial intervention.

A nation left to grieve in silence

The human cost of these events has rippled well beyond the courtroom. Kafwaya was a son of Northern Province, and his killing has become deeply entwined with the region’s collective mourning. The Bemba Royal Establishment, in an unprecedented decision reached during an urgent meeting on Friday night, cancelled the 2026 Ukusefya pa Ng’wena traditional ceremony, one of Zambia’s largest cultural gatherings, citing the region’s grief and the continued detention of prominent political figures from the area.

Former Northern Province minister Chungu Bwalya described the ceremony’s cancellation as entirely justified, noting that holding festivities while a son of the region lay dead and others from the province remained in detention would have signalled indifference to real suffering.

Constitutional stakes

Commentators tracing the sequence of events argue that what collapsed on August 13 and in the days after was not merely a political dispute but a structural safeguard: the presumption that state power, however forcefully exercised, remains answerable to judicial oversight in real time, not five days and a court order later.

Zambia now carries this into its second Hichilema term. Opposition figures Mundubile and Makebi Zulu remain in detention on treason-related charges connected to the same events, their case now moving through the ordinary channels of the courts. Kafwaya’s widow has secured, through legal action, the disclosure the state initially withheld. What remains unresolved is accountability for the raid itself, and for the five days during which the truth was denied.

World.title: Mundubile, Makebi on Hunger Strike?
World.content:
Uncertainty over what is happening inside Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility has deepened after reports emerged that detained opposition figures Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu have stopped eating food supplied by the institution, with their own legal team unable to fully explain why.

Defence counsel Sakwiba Sikota, part of the team representing both men, stopped short of confirming the hunger strike outright, but his account painted a picture of a legal team locked out of the very access it needs to know what is happening to its clients.

“I haven’t been to them today or yesterday, but we will be going there,” Sikota said, describing a pattern of restricted visits that has left even the lawyers uncertain about conditions inside the facility.

He traced the immediate concern back to the question of food safety. According to Sikota, Mundubile and Zulu have specifically asked for meals to be brought to them from outside the correctional facility rather than eating what is prepared internally, a request that prison authorities have repeatedly turned down.

“You see how they refuse the food being provided by the facility… So they have opted not to take food from the facility,” he said, describing the decision as a direct response to that refusal rather than an unprompted protest.

Behind the food dispute lies a broader breakdown in trust, Sikota suggested. He linked the difficulty in visiting the two men to what he called an unhelpful posture from officials at the facility, saying restricted access has made it impossible for the legal team to independently verify what the two detainees are being given to eat.

“There is a real need for them to be wary of the fact that they cannot be sure of what they are being given by the authorities, because the attitude of the authorities has shown no interest in that of goodwill,” he said.

Asked directly whether fears of poisoning were behind the men’s refusal to eat, Sikota declined to confirm this, saying he was not in a position to state it as fact. His caution reflects the wider information gap surrounding the case, in which claims and counter-claims have circulated without official confirmation from correctional authorities.

Sources close to the matter say the current standoff is not the first of its kind. This, according to those sources, is the second occasion since their detention began that Mundubile and Zulu have refused prison meals, suggesting a recurring pattern of distrust rather than an isolated incident.

Additional claims have surfaced regarding who is actually guarding the pair. Sources allege that Zambia Army commandos, rather than the ordinary correctional officers typically assigned to Mukobeko, have been posted around the two detainees, a security arrangement described as unusual and, by some accounts, without precedent in recent Zambian correctional practice.

Compounding the concern is the reported difficulty faced by friends and relatives attempting to visit the two men. Multiple sources say access for family members has been tightly restricted since the detention began, limiting independent channels through which the public could otherwise verify the detainees’ condition.

Taken together, the restricted legal access, the reported presence of military personnel and the refusal to eat facility-prepared food have combined to raise serious questions about the treatment of Mundubile and Zulu more than a week into their detention on treason-related charges.

Correctional authorities and government officials had not, by the time of publication, issued any public response confirming or denying the reports of a hunger strike, the restrictions on visitors, or the presence of military guards at the facility. The silence has left the matter unresolved, with Mundubile and Zulu’s legal team indicating it intends to press for renewed access in the coming days.

World.title: Release Mundubile, Makebi, Demands Kalaba
World.content:
A widening rift between political rhetoric and judicial practice has drawn sharp criticism from Citizens First president Harry Kalaba, who says Zambia’s courts are being used selectively depending on whose electoral fortunes are at stake.

Kalaba has demanded the unconditional release of Tonse Alliance presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and lawyer Makebi Zulu, arguing that their continued detention reflects a broader climate of political intolerance rather than a genuine legal process.

His statement did not stop at the two men. Kalaba called for every political detainee currently held in the country to be released, describing this as a necessary precondition for dialogue, national reconciliation and healing after a bruising election season.

At the heart of his argument is a contradiction he believes exposes the government’s true priorities. Courts were closed to any challenge of the presidential election outcome, he noted, yet those same courts remain open and active for challenges brought against duly elected parliamentary candidates.

“It is deeply concerning that while the UPND leadership denied the people of Zambia an opportunity to validate the presidential electoral outcome by closing the courts of law, it has now turned to those same courts to challenge duly elected parliamentary candidates,” Kalaba said.

He described this as “a troubling pattern of expediency over principle,” warning that it risks eroding public confidence in the justice system altogether.

Detention practices came under equally pointed criticism. Kalaba said he had received reports of opposition supporters being held for as long as 14 days without appearing before a court, a practice he labelled an abuse of the justice system.

“Such actions amount to an abuse of the justice system and point to a dangerous trend of its weaponisation. This must come to an immediate end,” he said.

A further, more urgent concern surfaced in his remarks: alleged plans to abduct Mafinga South Member of Parliament Faith Munthali. Kalaba called on authorities to investigate the claims and guarantee her safety without delay.

He tied these domestic developments to international scrutiny, saying recent events lend weight to warnings already issued by United Nations Special Rapporteurs about a shrinking democratic space in Zambia.

Rather than direct his appeal solely at government, Kalaba turned to the country’s institutions of conscience. He urged civil society organisations, faith-based bodies and the clergy to speak out in defence of constitutional democracy, justice and national unity, cautioning that silence in the face of injustice only deepens the crisis.

Citizens First, he stressed, remains committed to non-violence, equity, justice and respect for the rule of law. His closing appeal was aimed squarely at the ruling party: an end to what he termed “hypocrisy in the application of the law,” and a single, uniform standard of justice for every citizen.

World.title: Angola: Cotton Revival In Busia - Hope Grows Amid Small Farms, Dry Spells And a Silent Ginnery
World.content:
The roads leading into the interior of Busia County tell a story of a region that is slowly changing, but perhaps not fast enough.

From Luanda to Bumala and Finyula, the journey is punctuated by dusty roads, boda bodas and stretches where getting to the farms is an exercise in patience. Away from the main roads, infrastructure remains a challenge, with motorcycles often providing the only practical means of reaching some farming areas.

It is here, amid small farms and modest homesteads, that cotton is quietly making a comeback.

But unlike Lamu County, where cotton farmers are taking advantage of the revival of the industry to expand production, farmers in this part of Busia are still growing the crop on very small pieces of land.

Most farmers cultivate no more than two acres, according to Bonventer Barasa, an accountant and manager at Luanda Farmers Cooperative Union.

“Currently, not more than two acres. Very small acreage hence low production despite what our modern ginnery can handle,” Barasa says.

For a crop whose revival is being seen as an opportunity to reconnect farmers to a market that once supported entire communities, the small acreage presents a major challenge.

Without enough cotton coming from farmers, the ginnery cannot operate at full capacity. And without a reliable market and attractive returns, farmers have little incentive to increase production. It is a cycle that the region is still trying to break.

For Vincent Okumu, however, cotton is more than just another crop. The farmer has grown cotton for more than two decades, taking over the enterprise from his parents. What began as a family livelihood became an important investment in his own future. Cotton proceeds helped him pursue his education. Today, he is using the same crop to educate his children. Two of his children have already graduated from university, while another is preparing to enrol.

For Okumu, this is proof that even small-scale cotton farming can change a family's fortunes when the crop performs well and farmers receive a fair return.

He farms about one and a half acres and expects to make at least Sh100,000 in profit from the current crop.

He also chairs Bwiri Farmers Cooperative Society, where he says the benefits of cotton are becoming visible beyond individual households. Livelihoods in his village, he says, have improved, with the gradual disappearance of thatched-roof houses among families whose incomes have increased. The transformation may not be dramatic, but it is visible. The same crop that helped one generation access education is now helping another pay school fees and improve their homes.

Yet Okumu's experience also exposes the limitations holding cotton farming back in Busia. He would like to increase his acreage from one and a half acres to five. But expanding production is easier said than done.

One of the biggest challenges is mechanisation. Land preparation is still largely done manually, making cotton production expensive and time-consuming. The county's available machinery cannot meet the demand from the number of farmers seeking the service.

The problem is particularly important in cotton because timing matters. Okumu says delayed distribution of seed affects production because farmers are working within a narrow planting and growing window.

By the time some farmers receive seed and prepare their land, they may have already lost valuable time.

It is a challenge that echoes concerns raised by the cooperative leadership.

Bernard Ojiambo, chairman of the Luanda Farmers Cooperative Union, says the cooperative has been seeking machinery, including tractors that farmers can hire to prepare their land. Without tractors and other equipment, farmers can fall behind the rains. “When it reaches time for planting farmers can hire, they go and plow to make it earlier plantation. We delay because we don't have machines like tractors and other things to support farmers,” Ojiambo says.

The consequence is a chain reaction of delays in planting and harvesting. The rains hold the key This year's crop has also had to contend with insufficient rainfall.

The cotton plants are about two months old, but the season has not been ideal. The dry conditions have affected the crop, with farmers now looking to the rains for a turnaround. During the visit, temperatures climbed to around 30 degrees Celsius. The heat was compounded by dusty roads and the dry conditions in the interior. Yet farmers remain hopeful. Ojiambo says the area's soils and climate can support cotton when rainfall comes at the right time. “It is the soil itself and the climate, though we don't have much rain, but once we get it between April and August, the harvest comes out well,” he says.

AllAfrica Vincent Okumu, a cotton farmer from Busia County inspecting his crop at his one and a half acre farm

For farmers like Okumu, a good harvest could provide the incentive to expand.

He praises the cooperative's buying price of Sh76 per kilogram, saying the price offers farmers a reason to remain in the crop. His own target of at least Sh100,000 in profit from one and a half acres shows why the crop continues to attract interest despite the difficulties.

At Luanda Ginnery, however, there is currently little evidence of the activity associated with harvest. The machines are silent. The last season ended about four months ago, and the ginnery is now waiting for the next crop to mature.

Inside the modern facility, the process is straightforward. Once cotton arrives, it is weighed and stored before being fed into the machinery. A suction system moves it from the store to a bale opener, where compacted cotton is loosened.

The cotton then passes through a pre-cleaner that removes dust and separates poor-quality cotton from the good lint. The good cotton is taken to the ginning machine, where the lint is separated from the seed.

The seed moves through a conveyor while the lint is transferred to a press, where it is compressed and tied into 200-kilogram bales ready for collection. But the ginnery's ability to operate depends entirely on what farmers bring from their fields. “If they don't grow cotton, then we don't have raw materials. That means we won't move on,” Barasa says. It is a simple relationship: the strength of the ginnery depends on the strength of the farmer.

Cotton has a long history in Busia. Ojiambo says cotton growing in the region dates back decades, when the crop was promoted among local farmers. But the industry eventually declined, with farmers becoming discouraged by delayed payments and poor returns. When cotton lost its appeal, many turned to maize. But maize also requires adequate rainfall, while cotton, Ojiambo argues, remains better suited to the area's conditions. “Cotton is more of a value than maize,” he says. With maize, the small acreage available to farmers is often used to feed the household. Cotton, on the other hand, is primarily a cash crop. Once harvested and sold, the money can be directed towards school fees, food and other household needs. That distinction is important in an area where many families are still farming on very small plots.

The challenges extend beyond production. Barasa says farmers also struggle with access to chemicals and implements, while limited working capital makes it difficult for both farmers and the ginnery to operate efficiently. The ginnery has also struggled to add value to cotton seed. A machine supplied by the Agricultural and Food Authority to process cotton seed has not performed efficiently, according to Barasa. He says a better-performing machine could allow the facility to produce cottonseed oil, seed cakes and soap. Such value addition would give the crop additional economic importance and potentially create more income from the same harvest.

The ginnery has, however, received a major boost through investment in solar energy. Barasa says the government provided solar panels worth Sh40 million. The move has reduced the facility's monthly electricity bill from about Sh150,000 to approximately Sh75,000. But the question remains whether there will be enough cotton to keep the machinery busy.

Busia's cotton revival is therefore a work in progress. The crop has a history here. Farmers know it. Cooperatives understand it. The ginnery has the machinery to process it. What is missing is scale. Farmers are still cultivating small pieces of land. Seed distribution needs to be timely. Mechanisation remains inadequate. Rainfall is unpredictable. And the market needs to offer farmers sufficient confidence to invest more.

For Vincent Okumu, however, the argument for cotton is already settled. The crop paid for his education and is now paying for his children's education. He believes the same opportunity exists for his neighbours. As chairman of Bwiri Farmers Cooperative Society, he is encouraging other farmers to return to cotton and take advantage of the improving fortunes of the crop. His own ambition is to move from one and a half acres to five. But for that ambition to become reality, the tractors must arrive, seed must reach farmers on time and the market must remain attractive.

For now, the cotton plants are still young. The ginnery remains quiet. The roads remain dusty and difficult. But the clouds are gathering, and with them comes the possibility of a better harvest. In the small farms of Busia, cotton may not yet be the booming commercial enterprise seen elsewhere. But for farmers like Okumu, it has already proved that a small farm can produce something much bigger than cotton—a pathway to education, better homes and a more hopeful future.

World.title: Sudan: Seven Democratic U.S. Senators Call On UN Security Council to Pass Sanctions on Sudan to Cut Off Conflict Cash Flows
World.content:
document

U.S. Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) on Friday led seven of his colleagues in sending a letter to U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz calling for the U.S. to push to pass additional sanctions measures in Sudan that would limit the flow of funds to the warring parties driving the largest humanitarian crisis in the world.

Murphy specifically advocated for international prohibitions on the sale of precursor chemicals utilized in certain types of gold extraction and development of due diligence guidelines for the procurement of gum arabic, a natural resource frequently smuggled by belligerents to finance their operations. Murphy also called for increasing transparency in reporting by the Security Council’s Sudan Panel of Experts to explicitly identity countries that have circumvented international restrictions to provide weapons and financial support to the warring factions in Sudan. Exploitation of natural resources such as gold and gum arabic is a prominent source of income and foreign currency for both sides of the devastating war in Sudan, which has driven over half of the country’s population into severe hunger and displaced over 14 million people.

“Any resolution put forward to renew sanctions pursuant to United Nations Security Council Resolution 1591 (2005) should also prohibit the export or transfer of precursor chemicals used in Sudan’s artisanal mining industry, target the illicit sale of Sudanese gum arabic (also known as acacia gum), and improve reporting by the Panel of Experts to explicitly identify arms embargo violations and the parties responsible,” said Murphy.

Murphy argued ordinary sanctions on gold are not enough to disrupt the economic engine of the war: “Restrictions meant to disrupt transactions at the point of sale must be combined with a coordinated effort to restrict access to the precursor chemicals that enable unregulated gold extraction in the first place. This is especially critical to curtail other sources of profit tied to the gold sector but outside material sales, such as informal taxation schemes, security fees, and transportation fees levied against mining firms in RSF-held territory.”



He explained why a ban on the transfer or sale of precursor chemical would severely disrupt the illicit gold market: “Artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) operations account for approximately 80-90% of Sudan’s gold production. ASGM mining employs various methods of extraction, but it typically relies on mercury and sodium cyanide as relatively cheap and simple chemicals to easily find and process gold particles… According to a 2025 report, most of these precursor chemicals are imported from China, the United Arab Emirates, and some European Union (EU) nations… the diverse supply chain necessitates a more comprehensive prohibition to eliminate the transfer of mercury and sodium cyanide to ASGM miners. Adoption of an export ban on mercury and sodium cyanide as part of the Security Council’s Sudan sanctions regime, with appropriate exceptions for humanitarian purposes, would help sever the link between the gold sector and the ongoing conflict.”

Murphy called for new measures to undercut funding streams tied to gum arabic: “Gold is not the only natural resource being exploited to fund the war… revenue tied to gum arabic production is small relative to gold, but profits from its sale and control over of trade networks now help sustain the conflict… the RSF has engaged in looting and extortion to exert control over trade routes and border crossings, leveraging the proceeds to bankroll their side of the war. Cross-border smuggling and re-labelling of Sudanese gum arabic to avoid heightened scrutiny about sourcing is also pervasive in neighboring countries such as Chad, South Sudan, and Egypt. As the Security Council has done in response to other conflicts where natural resource exploitation has contributed to instability, it should mandate the Panel of Experts to develop due diligence guidelines to improve gum arabic procurement practices, prevent smuggled products from entering the supply chain, and avoid inadvertently enriching the belligerents.”

Murphy also advocated for the adoption of an aggressive reporting regime, including naming and shaming third-party countries who are fueling the violence in Sudan: “We encourage the U.S. to ensure the Panel of Experts’ extended mandate requires annual reporting that includes explicit documentation of all violations of the arms embargo and the parties responsible. Given the outsized role that external actors play in shaping the war, the Panel must improve transparency about the transfer of arms and financial support to the warring parties, including engagement with illicit gold smugglers. Reporting by other UN-sanctioned panels, including the Panel of Experts on Libya, demonstrate a level of naming and shaming that the Sudan panel should strive for. Countries who blatantly circumvent the arms embargo and other UN restrictions to prolong the conflict cannot be permitted to continue hiding their role and must be publicly held to account for their actions.”

In conclusion, Murphy stressed the UN’s current approach has proven incapable of ending the conflict and new strategies must be pursued: “The war in Sudan is now into its fourth year. A straight renewal of the UN Security Council Resolution on Sudan that maintains the status quo will not bring an end to the unimaginable violence and devastation that has affected millions of Sudanese. The international community should urgently adapt its strategy to creatively deploy the entire range of tools at its disposal. Coordinated, comprehensive measures to increase the pressure on the economic engine of the war, particularly on natural resources supply chains, can raise the cost of the war, making it too costly and burdensome to continue.”U.S. Senators Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Bernard Sanders (I-Vt.), and Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) also joined the letter.

A copy of the letter is available here.A full transcript of the letter is available below.

Dear Ambassador Waltz,

As the United Nations (UN) Security Council considers the renewal and possible expansion of the Sudan sanctions regime, we write to request that the U.S. Mission put forth additional measures that would target key funding sources actively enabling the horrific violence in Sudan. The recent proposal from U.S. Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos to expand the scope of the Darfur arms embargo to the entirety of the country is encouraging. We also appreciate his recognition that external financial support to all parties remains a driver of conflict and agree that the UN has the tools to address these issues. We therefore urge the U.S. Mission to engage accordingly and advocate for the passage of additional provisions to eliminate financial channels that belligerents depend on to perpetuate the conflict.

Specifically, any resolution put forward to renew sanctions pursuant to United Nations Security Council Resolution 1591 (2005) should also prohibit the export or transfer of precursor chemicals used in Sudan’s artisanal mining industry, target the illicit sale of Sudanese gum arabic (also known as acacia gum), and improve reporting by the Panel of Experts to explicitly identify arms embargo violations and the parties responsible.

Gold is widely considered the most significant source of income and foreign currency for both sides of Sudan’s war, which use the proceeds to purchase weapons and compensate personnel. The Treasury Department has previously targeted operatives in the RSF’s financial network that facilitate the sale of gold, recognizing the role that the sector plays in funneling cash to the militia group. However, restrictions meant to disrupt transactions at the point of sale must be combined with a coordinated effort to restrict access to the precursor chemicals that enable unregulated gold extraction in the first place. This is especially critical to curtail other sources of profit tied to the gold sector but outside material sales, such as informal taxation schemes, security fees, and transportation fees levied against mining firms in RSF-held territory.

Although it is difficult to determine precise figures because a substantial amount of Sudan’s gold is smuggled out of the country and gold production in RSF-controlled territory is not reported, artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) operations account for approximately 80-90% of Sudan’s gold production. ASGM mining employs various methods of extraction, but it typically relies on mercury and sodium cyanide as relatively cheap and simple chemicals to easily find and process gold particles. In addition to the chemicals’ vital role in the wartime economy, numerous studies have found prolonged exposure can lead to severe health complications and is harmful to the local environment. According to a 2025 report, most of these precursor chemicals are imported from China, the United Arab Emirates, and some European Union (EU) nations. While the EU recently unveiled a suite of regulations restricting the sale of precursor chemicals to Sudan, the diverse supply chain necessitates a more comprehensive prohibition to eliminate the transfer of mercury and sodium cyanide to ASGM miners. Adoption of an export ban on mercury and sodium cyanide as part of the Security Council’s Sudan sanctions regime, with appropriate exceptions for humanitarian purposes, would help sever the link between the gold sector and the ongoing conflict.

Gold is not the only natural resource being exploited to fund the war. As documented by the UN Office of the High Commission for Human Rights, revenue tied to gum arabic production is small relative to gold, but profits from its sale and control over of trade networks now help sustain the conflict. Sudan was one of the world’s largest exporters of gum arabic prior to 2023, but widespread disruption to the industry has caused output to plummet and its value to skyrocket. Consequently, the RSF has engaged in looting and extortion to exert control over trade routes and border crossings, leveraging the proceeds to bankroll their side of the war. Cross-border smuggling and re-labelling of Sudanese gum arabic to avoid heightened scrutiny about sourcing is also pervasive in neighboring countries such as Chad, South Sudan, and Egypt. As the Security Council has done in response to other conflicts where natural resource exploitation has contributed to instability, it should mandate the Panel of Experts to develop due diligence guidelines to improve gum arabic procurement practices, prevent smuggled products from entering the supply chain, and avoid inadvertently enriching the belligerents.

Close 

Finally, we encourage the U.S. to ensure the Panel of Experts’ extended mandate requires annual reporting that includes explicit documentation of all violations of the arms embargo and the parties responsible. Given the outsized role that external actors play in shaping the war, the Panel must improve transparency about the transfer of arms and financial support to the warring parties, including engagement with illicit gold smugglers. Reporting by other UN-sanctioned panels, including the Panel of Experts on Libya, demonstrate a level of naming and shaming that the Sudan panel should strive for. Countries who blatantly circumvent the arms embargo and other UN restrictions to prolong the conflict cannot be permitted to continue hiding their role and must be publicly held to account for their actions.

The war in Sudan is now into its fourth year. A straight renewal of the UN Security Council Resolution on Sudan that maintains the status quo will not bring an end to the unimaginable violence and devastation that has affected millions of Sudanese. The international community should urgently adapt its strategy to creatively deploy the entire range of tools at its disposal. Coordinated, comprehensive measures to increase the pressure on the economic engine of the war, particularly on natural resources supply chains, can raise the cost of the war, making it too costly and burdensome to continue. In the coming weeks, we hope that you and your team at USUN will consider incorporating these solutions into any forthcoming resolution to provide for the continuation and possible expansion of the Sudan sanctions measures.

Thank you for your consideration.

World.title: Africa: The Continent Has the Capital - It Needs the Alignment.
World.content:
Africa's industrial moment is not waiting for more money. It is waiting for the right kind — structured correctly, sequenced intelligently, and aimed at the right stage of a project's life. Afreximbank's Oluranti Doherty on why the continent's financing problem is really a coordination problem.

Why this series exists

Our new editorial initiative seeks to unearth an answer to a question that most development institutions have debated but few have answered: why does a continent that grows the world's finest cotton wear clothes made somewhere else — and what would it actually take to change that?

The answer is not, as it is so often presented, a story about roads or ports or missing technology. For centuries, the processing of Africa's raw materials into finished goods happened elsewhere by design — and the wealth that process generated remained elsewhere by consequence. That is the inheritance this generation of African industrialists, financiers, and policymakers is trying to overturn. Our programme is the journalistic record of whether they are succeeding.

The initiative is built on a straightforward premise. Africa's industrial potential is not poorly understood because the facts are unavailable. It is poorly understood because the right stories are not being told, to the right audiences, in the right register. A $40 million commodity export that could be an $800 million manufacturing industry is not, primarily, a financing problem. It is a narrative problem — and a narrative problem is one that journalism, data, and sustained institutional distribution can address.

The programme is anchored in cotton and textiles because the value chain is visible, traceable, and human — from the smallholder farmer harvesting seed cotton by hand to the factory floor where garments leave for European retailers. But it is not, ultimately, a story about cotton. It is a story about whether Africa can manufacture, add value, and compete globally — and what the continent's own financial institutions, entrepreneurs, and policymakers are doing to make that happen.

We distribute our journalism through the institutional wire network that reaches the fund managers, analysts, trade ministers, and development finance executives who price African risk every day. The argument is simple: the story Africa tells about itself is not the story its industrial performance warrants.

To begin that work, our editorial team sat with Ms. Oluranti Doherty — Managing Director for Export Development at Afreximbank — to understand what two decades inside the actual mechanics of African industrial finance looks like from the inside. The conversation ranged from the mathematics of a cotton boll to the architecture of a $70 billion African capital coalition, from the five-year ramp-up period of a new factory to the $4.2 billion annual cost of a bad story.

The math behind the optimism

The numbers, when she lays them out, are startling less for the size of the loss than for the size of the opportunity still sitting on the table. Raw Beninese cotton, from farm to port, sells for $1,500 to $2,000 a metric tonne. Transformed into garments, the same fibre is worth $16,000 to $20,000 a tonne — a value increase of ten to fifteen times. Scale that across 40,000 tonnes of annual production, and a $40 million commodity export becomes an $800 million manufacturing industry.

"Africa produces and exports cotton lint," Doherty says, "but much of the value generated in the cotton, textile and garment value chain occurs through spinning, weaving, dyeing, finishing, garment manufacturing, branding and retailing" — steps that have historically happened somewhere else. Benin's industrial zone, known as Glo-Djigbé, was built specifically to bring those steps home.

« What we need to prove more is that it can be replicated programmatically in every cotton-producing country. »

Not as a copy-paste template, she is careful to say, but adapted to the politics, infrastructure and ambitions of each place that tries it.

A different theory of the challenge

For years, the general explanation for why more African countries haven't replicated that success has been simple: not enough financing. Doherty, whose job is quite literally to arrange that financing, disagrees. And her disagreement is, oddly enough, the most encouraging line in the whole conversation, because it points to a solvable problem rather than an intractable one.

"It is relevant," she says of financing, "but what you need is a combination of financing solutions" tailored to each stage of a project's life — patient equity for the earliest, riskiest years; long-term project debt once a factory is built; working capital structured around the actual rhythm of the business, whether that trade cycle runs 60 days or 360. The failures she has seen tend to come from mismatches — a seven-year project financed with three-year money — rather than from an absence of capital altogether.

Afreximbank The value at stake in AfricaÂs cotton-to-cloth chain, summarised in four key figures

« Having financiers who can understand that this is the reality of industrial and manufacturing projects is very important — and increasingly, I believe, they do. »

That is a fixable problem, and Afreximbank has spent the past several years building the tools to fix it: a dedicated project-preparation facility to help entrepreneurs get their first plans investment-ready, and FEDA, a Rwanda-based equity fund built specifically to supply the patient capital that traditional lending cannot.

Closing the coordination gap

When Doherty steps back from individual transactions to describe the larger architecture of African industrial finance, her diagnosis shifts from frustration to something closer to strategic clarity. The continent does not lack capital. It does not lack viable projects. What it has lacked — until recently — is the mechanism for connecting the two.

« Africa has capital. Africa has viable projects. What has been missing is not resources — but alignment »

"Africa has development institutions, commercial banks, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds," Doherty says. What has been missing is a problem she calls "systemic fragmentation," in which capable institutions work in silos rather than in partnership.

The Alliance for African Multilateral Financial Institutions (AAMFI), a coalition Afreximbank helped launch, has brought together African-owned lenders with a combined balance sheet of $70 billion — capital that can now move behind large industrial projects in a coordinated way rather than depending on any single institution to shoulder a deal alone.

Rewriting the risk premium

Researchers have estimated that negative media narratives about the continent add up to $4.2 billion a year in inflated sovereign borrowing costs; Doherty believes the true figure, once corporate financing is included, is considerably higher.

« We are not asking for favorable risk assessment as Africans. We are simply requesting an accurate one. »

An accurate assessment, she argues, is one that weighs a young, fast-urbanising, increasingly educated population and proven projects like Glo-Djigbé alongside the risks that any market carries, rather than pricing an entire continent off a single, outdated story.

"I would like the fund manager to look at projects such as the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone as evidence that African cotton can be processed sustainably in Africa into exportable garments at industrial scale," she said — proof that the story is already changing, one factory at a time.

A continent coming into alignment

The continent's most ambitious trade project, the African Continental Free Trade Area, drew a hopeful assessment. Its architecture, Doherty said, is "directionally aligned" with what a West African textile manufacturer needs — tariff schedules, rules of origin, and Afreximbank's own cross-border payment system, PAPSS, are all pointed the right way.

The destination she describes is a striking one — cotton grown in one African country, spun and woven in a second, sold in a third, with predictable rules and frictionless payments throughout. It does not yet exist at scale. But in this conversation, it did not feel like aspiration. It felt like a schedule.

Benin's twenty thousand new jobs, its rising share of processed cotton, its garments now hanging in European stores — these are not yet the full story of African industrialisation. But they are, Doherty insists, the proof that the story is real, that it is replicable, and that the only question that remains is speed.

About Ms. Oluranti Doherty

Ms. Oluranti Doherty is Managing Director for Export Development at Afreximbank, where she oversees export financing across manufacturing, agro-processing, extractives, and industrial parks and special economic zones. She brings more than twenty years in project finance, credit analysis and industrial policy advisory. Recent transactions include a $1 billion project-preparation facility with Shelter Afrique and a $15 million SME finance facility for Zimbabwean export value chains. She is a Fellow of ICAN, and studied at IMD Lausanne, the University of Leicester and Olabisi Onabanjo University.

World.title: Rome ramps up security around Colosseum with new ‘red zone’ targeting criminals
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Rome has declared a "red zone" around the Colosseum after predatory crime, drug dealing and a violent confrontation involving roughly 50 people turned one of the world’s most famous tourist destinations into a security flashpoint.

The "enhanced-control zone" covers the Colosseum, Imperial Forums and Colle Oppio and allows authorities to remove certain people whose violent, threatening or persistently disruptive behavior creates a public safety risk, according to a six-page order issued by Rome Prefect Lamberto Giannini.

The measure took effect Aug. 24 and will remain in place for four months, through Christmas Eve.

FIREWORKS REPORTEDLY TRIGGER MASS HORSE STAMPEDE THROUGH ROME STREETS, INJURING SEVERAL SOLDIERS

Officials said the area has experienced a "resurgence of disorder" that was "predominantly attributable to groups of young people of non-EU origin," according to the order.

The document cited predatory crimes, fights and fireworks near the ancient amphitheater, warning that the explosives may have been used to distract potential crime victims.

Officials said the trouble reached a breaking point July 1, when Rome Capital police officers responded after fireworks were set off near the Colosseum. A group of approximately 50 non-EU nationals allegedly resisted responding officers and damaged police property, according to the order.

The group surrounded local police officers and left two with minor injuries during what news agency ANSA described as an unauthorized gathering in Piazza del Colosseo.

Authorities also singled out Largo Gaetana Agnesi, a terrace overlooking the Colosseum and situated above the Colosseo subway station, as a regular gathering place for the groups at the center of the security concerns.

The nearby Colle Oppio park was also described as a problem area because of people officials said may be engaged in conduct harmful to public safety and public order.

SEATTLE MAYOR ANNOUNCES CRACKDOWN ON CRIME-PLAGUED NEIGHBORHOOD AFTER YEARS OF COMPLAINTS

The newly designated zone stretches through some of the most recognizable areas of central Rome, including Piazza Venezia, Via dei Fori Imperiali, Piazza del Colosseo, the Arch of Constantine and Piazza del Campidoglio.

Giannini issued the order following a proposal from Rome’s police chief and discussions by the Provincial Committee for Public Order and Security.

The order says the opening of the Metro C station serving the Colosseum has also contributed to the security challenges by creating a direct connection between the historic center and neighborhoods in eastern Rome.

The station and another subway stop inside the designated area draw large numbers of commuters and tourists who could be exposed to criminal activity, officials said.

TOURIST HOT SPOT SLAPPED WITH US TRAVEL WARNING RENEWAL DUE TO CRIME AND TERROR

Under the order, authorities may remove people who engage in violent, threatening or persistently disruptive behavior and who were reported during the previous five years for specified offenses. Those include intentional crimes against people or property, certain drug offenses, weapons violations and crimes carrying a particular hate-crime aggravating circumstance.

The order is part of a broader push to protect residents and a flood of tourists visiting the Italian capital. Officials described Rome as facing an unusually complex security situation because of major international and historic events, the heightened geopolitical threat environment and the continuing influx of visitors.

AMERICAN TOURISTS STABBED OUTSIDE ATHENS' ACROPOLIS AS POLICE DETAIN SUSPECT IN APPARENT RANDOM ATTACK

Authorities said ordinary patrols, surveillance systems, fixed security posts and joint "High Impact" operations had produced results but had not stopped repeated criminal conduct or fully restored public spaces to residents and visitors.

Officials also extended a separate security zone in Esquilino, covering streets around Rome’s main Termini train station and the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore.

ITALY SHUTS DOWN EFFORT LINKED TO GAZA FLOTILLA GROUP TO TRACK JEWISH, ISRAELI TOURISTS

Officials said demonstrations around Termini continue to require close attention. They also cited the increased number of visitors and pilgrims traveling to Santa Maria Maggiore, where Pope Francis is buried, warning that large crowds can become targets for predatory crimes.

An earlier enhanced-control designation covering the Valle Aurelia area, including the Battistini and Cornelia subway stations, was discontinued after authorities determined that continuing the special measures there was no longer useful.

World.title: MLB tells umpire Doug Eddings he made a mistake in demanding Cardinals pitcher straighten his hat
World.content:
It's not often you see Major League Baseball criticize umpires or an individual umpire, as the league office prefers to downplay any mistakes or poor calls. But what veteran umpire Doug Eddings did on Friday during the Colorado Rockies-St. Louis Cardinals game apparently warranted such unusual treatment.

Eddings inserted himself into the game, apparently believing that fans buy tickets to see umpires, when Cardinals rookie reliever Hancel Rincon entered the game to make his major league debut. Rincon had his had tilted to the side, obviously not the traditional way to wear a baseball hat, but hardly anything exception or unusual in the modern game. Bizarrely, though, Eddings felt it necessary to instruct him to fix it.

Cardinals manager Oli Marmol was unsurprisingly furious, rushing out to defend the 24-year-old pitcher. Marmol could be seen telling Edings to "grow the f*** up" before getting tossed from the game, then went off about Eddings behavior afterward.

HOT MIC CATCHES HEATED ARGUMENT BETWEEN MLB MANAGER AND UMPIRE AFTER CONTROVERSIAL EJECTION

"I had an issue with Doug," he said to the media after the game. "Just Doug. He took it upon himself to tell our rookie pitcher the kid’s ‘not going to wear his hat on my field that way.’ You got Dontrelle Willis, CC Sabathia, Pedro Strop -- plenty of guys that have worn it way more tilted. I have an issue with that. That’s just a power-hungry move, in my opinion."

Eddings then defended himself by telling reporters that he'd made the decision to step in after a hitter from the Rockies complained about the hat.

"The batter said, ‘Hey, can he wear his hat like that?’" he explained after the game. "I really didn't know, but it was really, really crooked. I asked the catcher to tell him to straighten his hat out, and the pitcher did. Nobody said anything until he gave up a couple runs."

Except only one Colorado player had been up to the plate when the warning was issued, Hunter Goodman, who promptly denied he'd said anything.

"I never once mentioned the hat," Goodman told reporters. "It doesn’t matter who’s pitching. I don’t care how they wear the hat. I’m trying to find out where the ball is coming out, and I’m trying to worry about what I’m doing in the box. I’m not worried about how his hat looks.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

"It was one of those situations — it’s kind of a wild, wild thing that happens in the game. But I didn’t like seeing that my name was a part of it today when I didn’t say anything like that. You watch baseball growing up. There are a lot of guys who have had their hat crooked or however. Honestly, before today, when I went back and looked, I didn’t even notice the hat was messed up or looked like that when I was hitting. Anyway, I don’t pay attention to that stuff."

From Rincon's perspective, he addressed it by saying that Eddings had "apologized" to him and that he'd put the incident behind him.

CINCINNATI REDS PITCHER RIPS 'F—ING FATA–' UMPIRE FOR GETTING IN DEFENDER'S WAY ON GROUND BALL

"I understood a couple words and it looked like he apologized to me for what happened last night, and he also told me good luck the rest of my career as a big leaguer," Rincon said. "I told him don't worry, it's nothing personal, and everything stays here."

Still, in a very obvious gesture, many Cardinals players wore their hats purposefully tilted in the dugout before Saturday's game, and seemingly added a celebratory helmet tilt when reaching base.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

On Sunday, the Athletic reported that MLB had formally spoken to Eddings and told the veteran umpire he'd gone too far by telling Rincon to fix his hat.

Ken Rosenthal spoke to sources within the league about the incident, writing, "Umpires operate with broad discretion if they believe a player's actions are distracting, but according to two people briefed on the matter who were granted anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly, the league viewed Eddings' admonishment of Rincon as going too far."

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Frankly, it did go too far. Wearing a hat tilted a bit one way or another isn't an offense, and as Marmol brought up, it's hardly unprecedented. Is it every baseball fan's preferred way for a professional to wear a hat? No, of course not. But it isn't the type of infraction that warranted Edding's reaction.

Maybe Eddings thought he heard someone from the Rockies complain about the hat and took it upon himself to say something? Or maybe he thought it was some sort of violation then had to backtrack afterward?

Regardless, Rincon pitched again Saturday, with his hat tilted to his liking. Eddings, still part of the umpiring crew over the weekend, let it go.

World.title: Socialism 2026 speaker slams diet industry for policing 'Black fat flesh,' calls it 'body fascism'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An activist at the Socialism 2026 conference in Chicago slammed the "diet industry" for policing "Black fat flesh," characterizing modern health standards and weight management as forms of "body fascism".

During a session on "Health Fascism" on Saturday, author Da’Shaun L. Harrison said that the policing of "Black fat flesh" is foundational to broader "entire systems of governance."

"Black fatness is made meaningful through suffering, through surveillance, and through control and the policing of Black fat flesh anchors entire systems of governance. Without a population to discipline, there would be no BMI, no obesity epidemic, and no medical or scientific institutions organized around managing fatness," Harrison said.

"The diet industry reflects this logic. It operates through what I once defined as formal and informal relationships among major food corporations, the medical-industrial complex, and individual wealthy benefactors to sustain a social order in which fat people are monitored, restricted, guilted, stolen from, and punished. Diet culture has always linked food to morality, framing restraint as virtue and pleasure as danger through language like 'guilty pleasure,'" Harrison said.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ERUPT OVER 2028 ENDORSEMENT AS AOC SPECULATION GROWS: 'DANGEROUS PATH'

The four-day Socialism 2026 conference, held at the Hyatt Regency McCormick Place and organized by Haymarket Books, brought together activists, organizers, and communities from across the country and around the world, featuring over a hundred participatory discussions, lectures, and workshops, according to the event's website.

Harrison was one of three panelists — alongside podcast co-hosts Beatrice Adler-Bolton and Artie Vierkant—who spoke during a session titled "Health Fascism, Body Politics, and the Anti-State State". Over 200 people attended the discussion, which formed part of the conference's broader "Health Fascism" series. Clips of the conference were shared on X by Manhattan Institute investigative analyst Stu Smith.

"As governments retreat from care, and health increasingly becomes a signifier of discipline—rather than provision—fitness, disability, fatness, illness, Blackness, impairment, and bodily capacity are mobilized into measures of moral worth and political belonging. This panel examines how health, disability, body size, and race are instrumentalized by the state and being reorganized under health fascism," according to an event description.

In the session, Harrison argued that diet culture conditions "obedience," "self-denial," and "discipline" before framing those concepts as central components of "body fascism."

JILLIAN MICHAELS EXPOSES DANGERS OF SELF-DOSING ILLEGAL 'GRAY MARKET' WEIGHT LOSS DRUGS

"Abstaining from pleasure becomes a way to train obedience, to train self-denial, and to train discipline in service of a broader political order. Body fascism is not some relic of the past. It's an active feature of modern imperial regimes," Harrison explained.

Harrison also criticized GLP-1 weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, contending that efforts to treat fatness as a public-health issue are intrinsically connected to racial control.

"Every time a government decides whose body must be protected and whose bodies must be erased for the sake of national imagery, this is body fascism. Every time there is a call for sovereignty by state powers with the intent to maintain borders, this is body fascism. Every time Black flesh is wrangled, dismembered, abused, this is body fascism. Understanding this clarifies exactly how fascist ideologies operate through the body, not only by glorifying a narrow ideal, but also by violently repressing the Black fat," Harrison added.

Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist and author of "Therapy Nation," told Fox News Digital that Harrison's comments are a byproduct of ideology infiltrating everything.

"There are fair criticisms of BMI and how it’s used. But calling it ‘body fascism’ is what happens when ideology gets inserted into almost every part of life," Alpert said.

"We’re seeing more and more ordinary issues viewed through the same lens: Who has power? Who’s oppressed? How does race factor into it? Now even a conversation with your doctor about weight or diet can be framed as a form of oppression," he added.

"That fits neatly into the worldview being promoted at a conference like this. Instead of seeing people primarily as individuals who make choices and have some responsibility for their lives, everything gets explained through systems, identity and power," Alpert said.

"Socialism may be an economic philosophy, but the culture surrounding this version of it goes much further. Personal problems become political problems, and individual responsibility gets pushed aside in favor of identifying the system or group supposedly responsible," he explained further.

"As a psychotherapist, I think there’s a psychological cost to that. If you teach people to interpret uncomfortable information as an attack, they become less willing to hear things they may need to hear. Sometimes a doctor telling you that you need to lose weight or change your diet isn’t racism, oppression or an attempt to control your body. It’s medical advice," Alpert added.

Harrison and representatives for the Socialism 2026 panel did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s requests for comment.

TRUMP’S PENTAGON SHAKE-UP REVIVES A PRESIDENTIAL POWER PLAY WITH A LONG HISTORY

World.title: Kansas State Wildcats' mascot forced to complete absurd amount of push-ups during 71-3 victory

If you were one of the lucky ones to see your college football team score more than 70 points this weekend - and judging by the offenses we saw on Saturday, that likely isn't many of you - then you're probably feeling pretty good right now.

World.title: Group of fans kicked out of Portland Thorns NWSL match over pro-women apparel labeled 'transphobic'
World.content:
A group of eight people was confronted at their seats and ejected from a Portland Thorns match at Providence Park after stadium security flagged their pro-women apparel.

Footage obtained by OutKick shows Amy E. Sousa attempting to speak with a venue staff member for about a minute as the group sat in their assigned seats for the NWSL match against the Washington Spirit.

Attendees were wearing gear from XX-XY Athletics alongside shirts bearing slogans such as "Save Women's Sports," "Girls just wanna have fundamental rights," "Woman," and "It's common sense."

WNBA ADMITS SECURITY IN ATLANTA WAS WRONG TO MAKE FANS COVER SHIRTS AT DREAM-FEVER GAME

In the video, venue staff hand the group a card notifying them of an infraction of the Providence Park and NWSL Code of Conduct before escorting them out of the building.

The notice gave venue staff 72 hours to contact the group about additional penalties. It also warned that refusing to provide personal information on the spot could lead to a ban from all future events at the stadium.

Sousa later told OutKick that she was accused of being transphobic.

ADF SENDS LETTER TO WNBA AFTER CONTROVERSIES OVER TREATMENT OF SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SUPPORTERS

Following the ejection, Sousa took to social media to push back against any claim that the group caused a disturbance inside the venue before security stepped in.

"We did nothing. We had not even shown our shirts. We were dressed like this when ejected," Sousa posted on X in response to the incident.

WNBA FANS RECALL EJECTION THREAT OVER XX-XY ATHLETICS SHIRT AT FEVER-DREAM GAME: 'I WAS FLABBERGASTED'

The episode at Providence Park, which is owned by the City of Portland but operated by a private company, raises questions about how speech rules are enforced at a publicly owned stadium.

Fans face a core question: Who polices game-day gear, and when does safety cross into overreach? The incident also highlights a contrast in how Portland’s sports teams handle fan attire.

Sousa previously attended a WNBA game at the Moda Center between the Portland Fire and Indiana Fever wearing her XX-XY Athletics shirt. She was even featured on the arena’s massive jumbotron during the live broadcast, while the Thorns later booted Sousa and the other fans from Providence Park for wearing similar pro-women apparel.

"I didn't take it seriously," Sousa said regarding online warnings she received before Sunday's match. "I was like, what are they going to do? Arrest us for watching soccer?"

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SHARES TOUCHING MOMENT WITH YOUNG FEVER FAN AFTER GAME AGAINST PORTLAND

The security response at Providence Park followed public social media posts from a local LGBT group organizer, Hannah Perry, who lobbied municipal and state officials to intervene at the city-owned stadium.

Ahead of game time, Perry fired off a Facebook message to Sousa letting him know she’d already put the Portland PD, the mayor and Gov. Tina Kotek on notice.

Perry added that she was contacting Providence Park directly, alongside local organizations, to demand the group be removed. She called Sousa a "pathetic excuse of a human being" and wrote, "I hope that you're not allowed into the stadium."

Under the NWSL Fan Code of Conduct, spectators are prohibited from displaying signs, symbols, words or imagery used for political campaigning or advocacy. However, neither the league nor venue rules provide an objective standard for what turns basic slogan apparel into banned political expression, leaving enforcement largely to staff discretion.

Requests for comment sent to Providence Park venue management, Portland Thorns and NWSL league headquarters were not immediately returned.
