World.title: Perfect Day Mexico wasn’t dead after all. Now its opponents are headed to the Supreme Court
World.content:
Perhaps someone should have driven a stake through its heart.

Royal Caribbean’s Perfect Day Mexico was widely believed dead in May, when Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena announced that the massive water park planned for Mahahual, Quintana Roo, would not be approved.

But the massive, US $1 billion extreme water park proposal wasn’t buried after all. Royal Caribbean withdrew its environmental application before authorities could formally reject it, leaving the cruise giant free to return with a revised proposal.

Now the residents’ battle has reached Mexico’s Supreme Court, which on Aug. 10 agreed to hear three challenges to fast-tracked land-use changes that helped make Perfect Day possible.

The stakes reach well beyond the fate of a water park. The fight involves development alongside the Mesoamerican Reef, the world’s second-largest barrier reef system; a national campaign that drew more than 5 million petition signatures; and now a potentially precedent-setting question: How much opportunity must Mexican citizens be given to challenge development decisions that could permanently alter the places where they live?

A reef transformed

When Luis Fernando Amezcua first began diving off Mahahual nearly three decades ago, he remembers a very different Caribbean: water about 5 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit cooler, with coral reefs alive with color and an extraordinary variety of marine life.

The reef is still remarkable. A first-time visitor could easily be dazzled by its diversity. But to Amezcua, the losses are impossible to miss.

If he could take a visitor anywhere in Mahahual, he said, he would dive with them directly in front of town. Then he would show them photographs of that same reef 20 years ago, and let the contrast speak for itself.

Mahahual’s problems don’t stop at the shoreline. Amezcua says the wastewater system is already overwhelmed in a town of roughly 3,000 residents, where a single cruise ship can arrive with 6,000 passengers — and as many as four ships may call in a day.

And on the Yucatán Peninsula’s porous limestone, what happens on land doesn’t necessarily stay there. Contaminated water can quickly move through the underground aquifer toward the sea, adding another source of stress to an already vulnerable reef.

For Amezcua, who has lived in Mahahual for about 17 years and belongs to the citizens’ collective Salvemos Mahahual, the issue isn’t whether the town should develop. It’s what kind of development — and how much the ecosystem can withstand.

From four stories to 20

Accommodating the company required changing the rules.

In December 2025, the municipality of Othón P. Blanco approved changes to the urban development plan covering 107.67 hectares — roughly 200 football fields — in less than three weeks, a process attorney Irma Morales says normally takes eight months to a year.

Among the changes: The maximum permitted height on part of the property jumped from roughly four stories to about 20 — just what Royal Caribbean needed for the record-breaking water park it was proposing. The company had touted Jaguar’s Peak, at more than 170 feet tall, as the tallest waterslide tower in North and South America.

Morales, an attorney with Defendiendo el Derecho a un Medio Ambiente Sano (DMAS), said the changes were approved without the studies and public participation required by law.

Residents challenged them in federal court.

Their cases never got as far as the environmental questions. They were dismissed because judges found that residents had filed them too late — in one case applying a 15-day deadline for citizens to respond.

But Morales said the residents hadn’t even known the land-use plan had been changed while that clock was running.

Environmental justice and the rights of communities

That dispute has now landed Mahahual before the Supreme Court. At stake is a broader question of environmental justice: How meaningful is the right to challenge decisions capable of transforming a community and its environment if residents have only weeks to discover those decisions, understand their implications and get into court?

The justices are not deciding whether Royal Caribbean can build Perfect Day. But their ruling could establish new ground rules for when and how communities across Mexico can challenge land-use decisions with potentially irreversible environmental consequences.

That could affect communities fighting tourism, real estate and industrial projects far beyond Mahahual.

How a local fight went national

Long before the federal government intervened, Mahahual’s fight had become a national cause. Local residents had been organizing for months when Greenpeace Mexico and other national organizations joined.

The response surprised even veteran campaigners. A Greenpeace petition opposing Perfect Day ultimately drew 846,646 signatures. High-profile Mexican content creators, including film critic Javier Ibarreche and travel creator Alan Estrada, spoke out against the project, while Mexican BTS and Taylor Swift fan networks mobilized their formidable social media reach behind the cause.

For Ornela Garelli, campaigns director for Greenpeace Mexico, Mahahual tapped into a wider backlash against tourism, real estate and industrial megaprojects that communities say threaten ecosystems while giving residents too little voice over what happens to their territory.

Perfect Day became a particularly potent symbol: an enormous artificial attraction proposed beside one of the planet’s great natural ones.

The project anticipated as many as 21,000 visitors a day — seven times Mahahual’s resident population — while a Greenpeace analysis warned of impacts to vegetation, groundwater and biodiversity.

The campaign appeared to work.

The victory that wasn’t

In May, Bárcena announced that Perfect Day would not be approved. Semarnat requested additional information from Royal Caribbean, later saying the company failed to show how significant environmental impacts would be avoided.

On May 19, before Semarnat issued a final ruling on the main Perfect Day application, Royal Caribbean withdrew it. Morales says developers sometimes withdraw applications facing likely rejection to avoid a formal denial, allowing them to return later with another proposal.

Amezcua and his fellow activists understood immediately what that meant.

Asked whether Salvemos Mahahual believed in May that the fight was finally over, his answer was emphatic: “Not for a moment.”

Royal Caribbean, meanwhile, has made clear it is not walking away from Mahahual. On a July 28 earnings call, CEO Jason Liberty told investors the company was continuing to work “to develop a tourism destination” there, saying negotiations with government and community stakeholders would “affect our previously planned timeline.”

That is precisely what worries Amezcua: that attention will fade before Perfect Day returns in another form.

After nearly three decades watching Mahahual’s reef change, his message is simple: “Everything we do has consequences for the ecosystem we inhabit.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: What would a move from CONCACAF to CONMEBOL mean for Mexican soccer?
World.content:
Following arguably Mexico’s best World Cup finish since 1986, rumors have circulated online about El Tri potentially moving from its throne in CONCACAF to the much tougher South American confederation known as CONMEBOL. With FIFA’s presidential election coming up on March 18, 2027, rumors have swirled around current FIFA president Gianni Infantino granting the Mexican Football Federation’s ambition to switch over to CONMEBOL and host Club World Cup tournaments in exchange for its vote.

Historically, Mexico has dominated in CONCACAF, with its biggest rival being the United States in World Cup qualifiers, Gold Cup matchups and even friendlies. The occasional scare from countries like Costa Rica, Honduras and most recently, Canada, has threatened Mexico’s throne at the top. But it never fell lower than the third-best team in the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football.

The reality of a move to CONMEBOL

That narrative changes if Mexico switches over to CONMEBOL, where it would have to win or tie enough games against nations like Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, Chile and Uruguay to even think about qualifying for future World Cups.

It’s also worth noting that Liga MX teams would be eligible to play in the Copa Libertadores, which is the South American version of Europe’s Champions League, creating opportunities for Mexican pro teams to compete against the best of Latin America every season.

Even though it may be a daunting task for some fans, Mexico’s stellar performance in the 2026 World Cup gives lifelong fans like myself hope. El Tri won all of its group-stage games for the first time without conceding a single goal. Then, it won a knockout-phase game for the first time in 40 years. Then, it took eventual third-place finisher England down to the wire in a 3-2 loss at the historic Estadio Azteca in the round of 16.

A great mix of emerging talent like Julián Quiñones and young players like Gilberto Mora gives fans reason to be excited for the future if Mexico actually switches over to CONMEBOL.

New and greater challenges

There’s an old saying in sports: If you want to be the best, you need to beat the best. And if Mexico ever hopes to build off its momentum from the last World Cup, playing against quality footballing nations will benefit the squad.

Brazil has won the World Cup five times and has plenty of top players in Europe, including Vinicius Junior, Raphinha and Alisson Becker. Argentina has Lionel Messi and back-to-back World Cup finishes where it either won or finished runner-up. Colombia and Uruguay are also teams not to be taken lightly. But the good news is this will force players like Brian Gutierrez, Gilberto Mora, Mateo Chavez and Raul “Tala” Rangel to level up their games. All of them had their moments in the last World Cup, and that momentum needs to continue.

Being part of CONMEBOL also means playing in the Copa America, a tournament that will be Mexico’s next big test, whether it makes the switch or is simply invited to compete in 2028. A solid finish would strengthen Mexico’s position as an improving footballing nation capable of making deep runs among the elite.

Revival of old-school rivalries

Despite Brazil’s accolades on the global stage, Mexico has proven to be a worthy opponent over the years. In the 1999 Confederations Cup final, Mexico prevailed over Brazil 4-3 in front of 110,000 fans in Estadio Azteca. Mexico also upset Brazil in the 2012 Summer Olympics in London, beating a prime Brazilian squad 2-1 that included players like Neymar, Thiago Silva and Marcelo.

Mexico and Colombia also go way back, having played against each other in the 2001 Copa America final. The Mexican national team also has Colombian influence via Julián Quiñones, a Colombian-Mexican striker who was Mexico’s leading goalscorer in the last World Cup with four goals in five matches. It’s also worth noting Colombia was set to be the original host of the 1986 World Cup, but withdrew due to overwhelming stadium demands from FIFA — leading Mexico to step in its place, hosting what is now considered one of the greatest World Cups of all time.

The parallels between Mexico and many South American countries are endless, which can strengthen rivalries if El Tri ends up switching over to CONMEBOL. Looking at the drama leading up to Mexico’s 2-0 win over Ecuador in the round of 32, new rivalries may also be in the works.

Great economic opportunities

Though watching Mexico face off against the U.S. is always a treat, there isn’t much else for Mexican fans to look forward to between World Cups. It’s no secret that the Mexican Football Federation loves hosting friendlies with its American neighbors in cities like Los Angeles and Houston due to economic opportunities, but other nations within CONCACAF don’t present the same level of excitement.

Playing in CONMEBOL will change that and add more variety to El Tri’s calendar. Regular matches against Brazil, Argentina and Colombia will also attract South American fans — millions of people ready to pay top dollar to watch their respective national teams.

Not only can Mexico continue to play against the United States in friendlies, but it can also strategically host games in American cities with large Brazilian, Argentinian and other South American populations.

Would you rather see Mexico vs. a tiny island in a Gold Cup group-stage match or against Uruguay in a World Cup qualifier? Regular matchups against steep competition will not only make Mexican players better, but will also create buzz and excitement that won’t fade after a World Cup ends.

Do you think Mexico can thrive in CONMEBOL?

Like most rumors, the idea of Mexico switching over to CONMEBOL probably won’t materialize unless real action takes place. But if you want a taste of how well Mexico’s current national team could stack up against South American competition, three of its next four games are against Colombia, Peru and Chile.

So, do you think Mexico is good enough to compete against South America’s best? Let us know in the comments below.

Ian Ostroff is an indie author, journalist and copywriter from Montreal, Canada. You can find his work in various outlets, including Map Happy and The Suburban. When he’s not writing, you can find Ian at the gym, a café or anywhere within Mexico visiting family and friends.

World.title: From the archive: To friend or not to friend other expats in Mexico?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — is a humorous look at the often thorny issue of friendships among expats.

Any foreigners who’ve been in Mexico for more than two minutes know this truth: expat relationships are complicated.

I read with interest Louisa Rogers’ article on expat relationships, and found myself nodding along to much of it. Feeling threatened by large numbers of new foreigners moving to my area? Check! Hyper awareness of my ratio of Mexican-to-foreign-born friends? Check! Complaining about “those other gringos” who are messing up some designated “elsewhere”? Oh my goodness, please don’t make me look in the mirror.

Friends unless proven otherwise

My policy these days is to keep a very light grip on everything from my friendships to my own ideological musings. I pre-like everyone now, purposefully rather than by default. I haven’t met you, but I am sure you are a friend, until and unless you prove otherwise.

And I would really appreciate it if you wouldn’t prove otherwise.

But this attitude was hard-won, not discovered in a sudden stroke of coolness. It’s been over 20 years — uh-oh, am I bragging? — and it’s taken a long time to make peace with my identity both as an individual and as part of the greater foreigner-in-Mexico population. I don’t know if it’s my time here or just my age. Maybe it was a really good mushroom trip. But I just refuse to get worked up: if you want to be friends, we’re friends. I’ll try to help you if you need help. If you don’t like me, then, oh well. I guess we’re not friends.

The comment section of this humor piece I wrote made the “not friends” column abundantly clear; self-sorting, even.

And it got me thinking: is online communication among us all helping or hurting? After all, no one would be as nasty to people’s faces as we might be online. Online, we’re anonymous; we could be anyone; and we can’t get punched in the face for being rude as hell.

A polarized society, at home and abroad

Perhaps it’s a reflection as well of the general polarity we find in the United States. I’m certainly not immune from self-sorting, of course: finding common ground with friends who are openly enthusiastic about a felon president is not always easy. In any case, everyone has strong opinions either way.

Yes, we foreigners are a varied bunch, each of us as unique as a snowflake. Complicating matters is the fact that the average U.S. or Canadian citizen is not someone who would voluntarily move to Mexico. Right off the bat, then, you’re dealing with someone whose type you might not be too familiar with.

Overall, the most even-keeled people I’ve met have been retirees, though this isn’t a hard and fast rule. You can be a weirdo at any age!

People closer to my own age are a bit of a mixed bag, though, and I’ve had a few relationships with other paisanos end abruptly at this point. This has only happened once with a Mexican friend, a neighbor who blocked me after I friended her husband, who I thought was also my friend, on Facebook. Given the demographics, I’d say the number of times it’s happened with those from my own culture makes it conspicuously likely.

Abrupt endings to friendships

The first cut off was by a couple from the U.S. who wanted help translating and getting paperwork done upon arrival. We’d had some great conversations online beforehand, but in real life, our chemistry was pretty tense and weird. No matter; they were paying me for my help, and I was going to do whatever I could to make it worth it. Mostly, it was fine.

But then there was a misunderstanding about what exactly was being charged, and I suddenly found myself buried under some very intense, urgent messages. I gifted them some extra live interpretation time as a sign of goodwill and thought we were fine. Later, though, when I wanted to send a message to see how their house hunting had gone, I realized I’d been blocked on WhatsApp and Facebook.

Since then, I’ve found I’m not the only person to have received that treatment. A clear picture of kookiness has emerged, so I guess it’s not just me. The experience did convince me, however, that I definitely did not want to make a career of helping people settle down here.

Another cut-off came from someone who’d been a friend and mentor to me for over 20 years. That one was completely unexpected, and it hurt. I’d excused myself from what I saw as a minor favor, an action which my friend apparently interpreted as a sign of deep disrespect. I was oblivious that he was upset with me, and only learned that he was months later from another friend. By the time I wrote him to apologize, that was it. I never heard from him again.

The last incident was quite recent, with a friend of three years. I thought we were really close, but when I unwisely hounded her about getting her dog fixed so it wouldn’t get all the dogs in the neighborhood pregnant, that was it, too. I was asked to leave her house immediately, even though home was over three hours away.

Keeping an open mind on other expats

What is with these gringos and abruptly cutting people off? Mexicans may have a reputation for being dramatic, but my relationships with them have gone through rocky patches and come out just fine. Only my own paisanos have been so mad that they banished me from their lives. Is it something about North Americans, or is it just something about North Americans who live in Mexico? I will probably never know.

But I have not sworn off other U.S. Americans. Currently, we have a small breakfast group of foreigners in Xalapa that meets once a month. We share a nice meal and chat. We wouldn’t all necessarily be best friends were we in the U.S.

But this is different. When you’re in a foreign country without family, it’s nice to know people who know your culture and language on a native level. Real friendships, I still believe and have proven, are possible.

But for people who I know will definitely still be my friend even if I berate them about their unsterilized pets, I’m sticking with Mexicans.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, https://sarahedevries.substack.com/

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum delivers her second-year report as trade tensions simmer
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 31, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report, reflecting on the state of the nation as her second year in office draws to a close. She touted falling homicides and a stable economy, only to face a pointed rebuttal from opposition leaders who accused her administration of manipulating crime statistics and shielding officials tied to drug trafficking.

Mexico continues to grapple with security challenges on a variety of fronts, a fact underscored by a car bomb in Zacatecas Sunday night — the state’s third such attack in four days. But Mexico’s security forces remain active and on Monday claimed a high-profile target: Soldiers and marines killed Luis Enrique Barragán, alias “R5,” the accused leader of extortion against Michoacán’s avocado growers, in a shootout in Tocumbo.

Trade friction with Washington ran through much of the week. A dispute over cheese naming rights is complicating already-strained talks over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Mexico continues to push back against the threat of U.S. tariffs, and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 gathering Wednesday to press Mexico’s case against tariffs on steel, aluminum and cars.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum’s second-year report meets a sharp opposition response

President Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report Tuesday, a 67-minute address touting a 51% reduction in homicides since taking office, record foreign direct investment and a stable economy. She said her administration’s relationship with Washington “has had its challenges” but reiterated that “sovereignty isn’t negotiated, handed over or shared.”

Opposition senators offered a starkly different account. PAN’s Ricardo Anaya disputed the government’s homicide figures, arguing that reclassified deaths obscure a rising toll, while PRI’s Alejandro Moreno accused the administration of an unspoken “pact” with organized crime, pointing to the unresolved U.S. extradition request for Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya. Sheinbaum has said her administration won’t shield anyone who has committed a crime.

The president also used Wednesday’s press conference to accuse the Trump administration of trying to “create divisions” within her cabinet ahead of November’s U.S. midterms, calling it part of a long-standing U.S. pattern of pressuring “independent governments.” Her approval rating stood at 68% heading into the report, among the highest of any Mexican president at this point in a term, according to polling firm El Financiero. Along with the high approval rating, the newest results of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ found an almost 10-point increase in the president’s performance.

Security: Zacatecas car bomb and a cartel leader’s death

Eleven people, including a policewoman, were injured Sunday night when a car bomb exploded outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente — the third explosives attack in Zacatecas in four days. Authorities are investigating whether the blast was retaliation for the Saturday capture of an alleged Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) sicario. The explosion damaged 30 properties and 13 vehicles; classes were suspended and army troops deployed to the municipality.

The next day, Mexican Army and Navy forces killed Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, known as “El Güicho” or “R5,” in a shootout in Tocumbo, Michoacán. Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch identified Barragán as the leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes and the main coordinator of extortion against avocado producers in the state; the U.S. had offered a $3 million reward for his arrest on drug and firearms charges.

At her Friday mañanera in Zacatecas, Sheinbaum’s Security Cabinet reported the state’s daily homicide rate fell 85% in August compared to September 2024, and that more than 3,800 people have been arrested there since she took office. Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, responding to a Fox News report on U.S. anti-drone operations at the border, said the drones are mainly used by migrant smugglers and declined to confirm Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedowns.

Mexico-U.S. trade relations: Tariffs, cheese and an uncertain USMCA

Mexico-U.S. trade talks hit a snag over cheese this week, with U.S. officials pressuring Mexico to amend a May agreement with the European Union that grants regional-name protections to products like Parmigiano Reggiano and manchego. The U.S. government’s position is that these names are generic; the European Commission says the deal isn’t open to amendment, leaving Mexico caught between two trading partners.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina on Wednesday, pressing the U.S. to lift tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminum, which Mexico calls unjustified. Sheinbaum said Thursday her government is working to secure a better tariff agreement, noting that most Mexican exports still enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA.

The tariff dispute traces back to Washington’s decision not to renew USMCA in its current form for a further 16 years, leaving the pact’s future — and Mexico’s manufacturing-heavy states — in limbo pending ongoing bilateral talks.

Economy: The peso strengthens as growth forecasts improve

The peso hit a 28-month high against the dollar on Friday, trading at 16.863, reviving talk of a “super peso.” Analysts attribute the gains partly to peso strength and partly to the dollar’s weakness. A stronger peso cuts import costs and inflation but squeezes exporters’ margins and remittance values, with agricultural states like Michoacán most exposed.

Earlier in the week, Banxico raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.5%, up from 1.1%, citing stronger-than-expected second-quarter growth, while flagging USMCA uncertainty and geopolitical tensions as downside risks.

Mexico’s tourism sector added a bright note: The World Travel & Tourism Council ranked Mexico fourth globally in tourism-generated GDP, behind only the U.S., China and Germany, with Quintana Roo cited as the main driver.

Looking ahead

Trade talks with Washington remain unresolved on both cheese labeling and industrial tariffs, with no clear timeline for a new USMCA agreement as bilateral dialogue continues. Meanwhile, Hurricane Marie, a Category 2 storm off Baja California Sur, is expected to weaken to a Category 1 by Saturday as it moves out to sea, though Conagua warned that atmospheric instability could keep bringing rain to the country’s interior into next week. Zacatecas remains under heightened security following last week’s car bomb attack, with federal, state and municipal forces reinforcing operations in Ojocaliente.

Some good news to end the week

World.title: DR Congo: Kinshasa Comics Festival Returns After Six Years
World.content:

DR CONGO · CULTURE

Key Facts —What happened: SABDAM returns to Kinshasa from 11 to 13 September 2026, its first edition since 2019. —How big it is: The 2019 edition drew nearly 2,500 visitors and more than 30 cartoonists; the 2026 edition is expected to be larger. —What it means: Organizers want to make Kinshasa Africa’s comic-book capital, with Senegal as guest of honor. —The catch: The venue changed from the judo center to the Beaux-Arts academy, and no budget is public. —Who it hits: Artists from Goma and Bukavu may not attend because rebels hold those cities. —What comes next: A three-country comics corridor linking Kinshasa, Dakar, and Tetouan launches at the festival.

The Kinshasa comics festival returns in September 2026 after a six-year pause. Senegal is the guest of honour, and organisers will launch a three-city African comics corridor.

A long-awaited return

SABDAM returns to Kinshasa from 11 to 13 September 2026. It is the first edition since December 2019.

The salon began in 1991, making it one of Africa’s oldest comics festivals. Its return after six years is the news, and organizers are billing it as a comeback.

Who runs the show

SABDAM is organized by ACRIA, an arts workshop founded in 1989 and chaired by cartoonist Barly Baruti. His deputy is Thembo Kash, and they work with the Agence congolaise pour l’action culturelle (ACAC).

Baruti is the public face, but the salon is a team effort. The Ministry of Culture, Arts and Heritage has declared its support, though no budget has been published.

Senegal takes the spotlight

Senegal is the guest of honor, with a large delegation expected, as Radio Okapi reported on 5 September. Belgium, Mexico, Colombia, Canada, Gabon and the Central African Republic are also sending artists.

Japan was an earlier headline guest, paired with the DRC as rumba’s home. The salon’s full name includes ‘the other music.

This year’s music strand is curated by guitarist Pépé Felly Manuaku Waku, a Zaïko Langa-Langa founder.

A corridor for African comics

In May, ACRIA approached the DRC’s ambassador in Dakar, Christophe Muzungu, and Senegal’s culture minister. Baruti told ACP that Kinshasa must become Africa’s comic-book capital.

In June, Baruti announced a three-hub corridor at Dakar’s third comics festival. Kinshasa serves the east, Dakar the west, Tetouan the north.

The goal is visa-free artist travel. The corridor launches at SABDAM.

Venue questions linger

The salon was announced in April for the Centre sportif de judo in Lingwala, a symbol of Congo-Japan friendship. But Radio Okapi reported on 5 September that it will be at the Académie des Beaux-Arts.

No official explanation has been given for the change. The Académie is a working art school, which fits the program’s focus on heritage.

A tribute to a sculptor

The program includes an immersion in the work of Alfred Liyolo, a pioneer of bronze sculpture in Congo who died in 2019. Baruti told Radio Okapi that the salon will honor ‘these giants’ in the academy’s gallery.

A mural on the academy site shows miners as bees producing honey that flows from Congo to a queen bee. Baruti reads this as the theme: life, nothing but life.

The shadow of war

ACRIA has promised that authors from Goma and Bukavu will attend, but those cities remain under rebel control. As of September 2026, the AFC/M23 group holds both, and the government has not restored control.

Whether those artists can travel is the real question. The salon’s theme of resilience is tested by the east’s ongoing conflict.

Government support, with limits

Prime Minister Judith Suminwa received Baruti on 13 August, and he asked for help with visas for international guests. The culture minister, Yolande Elebe, has given an agreement in principle.

The salon’s partners include the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, the Centre Wallonie-Bruxelles, the Angoulême festival, and the Kyoto Manga Museum. No budget has been made public.

Who is Barly Baruti?

Barly Baruti is a Congolese cartoonist and the president of ACRIA, the workshop behind SABDAM. He has been a central figure in Congolese comics for decades.

His deputy, Thembo Kash, is also a cartoonist. Together they run the salon with the Agence congolaise pour l’action culturelle, a state cultural agency.

What is the Genocost?

Genocost refers to the cost of the genocide in the Democratic Republic of Congo. It is a term used by activists to describe the ongoing suffering from decades of conflict.

At a meeting on 13 August 2026, Baruti discussed the salon with Prime Minister Judith Suminwa. The Genocost was mentioned in that context, as reported by Congo Quotidien.

What else is on the program?

Besides the Liyolo tribute, there is a comics-and-song competition for young people. Winners will be presented in September.

The music strand, called Autre Muzik, is curated by guitarist Pépé Felly Manuaku Waku. He is a founder of the legendary band Zaïko Langa-Langa.

What to watch

Watch whether the Goma and Bukavu authors make it to Kinshasa. Their presence would be a statement against the war.

Also watch for the corridor’s launch and any publishing deals. The measure of success is what artists take home.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Kinshasa comics festival? SABDAM runs from 10 to 14 December 2026 at the Académie des Beaux-Arts in Kinshasa. It is the first edition since 2019. Who organizes the festival? ACRIA, an arts workshop founded in 1989, organizes it with the Agence congolaise pour l’action culturelle. Barly Baruti is the president. What is the theme this year? The theme is ‘Bomoyi, Kaka Se Bomoyi,’ Lingala for ‘life, nothing but life.’ It reflects resilience and creativity. What is the Genocost? The term refers to the deaths from decades of conflict in Congo, as used by civil society. It was mentioned at a meeting with the prime minister in August. Why is Senegal the guest of honor? Senegal is the guest of honor, and a large delegation is expected. The festival also launches a comics corridor linking Kinshasa, Dakar, and Tetouan.

World.title: Kagame in Oman: Rwanda’s President Seeks Gulf Investment
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

RWANDA · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts —What happened: President Paul Kagame of Rwanda makes a two-day official visit to Oman on 7 and 8 September 2026. —How big it is: It is the highest-level contact yet between the two governments, which have signed several cooperation agreements since January. —What it means: The visit aims to turn those agreements into trade, investment and economic ties. —The catch: Rwanda faces US sanctions over its alleged support for M23 rebels in Congo, which it denies. —Who it hits: Rwandan officials and companies, including a gold refinery and three mining firms, are under US sanctions. —What comes next: Watch for any investment commitments or named projects in the joint statement after the visit.

President Paul Kagame of Rwanda arrives in Muscat on 7 September for a two-day official visit. Kagame in Oman marks the most senior contact yet between the two governments.

What the visit is meant to produce

President Paul Kagame of Rwanda arrives in Muscat on Monday, 7 September, for a two-day official visit. It is the most senior contact yet between two governments that have signed several cooperation agreements since January 2026.

The stated purpose is to move a warming diplomatic relationship into trade, investment and economic substance. Both governments have listed the same sectors in their pre-visit statements.

Those sectors are energy and renewables, mining, logistics, airports, hospitality, healthcare, education and technology. It is a wide list, which usually means the specifics are still being negotiated.

The visit was announced on 5 September by the Diwan of the Royal Court, the Sultan’s court. Kagame is expected to meet Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said, who has ruled Oman since January 2020.

The aviation link came first

SalamAir, a low-cost Omani airline, began flying twice a week between Muscat and Kigali on 21 July 2026. It is the most concrete development in the relationship so far.

The legal foundation was laid earlier. A 2023 air services pact took effect on 12 January 2026, and airport plans were in January’s memoranda.

Kigali has built its strategy around exactly this. The airport, the convention business and the national carrier are the instruments of a small landlocked economy trying to be a hub.

Why the Gulf keeps looking at East Africa

Gulf states have become significant African investors over the past decade, in ports, logistics, agriculture and increasingly in minerals. The Horn and East Africa are the nearest African markets to the peninsula.

The competition is not only commercial. The UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar have built positions on Africa’s Red Sea coast, each with political weight.

Oman is quieter than its neighbours. It avoids taking sides and diversifies from hydrocarbons.

What Rwanda is selling

The pitch is a small, well-run, predictable jurisdiction with an international convention business and a growing services sector. Rwanda has used it to attract capital well beyond what its size would suggest.

There is a mining dimension too. Rwanda handles a substantial volume of regional minerals, but that trade is now under scrutiny.

On 25 June 2026, the US Treasury designated Gasabo Gold Refinery and three Rwandan mining companies over conflict minerals financing M23. Rwanda’s foreign minister, Olivier Nduhungirehe, called the sanctions ‘biased’ and ‘unjustified’.

Kagame has separately said Rwanda wants a stake in a proposed refinery at Lamu, Kenya. On 24 August 2026 he said Rwanda ‘would be very happy to be part of that kind of investment.

He added that it was too early for details.

What Oman gets

Oman is diversifying away from hydrocarbons under Oman Vision 2040, and outbound investment is part of that. African logistics and airport concessions fit the model.

Duqm, Oman’s deepwater port and special economic zone, needs cargo and partners. East African trade routes are one answer.

The Swahili coast diaspora gives Omani business regional familiarity. Few Gulf states match this historical connection.

The sanctions cloud

Rwanda’s involvement in the war in eastern Congo is the single largest risk to any investment case built on Kigali. The West, UN, and US Treasury accuse Rwanda of backing M23 rebels.

Kigali denies this.

On 2 March 2026, the US Treasury designated the Rwanda Defence Force itself and four senior commanders over operational support to M23. Rwanda’s Office of the Government Spokesperson said the measures ‘misrepresent the reality and distort the facts’.

The EU imposed sanctions on M23 figures and Rwandan officials in March 2025, and the UK suspended bilateral aid in February 2025. Neither has been reported as lifted.

Gulf states have continued signing agreements with Kigali through this period.

The Gulf portfolio beyond Oman

Rwanda’s Gulf ties extend beyond Oman. Qatar Airways agreed in December 2019 to take a 60% stake in Bugesera Airport.

The project costs about US$2 billion and remains under construction.

A Qatar Airways acquisition of 49 percent of RwandAir has been reported as close for years but has not closed. The UAE and Rwanda have been negotiating a comprehensive economic partnership agreement since at least November 2025, but it is not signed.

Saudi Arabia and Rwanda concluded a general cooperation agreement and a trade and investment agreement in February 2025. These are framework instruments, not capital commitments.

What could get in the way

The sanctions are a live issue, not a historical one. They directly touch the mining and aviation sectors that this visit is meant to promote.

Rwanda’s domestic market is small, so almost any project has to make sense as a regional play. That limits the scale of what Oman can expect.

The other constraint is trust. Western governments have questioned Rwanda’s actions in Congo, and that affects how investors everywhere assess risk.

The measure of success

Memoranda are cheap and frequent. The test of this visit will be whether anything signed carries a number, a counterparty and a date.

Watch for an investment fund commitment or a named airport or logistics concession. Those are the deliverables that turn a state visit into a transaction.

What to watch next

Watch the joint statement at the end of the second day, and whether Omani sovereign investment vehicles are named in it.

Watch the Muscat to Kigali route as well. A move from two flights a week to daily would say more than any communiqué.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Kagame visiting Oman? On 7 and 8 September 2026, for a two-day official visit to Muscat. It follows a Rwandan ministerial delegation led by Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe on 10 and 11 January 2026. What sectors are Rwanda and Oman discussing? Energy and renewables, mining, logistics, airports, hospitality, healthcare, education and technology. In January 2026 they signed a memorandum of understanding on airport development and two cooperation programmes on logistics and data centres. Is there a direct flight between Oman and Rwanda? SalamAir launched twice-weekly Muscat-Kigali flights on 21 July 2026. This follows an air services agreement effective 12 January 2026. Why is the Gulf investing in East Africa? The region is Africa’s closest market to Arabia. Gulf states have built port, logistics, farm, and mineral positions there over ten years. What are the US sanctions on Rwanda about? The US Treasury says Rwanda backs M23 rebels in eastern Congo, which Kigali denies. It sanctioned Rwanda’s army and four commanders in March 2026 and four mining firms in June.

World.title: Malawi El Niño Plan Is Only One Third Funded
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

MALAWI · CLIMATE

Key Facts —What happened: Malawi’s government published a preliminary El Niño preparedness plan on 4 September 2026. —How big it is: The plan needs 488.5 billion kwacha (about US$282 million), with 163.7 billion (US$94 million) mobilised. —The gap: The shortfall is 324.8 billion kwacha (about US$187 million), two-thirds of the total. —Who it hits: Up to 2.6 million people, 14% of the population according to the plan, across 23 districts. —The catch: The mobilised money comes from existing programmes, not new pledges, and the largest potential fund is conditional. —What comes next: The World Bank’s US$190 million releases only after drought impacts are verified in early 2027.

The Malawi El Niño preparedness plan needs about US$282 million. The government has mobilised about US$94 million from existing programmes, leaving a US$187 million gap.

The plan and its price tag

Malawi drafted a national plan for the 2026/27 El Niño dry spell. Announced on 4 September 2026, it costs 488.5 billion kwacha (about US$282 million).

That sum is meant to cover two pillars: preparedness and resilience. They span fourteen priority areas, including agriculture, food security, nutrition, health, water, energy, and logistics.

The most concrete item is grain. The plan calls for securing 440,000 metric tonnes of maize for national food reserves.

What has been mobilised so far

The government says 163.7 billion kwacha (about US$94 million) has already been mobilised through ongoing programmes. That means existing budget lines and donor projects, not new money pledged for this plan.

The remaining gap is 324.8 billion kwacha (about US$187 million), which is two-thirds of the total. The figures come from the government’s own document, dated 4 September 2026.

The government calls the requirement preliminary, and the gap could widen if needs grow.

Why the gap matters for people

The plan projects that 2.6 million people, about 14% of Malawi’s population, could be affected. Of those, 2.5 million live in rural areas, spread across 23 priority drought-prone districts.

Malawi’s economy relies on rain-fed maize. A poor season causes hunger.

The 2023/24 El Niño led to a disaster declaration in March 2024.

According to the Ad Hoc Cabinet Committee on El Niño, the 2023/24 event left many households without enough reserves. That makes them more vulnerable to another shock.

The forecast: a strong El Niño is here

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed a developing El Niño on 2 June 2026. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) declared its arrival on 11 June.

Forecasters expect the peak from December 2026 to February 2027. Malawi’s south faces below-normal rain from October to December 2026, with fewer rainy days from January to March 2027.

The WMO’s August update says the event is near-certain to continue through the September-to-November period. The peak comes later.

The money problem: forex and fiscal limits

Malawi lacks foreign exchange, hindering maize imports. The official rate was 1,734 kwacha per dollar on 4 September 2026; the parallel rate was about 4,400 in July 2026.

The government has ruled out devaluing the kwacha. Finance Minister Joseph Mwanamvekha said in June that there would be ‘no discussion on devaluation’.

The extended credit facility from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) lapsed in May 2025 with about US$35 million disbursed. A June 2026 IMF mission ended without an agreement.

The 2026/27 budget allocates only 590 million kwacha (US$340,000) to disaster risk management. Of that, 114 million (US$66,000) is for interventions.

Where the money could come from

The UK pledged US$3 million on 4 September, about 5.3 billion kwacha. FAO and WFP appealed for US$202 million on 29 June for twelve countries, including Malawi, with no breakdown published.

The World Bank found up to US$190 million available, but conditionally. Funds release only after drought checks in February and March 2027, post-planting.

African Risk Capacity and the African Development Bank paid Malawi US$11.2 million in 2024. They also paid US$14.2 million in recovery cover, totaling about 9% of the US$282 million need.

Voices from the ground

Chief Secretary Justin Saidi chairs the El Niño committee. President Mutharika set it up. ‘We cannot wait for impacts before responding,’ Saidi said.

He added that early action remains Malawi’s best defence. Innocent Pangapanga, director of the Centre for Agricultural Research and Development, said: ‘After the plan, next should be action.’

Economist Christopher Mbukwa urged the private sector to shift from disaster donations to building pre-disaster resilience. These voices underline the urgency, but the funding gap remains the central challenge.

What preparedness money buys

According to an IFPRI policy note, pre-positioning supplies in districts before roads deteriorate costs a fraction of what airlifted relief costs later. The plan includes drought insurance and livestock support, with policies that pay automatically when rainfall falls below a set level.

Early warning systems are the cheapest line, per the note, yet often first cut. World Bank money, if any, arrives post-drought.

The gap between the need and the mobilised funds is the story. It is a race against the rains.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does Malawi need for El Niño preparedness? The government’s preliminary plan requires 488.5 billion kwacha (about US$282 million). Only 163.7 billion (US$94 million) has been mobilised from existing programmes. Who is coordinating Malawi’s El Niño response? The Department of Disaster Management Affairs coordinates, with district councils leading implementation. President Peter Mutharika set up the Ad Hoc Cabinet Committee on El Niño, chaired by Chief Secretary Justin Saidi. What does the preparedness plan cover? It covers fourteen priority areas, including agriculture, food security, nutrition, health, water, energy, and logistics. A key goal is securing 440,000 metric tonnes of maize for national reserves. When is the El Niño expected to peak? Forecasters expect the peak between December 2026 and February 2027. Malawi may see below-normal rain in the south from October and dry spells from January. How many people could be affected? The plan projects 2.6 million people, about 14% of the population, could be affected. They are spread across 23 priority drought-prone districts.

World.title: Watchdog Seeks Audit of Mali Military Contracts Since 2020
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

MALI · GOVERNANCE

Key Facts —What happened: The RAMLCDF network filed an audit request with Mali’s Auditor General on 4 September 2026. —How big it is: The audit would cover six years of contracts, including a 15.6 billion CFA franc (US$27.6 million) command aircraft. —The catch: The government says the aircraft’s net cost was 5.6-6 billion CFA francs after insurance and resale. —Who it hits: The military government of General Assimi Goita, which has restricted civil society and dissolved parties. —What comes next: The Auditor General’s office has not yet responded; the network awaits a decision. —The number that matters: Defence is Mali’s largest budget line at 516 billion CFA francs (US$914 million) in 2026.

A watchdog network has asked Mali’s Auditor General to examine Mali military contracts signed under six years of army rule. The request takes in defence, infrastructure, energy and hydrocarbons.

Who is asking for the audit

The RAMLCDF filed the request on Friday 4 September 2026. It is an umbrella body grouping about a hundred Malian associations.

The network went to the Vérificateur général, Mali’s Auditor General, an independent office that reviews state spending. The office is headed by Abdoul Aziz Aguissa, installed on 24 May 2025 for a single seven-year term.

Neither the government nor the Auditor General’s office had responded publicly as of Sunday 6 September 2026. The network’s request is public, but the office has not said whether it will take it up.

What the audit would cover

The demand covers contracts awarded since the transition began with the coup of 18 August 2020. It targets defence, infrastructure, energy and hydrocarbons, and singles out single-source awards, known as ‘gré à gré’ contracts.

These are contracts given directly to a chosen company without open competition. The network says such awards have escaped proper oversight.

A network official said: ‘All files for the acquisition of military equipment and materiel escape the control mechanisms. The network did not name the official, and reports of the filing do not identify the speaker.

The aircraft example and its real cost

The network cites a modernised Boeing 737 bought as a command jet for 15.6 billion CFA francs (about US$27.6 million). That gross price contrasts with the government’s net outlay of 5.6 to 6 billion CFA francs (US$9.9 to 10.6 million).

The lower figure follows about 6 billion CFA francs (US$10.6 million) recovered from insurance on the damaged aircraft. It also includes a further 3 to 4 billion CFA francs (US$5.3 to 7.1 million) from selling salvageable parts and equipment.

The finance ministry says the state recovered 9 to 10 billion CFA francs in all. The attack on 17 September 2024 was claimed by JNIM, the al-Qaeda affiliate in the Sahel.

The new aircraft replaced the one damaged beyond economic repair that day. The ministry said the old aircraft was damaged beyond economic repair.

The transition has no end date

The transition began with the 2020 coup, and in July 2025 General Assimi Goita was granted a five-year presidential mandate. That mandate is renewable ‘as many times as necessary’ until the country is pacified, with no election date.

Political parties were dissolved in May 2025, and a 2024 decree suspended political associations. At least five civil-society organisations have been dissolved, including a governance watchdog, the Observatory for Elections and Good Governance, according to CIVICUS.

Civil society under pressure

CIVICUS, a global alliance, rates civic space in Mali as ‘repressed’. Amnesty International’s 2026 report records detentions of activists and a one-year sentence for former prime minister Moussa Mara over social-media criticism.

The RAMLCDF itself has not been dissolved and can still operate. That makes its demand one of the few remaining channels for scrutiny, according to the network’s own statements.

RFI, the French broadcaster that first reported the filing, has been banned from broadcasting in Mali since April 2022. PressAfrik, Bénin Web TV and Leral carried the same account.

Defence spending is large but falling

Defence leads Mali’s 2026 budget at 516 billion CFA francs (US$914 million). That is 11 billion less than 2025.

Security spending fell by 129 billion CFA francs (US$228 million) to 376 billion (US$666 million). Health spending rose by 61 billion CFA francs (US$108 million) to 206 billion (US$365 million).

Mali has bought military aircraft, drones and vehicles since 2021, largely from Russia and Turkey. Russia is the government’s strategic partner.

The Auditor General has audited other bodies

The Bureau du Vérificateur général audited OCLEI. It reported over 350 million CFA francs (US$620,000) in suspected irregularities from 2021 to 2025, citing management and procedural failings.

OCLEI is headed by Dr Modibo Sacko. That shows the office can scrutinise other state bodies.

Whether it will take on the network’s request is another matter. The Auditor General can examine documents and publish findings, but it cannot prosecute.

It refers files to the courts.

Gold and mining disputes

Mali is among Africa’s largest gold producers, and the transitional government has rewritten terms for foreign miners. Several disputes and detentions have followed, according to Reuters and Bloomberg.

The network’s audit request does not cover mining contracts directly. But the sectors it names—defence, infrastructure, energy—are where single-source awards are common, according to a 2023 report by Transparency International.

What to watch next

Watch whether the Auditor General acknowledges the request publicly and gives a timetable. The office has not responded as of Sunday 6 September 2026.

Watch how the government reacts to the demand. The network remains legal, but its request challenges the military’s control over spending.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the RAMLCDF? It is the Network of Associations Against Corruption and Financial Crime, an umbrella body of about a hundred Malian groups. It filed the audit request. What does the audit cover? It covers public contracts awarded during the six-year military transition, focusing on defence, infrastructure, energy and hydrocarbons. It targets single-source awards. Why is the aircraft cost disputed? The gross price was 15.6 billion CFA francs, but the government says the net outlay was 5.6-6 billion after insurance and resale. The network cites the gross figure. Has the government responded? No, neither the government nor the Auditor General’s office had responded publicly as of 6 September 2026. The network awaits a decision. Can the network operate freely? Yes, the RAMLCDF has not been dissolved, but civil society in Mali faces restrictions. Political parties are banned, and several groups have been shut down.

World.title: Zambia’s State Firm Puts Ndola Refinery at US$1.2 Billion
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

ZAMBIA · ENERGY

Key Facts —What happened: The Industrial Development Corporation said the Ndola refinery will cost US$1.2 billion. —How big it is: The refinery will make 3 million tonnes a year, about 60,000 barrels per day. —Who is building it: Zambia Petrochemical Energy Company, a joint venture between the state IDC and China’s Fujian Xiang Xin. —The catch: The licensed value is US$1.1 billion, and the difference is not explained. —Who it hits: Zambian fuel buyers, who pay among the highest prices in the region. —What comes next: Completion is targeted for the end of 2028. No cabinet is in place yet.

Zambia is landlocked and has not refined fuel since 2022. The state firm says its Ndola refinery will cost US$1.2 billion, above the licensed US$1.1 billion.

What the state holding company said

The Industrial Development Corporation (IDC) is the state’s main holding company for commercial assets. Its chief executive, Cornwell Muleya, said on 5 September that the refinery will cost US$1.2 billion.

He spoke to the state broadcaster ZNBC, as Lusaka Times reported. The refinery is already under construction next to the old Indeni plant at Ndola, on the Copperbelt.

Muleya also gave jobs figures that conflict with earlier official numbers. He said 3,000 construction jobs and 800 permanent ones, but earlier official figures were 2,200 construction and 600 direct operational jobs.

The project that is already being built

The developer is Zambia Petrochemical Energy Company (ZPEC), a joint venture between IDC and China’s Fujian Xiang Xin Corporation. The shareholding split is not public.

ZPEC got an investment licence from the Zambia Development Agency on 28 November 2025. It signed an investment protection agreement in mid-May 2026, and the environmental regulator ZEMA approved it in June 2026.

The groundbreaking was on 10 April 2026, officiated by the then energy minister, Makozo Chikote. He held the portfolio until Parliament was dissolved on 15 May 2026 ahead of the election.

Why the cost figure matters

The licensed value of the project is US$1.1 billion. Muleya’s US$1.2 billion is higher, and IDC has not explained the difference.

That gap is about 9 percent. For a project of this size, even a small percentage change is a lot of money.

The cost matters because Zambia is still recovering from a debt default. The government restructured its bonds in 2024, and rating agency S&P raised Zambia to CCC+ in November 2025.

What the refinery will do

The plant will make 3 million tonnes of fuel a year, about 60,000 barrels per day. That is two and a half times the old Indeni refinery’s design capacity of 24,000 barrels per day.

Zambia has no working refinery today. Indeni stopped refining in 2022, after going onto care and maintenance in November 2021.

Indeni now operates as a state-owned fuel marketing company under IDC. It imports and sells petrol, diesel, jet fuel and other products, and runs the largest single-site fuel storage in Zambia.

Where the crude will come from

Zambia does not produce its own crude oil. The refinery will need to import it, and reported sources are the Middle East and Angola.

How the crude will reach Ndola is not clear. The TAZAMA pipeline from Dar es Salaam has carried low-sulphur diesel, not crude, since 16 March 2023.

TAZAMA, owned 66.7 percent by Zambia and 33.3 percent by Tanzania, used to pump crude to Indeni. Whether it will be converted back or a new line built is an open question.

The politics around the project

President Hakainde Hichilema was sworn in for a second term on 1 September 2026, after a disputed election. No cabinet had been named at the time of writing.

That means there is no sitting energy minister. Muleya argues the refinery will give Zambia more control over fuel supply and prices.

But he has not said how the difference between the two figures will be funded.

What fuel prices are doing now

The Energy Regulation Board (ERB) reviews pump prices every month. It cut prices for three months running, and held them unchanged for September 2026.

Petrol costs 25.29 kwacha a litre, about US$1.32, and diesel 26.86 kwacha, about US$1.40. The kwacha traded at about 19.1 per US dollar on 4 September 2026.

The ERB says prices are driven by international oil prices and the exchange rate. A stable kwacha has helped bring prices down.

How this fits the region

Nigeria’s Dangote refinery cut petrol imports by 96% in early 2026. Output fell from 81,000 to 10,000 barrels daily by June.

On 21 August 2026 Aliko Dangote offered Kenya, Ethiopia and Rwanda a combined 30 percent stake in a planned refinery. The project reportedly costs US$17 billion.

For Zambia, the new refinery is sized for its own demand. It will not export much, but it could reduce the country’s reliance on imported finished fuel.

What to watch next

Watch for a new cabinet and an energy minister. They will have to explain the cost difference and the funding plan.

Watch for how crude will reach Ndola. The pipeline question is central to whether the refinery can run at full capacity.

Watch for updated jobs figures. The conflict between Muleya’s numbers and earlier official ones needs to be resolved.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much will the Ndola refinery cost? The Industrial Development Corporation says US$1.2 billion. The licensed value is US$1.1 billion, and the difference has not been explained. Who is building the Ndola refinery? Zambia Petrochemical Energy Company, a joint venture between the state’s IDC and China’s Fujian Xiang Xin Corporation. The shareholding split is not public. When will the Ndola refinery be finished? Completion is targeted for the end of 2028. The groundbreaking was in April 2026. Why does Zambia need a new refinery? Zambia is landlocked and has not refined its own fuel since 2022. The new plant would make about 60,000 barrels a day, two and a half times the old Indeni capacity. How will the refinery affect fuel prices? The government argues it will give more control over supply and price. But the cost of crude and the exchange rate will still matter.

World.title: Burundi Inflation Falls to 8.7%, 15 Months After Peak
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

BURUNDI · ECONOMY

Key Facts —What happened: Annual inflation in Burundi fell to 8.7% in July 2026, from 45.5% in April 2025. —How big it is: The 2025 average was 34%, up from 20.2% in 2024; 2026 forecasts range from 14.5% to 22.1%. —The catch: The parallel exchange rate was about double the official rate in April 2026, so prices feel higher. —Who it hits: Households still face high food and fuel costs, with reserves covering only 1.4 months of imports. —What comes next: No IMF programme is active; the June 2026 Article IV was surveillance only. —The number that matters: The gap between official and parallel exchange rates was about 100% in April 2026.

Burundi inflation fell to 8.7% in July 2026, down from a 45.5% peak fifteen months earlier.

Inflation in Burundi has dropped sharply

Consumer prices in Burundi rose 8.7% in July 2026 compared with a year earlier, according to the national statistics institute, INSBU. That is down from 45.5% in April 2025 and 10.8% in March 2026.

The drop is real, but it does not mean prices are stable. The 2025 average inflation was 34%, up from 20.2% in 2024, and forecasts for 2026 range from 14.5% to 22.1%.

Why inflation fell: budget discipline, not gold

The IMF said on 18 May 2026 that stricter budget discipline and less central bank financing drove the slowdown. The World Bank credits curtailed monetary financing and a good harvest.

Gold and coffee exports eased forex pressure, narrowing the deficit. They did not cut inflation directly; AfDB cites budget deficit monetization.

The parallel exchange rate tells the real story

The official exchange rate is about 3,000 Burundian francs to the dollar. But the parallel rate was above 7,500 before October 2025 and fell to 5,300-5,500 in mid-October 2025.

The IMF put the gap at about 100% in late April 2026. Many goods use the parallel rate, so felt inflation may exceed the official figure.

Gold exports tripled, but the currency fell

Gold exports rose from about 400 kilograms in 2024 to 1.2 tonnes in 2025, according to the IMF. Coffee receipts also rose, from 78.9 billion to 230.2 billion Burundian francs, and gold from 93.2 billion to 408.9 billion.

But those figures are in a currency that has lost 87.7% against the dollar since 2015. The World Bank notes that traditional exports like coffee and tea have declined over the long term.

Growth is slowing, not accelerating

The economy grew 4.1% in 2024. For 2025, the AfDB estimates 4.6% growth, the IMF 4.2%, and the World Bank 4.0%.

The IMF projects 3.9% for 2026. So growth is not accelerating; it is slowing, and the country remains one of the poorest in the world.

Current account deficits vary by source

The current account deficit is projected to narrow in 2026. The AfDB says 6.3% of GDP, the IMF says 6%, and the World Bank says 8.6%.

The IMF credits higher gold exports for the improvement. The World Bank sees a smaller improvement, from 9.3% in 2025.

Reserves are thin, and debt is a risk

Foreign reserves cover only 1.4 months of imports, according to the French Treasury. The IMF expects reserves to rise to about US$500 million, or 2.8 months, over the medium term.

Burundi is at high risk of debt distress. Public debt is about 42% of GDP on the IMF’s measure, and 67.1% on the World Bank’s.

No active IMF programme

Burundi has no active IMF programme. The US$271 million extended credit facility approved in July 2023 expired automatically in January 2025 with no reviews completed.

The June 2026 Article IV consultation was surveillance only, with no money and no conditions. So when the IMF speaks, it is advice, not a programme.

Fuel shortages and daily life

Fuel and foreign currency shortages persisted through 2025, even as inflation fell. Queues at petrol stations are common.

Landlocked Burundi imports all its fuel, making supply chains costly. The gap between official statistics and daily life is wide, and the parallel rate explains part of it.

Who runs Burundi’s economy

President Évariste Ndayishimiye has led Burundi since 2020. He named himself the ruling party’s candidate for the 2027 election in April 2026.

The central bank is the Bank of the Republic of Burundi, or BRB. Its governor, Édouard Normand Bigendako, took office in October 2023.

His predecessor was removed and arrested on corruption charges. The BRB sets monetary policy and publishes monthly and quarterly reports.

What the IMF and World Bank say

The IMF’s mission chief for Burundi, Alexandre Chailloux, spoke on 18 May 2026. He said the current account deficit would narrow to 6% of GDP in 2026, helped by gold exports.

He also said reserves should rise to about US$500 million over time. That equals 2.8 months of imports, but it is a target, not today’s figure.

The World Bank sees a smaller improvement in the current account. It projects an 8.6% deficit for 2026, after 9.3% in 2025.

Why the official numbers may understate prices

The official exchange rate is about 3,000 Burundian francs to the dollar. But many goods are priced at the parallel rate, which was far higher.

The IMF says the gap between official and parallel rates was about 100% in late April 2026. That gap means official inflation may feel lower than reality.

The parallel rate has narrowed since late 2025, but it still exists. Watch it as a sign of real price pressure.

What the government’s plan aims to do

In January 2026, the government launched a Macroeconomic Stabilization Plan. The IMF credits this plan for the drop in inflation.

The plan focuses on budget discipline and less central bank financing of the deficit. It also aims to boost foreign exchange reserves.

Success is not guaranteed. The IMF warns that reforms must continue for the outlook to stay positive.

What to watch next

Watch INSBU’s monthly inflation prints. July’s 8.7% nears the EAC’s 8% target.

The annual average will be higher.

Watch the parallel exchange rate. A narrower gap may stabilize prices.

A wider gap could reignite inflation.

Background: ECLAC: Panama Canal Economy Still the Engine as Growth Seen at 4.4%.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much has inflation in Burundi fallen? Inflation in Burundi fell to 8.7% in July 2026, from 45.5% in April 2025. The 2025 average was 34%, and 2026 forecasts range from 14.5% to 22.1%. What drove the drop in inflation? The IMF and World Bank credit stricter budget discipline and less central bank financing of the deficit. Gold and coffee exports helped the exchange rate, but did not directly cut inflation. Why does the official inflation rate feel wrong? The parallel exchange rate was about double the official rate in April 2026. Many goods are priced at the parallel rate, so the real cost of living may be higher than the official number. Is Burundi under an IMF programme? No. The extended credit facility expired in January 2025 with no reviews completed. The June 2026 Article IV was surveillance only. What are the risks to Burundi’s economy? Reserves cover only 1.4 months of imports, and debt is at high risk of distress. Growth is slowing, and the parallel exchange rate gap remains wide.

World.title: Libya Shuts 490 Petrol Stations Over Alleged Smuggling
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

LIBYA · ENERGY

Key Facts —What happened: On 2 September, Libya’s Tripoli-based government closed 490 petrol stations over alleged fuel smuggling. —How big it is: About 365 stations were approved to keep operating, based on what the ministry calls actual need. —What it means: The closures target smuggling, which thrives because subsidised fuel is far cheaper than market prices. —The catch: The closures are not permanent; stations can reopen if they meet approved specifications, the minister said. —Who it hits: The order applies in western Libya, not the east, which is under a rival administration. —What comes next: Watch whether the closures hold and whether fuel demand falls from its post-Eid spike.

On 2 September, Libya’s Tripoli-based Government of National Unity announced the closure of 490 petrol stations over alleged fuel smuggling. The interior minister said no station will open unless it meets approved specifications.

Why Libya petrol stations are closing

On 2 September, the Interior Ministry of Libya’s Tripoli-based Government of National Unity announced the closure of 490 forecourts. The move targets stations accused of involvement in fuel smuggling.

Major General Emad Trabelsi said no station opens unless approved. Closures are conditional, not permanent.

The order applies in western Libya, where the Government of National Unity has authority. The east is controlled by a rival administration, so the closures do not extend there.

The demand spike that raised alarms

After Eid al-Adha, Libya’s petrol demand surged in early June. NOC chief Masoud Suleiman said daily distribution hit 9-9.5 million litres, versus 6.5 million normally.

Suleiman attributed the spike to holiday travel and panic buying. The jump of about 46 percent was not seen as a sign of smuggling by the NOC, but it strained the system.

The August shortage that followed was separate, and the government responded with emergency diesel supplies.

The minister’s blunt words on smuggling

At a cabinet meeting in Zliten on 19 July, Trabelsi said he ‘cannot clash with other security agencies and state entities. He called diesel smuggling ‘blatant and well-known.’

His remarks were an unusual public acknowledgment of the problem. But they were not a direct admission that state entities smuggle fuel.

The closures are an attempt to cut off the retail end of the smuggling trade, which the minister says is widespread.

The subsidy gap that fuels smuggling

Libya sells diesel at an official price of 0.15 Libyan dinars per litre. During the August shortage, the black-market price peaked at 8.00 dinars per litre, a gap of more than fifty times.

That gap makes smuggling highly profitable. In 2025, Central bank governor Naji Issa said fuel subsidies cost 60 billion dinars (about US$7 billion), with 30 percent smuggled out.

Until the price gap narrows, the incentive to smuggle will remain, regardless of station closures.

Security threats to fuel infrastructure

A drone crashed near a Tripoli fuel depot on 3 September. Brega Petroleum Marketing Company reported minor damage to pipelines and two tanks.

No casualties were reported, and supply was not interrupted. Technical teams drew down fuel levels in the affected tanks as a precaution.

That attack followed a drone strike on 11 August that caused a large fire at the Zawiya refinery complex. Fuel infrastructure has become a target.

Oil production remains strong

Libya’s crude oil production stood at about 1.44 million barrels per day in late June, according to the National Oil Corporation. Including condensate, a lighter form of oil, total output was close to 1.49 million barrels per day.

That production is vital for Libya’s budget, which relies heavily on oil revenue. The fuel smuggling problem does not directly threaten output, but it drains state finances.

The government’s crackdown on petrol stations is a signal that it is willing to act against networks that have operated with impunity.

Two governments complicate enforcement

Libya has two rival administrations: the Government of National Unity in Tripoli and a separate government in the east. Fuel distribution crosses that divide, but the closure order only applies in the west.

Smuggling routes run south into the Sahel and north by sea, often involving armed groups. Closing a petrol station does not close a smuggling route.

The National Oil Corporation has largely stayed neutral in the political split, making its statements a reliable source on the sector.

What to watch next

Watch whether the 490 closures hold through the autumn, or whether stations quietly reopen after meeting specifications. Also watch daily fuel demand: if it falls back toward 6.5 million litres, the crackdown may be working.

The government’s next steps will show whether it can enforce its rules against powerful smuggling networks.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many Libya petrol stations have been closed? On 2 September, the Tripoli-based government closed 490 filling stations over alleged fuel smuggling. About 365 stations were approved to keep operating. Will the closed stations reopen? Interior Minister Emad Trabelsi said no station will be permitted to open unless it meets approved specifications. That means stations can reopen if they comply. Why is fuel smuggling a problem in Libya? Fuel is heavily subsidised, so it is much cheaper than on the open market. Smugglers buy subsidised fuel and sell it abroad or on the black market for a large profit. Did a drone attack damage Libya’s fuel infrastructure? Yes, on 3 September a drone caused minor damage to pipelines and two tanks at a Tripoli depot. Brega Petroleum Marketing Company reported the damage. What is the current fuel demand in Libya? In early June, after Eid, petrol demand spiked to between 9 and 9.5 million litres per day. The usual rate is about 6.5 million litres.

World.title: Guinea Buries 36 Killed in Conakry Landfill Collapse
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

GUINEA · SOCIETY

Key Facts —What happened: A rubbish dump collapsed onto homes in Conakry overnight on 22-23 August, killing 36 people. —How big it is: The dead included 19 Guineans and 17 Sierra Leoneans, buried on 4 September. —The catch: The 17 Sierra Leonean deaths were announced by Freetown on 31 August, not at the funeral. —Who it hits: Waste-pickers and families living beside the dump in Gbessia commune lost homes and loved ones. —What comes next: Guinea plans to rehouse about 1,500 people and demolish at-risk homes near the site. —The number that matters: 33 people were injured in the collapse, and 542 survivors were sheltered at a school by late August.

Guinea buried 36 people on Friday, twelve days after the Conakry landfill collapse. Seventeen of the dead were Sierra Leonean, a figure Freetown had already confirmed.
