World.title: Second man pleads not guilty over Coles Bay home invasion and arson
World.content:
One of three men accused of attacking and robbing a 76-year-old man on Tasmania's east coast in July has pleaded not guilty.

Hayden James Morrison, 31, appeared in the Launceston Magistrates Court via video link from prison on Monday.

The Invermay man has been charged with a string of offences stemming from the alleged July 11 incident at Coles Bay, including aggravated armed robbery, aggravated assault, motor vehicle stealing and arson.

Police believe Mr Morrison was part of a trio that tied up home owner Grant Whelan, stole his firearms and torched his Coles Bay home.

Police allege Grant Whelan was attacked, had his guns stolen and his Coles Bay home torched. (Supplied)

What remains of Grant Whelan's house in Coles Bay. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Mr Whelan spent six days in hospital after the incident.

The stolen guns remain missing.

Report crime Call Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000

Report anonymously via the Crime Stoppers website

Another man, 33-year-old Jason Robert Burns, is set to appear in the Supreme Court later this month after also pleading not guilty.

Ravenswood man Charlie Hills, 30, was granted bail in July, with his lawyer indicating a plea of not guilty would be entered.

Grant Whelan spent six days in hospital. (Supplied: Chantel Yates)

Mr Morrison on Monday entered a not guilty plea through his lawyer Fran McCracken.

He was remanded in custody by Deputy Chief Magistrate Ken Stanton.

World.title: Sydney mother challenges Liberal seat following son's hospital death
World.content:
Kellie Sloane and the NSW Liberals face a fresh challenge ahead of the March election, with Elouise Massa announcing she will contest the seat of Manly as an independent.

It comes just days after Liberal frontbencher James Griffin revealed he would not recontest the northern beaches seat.

Ms Massa already has a high profile in the community, having successfully spearheaded a campaign to transfer Northern Beaches Hospital to public hands, following the death of her son Joe in 2024.

Toddle Joe Massa died in 2024. (Supplied)

A review identified multiple failures in the two-year-old's treatment and the Massa family's campaign also resulted in a new system by which families can escalate concerns over a child's care.

It also led to "Joe's Law" which bans future public-private partnerships in major hospitals.

Ms Massa said her family's campaign had shown her what can happen when "courage in the community is met by people in government who genuinely listen and act".

"I am not the same person I was before Joe died," she said.

"Creating meaningful change has become a vocation.

"It's my way of saying thank you to our community for backing [my husband] Danny and me through our campaigns."

The Massa family's advocacy was credited with helping transfer Northern Beaches Hospital back to public hands. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

The former journalist from North Balgowlah said people have stopped her in the street and told her to "keep going".

"This is how I want to keep going, by listening, discerning, and taking our community's voice to parliament."

Liberals risk losing more territory

The seat of Manly has been held by The Liberal Party for almost 20 years, after it was won by former premier Mike Baird.

However, between 1991 and 2007 it was held by independent MPs — first Peter Macdonald and then David Barr.

At a federal level, the Manly area is represented by teal independent Zali Steggall, who unseated former prime minister Tony Abbott in the seat of Warringah in 2019.

In April, Northern Beaches Hospital officially transferred to public ownership. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The Liberals are yet to announce their candidate to replace Mr Griffin in Manly, but the party is expected to campaign hard to keep a foothold on the northern beaches.

In 2024, independent Jacqui Scruby won the seat of Pittwater from the Liberals in a by-election.

A year earlier, independent Michael Regan won the seat of Wakehurst in the general election.

Ms Massa said an independent would better serve the needs of the community, vowing to campaign on issues like healthcare, housing and transport.

"I've seen what happens when nobody is held accountable and I've seen what can happen when a community demands better," she said.

"I'm running because the Member for Manly should answer to the people who live here, not to a party room."

World.title: Maternity unit problems persist at Toowoomba Hospital, review finds
World.content:
Longstanding issues at Toowoomba Hospital's troubled maternity unit remain unresolved, an independent review of the ward says.

The assurance review of the unit, released today, found that while some changes were underway, several areas, including complaint processes, still needed fixing.

Queensland Health commissioned the review in February after years of complaints from mothers and families about maternity services at the major regional hospital.

Most recently, a Toowoomba mother revealed footage that showed her support person being unnecessarily removed from the birth of her son.

Toowoomba maternity concerns A confrontation caught on body-worn security footage in the halls of the Toowoomba Hospital maternity unit highlights concerns raised by local mothers.

A panel wrote the report, which was prepared by independent experts who examined Darling Downs Health's response to five previous reviews and investigations into the service since 2018 and the 117 recommendations made.

The experts highlight how long the report took to finalise: an Internal Maternity Services Review Report was commissioned in August 2018 but was not received by the chief executive until October last year.

Focus on complaints

A significant portion of the review focused on how complaints were handled at the hospital, particularly on maternity outcomes since January 1, 2025.

It found the hospital had no dedicated maternity complaints service and described "barriers to raising concerns, poor visibility of complaint pathways, dissatisfaction with responses, poor communication, lack of follow-up, and a perception that complaints did not lead to meaningful resolution or change."

"In particular, concerns raised in real time during care were sometimes experienced as dismissed, minimised or redirected into formal processes without meaningful response."

The review found policy change was "early in its lifecycle" and not yet embedded into routine practice at the maternity ward.

"The service is still transitioning from a reactive model of governance to a more proactive, evidence-based approach," the report said.

The panellists identified a "significant risk" that the specific details from the 117 previous recommendations may have been "inadvertently overlooked" when being broadly summarised in Darling Downs Health' Master Action Plan.

Director-General of Queensland Health David Rosengren said Darling Downs Health was considering the opportunities identified by the review to strengthen the complaints process and support community confidence in maternity outcomes "as a matter of priority".

"Queensland Health values the opportunity to improve its processes and services, and I thank staff and consumers for their participation in the assurance review."

World.title: Hunt continues for man who allegedly attacked parents and brother with axe
World.content:
Police are urging people to remain vigilant and report any sightings of a man who allegedly attacked his parents and brother with an axe in Victoria's east.

On Saturday, Peter O'Ryan, 48, allegedly set upon his elderly mother and father, and brother with an axe at a home in Tyers, about two hours east of Melbourne.

Police are continuing their investigation at the Cowies Road home and have issued a warrant for his arrest.

Police gathering evidence at the crime scene in Tyers on Monday morning. (ABC Gippsland: Jack Colantuono)

The man's 76-year-old father and 47-year-old brother were yesterday flown to The Alfred hospital in Melbourne with life-threatening injuries, while his 74-year-old mother was also transported to hospital with critical injuries.

All of the victims are in stable condition.

Detective Inspector Mark Rossiter said extra police resources had been called to the area to continue the manhunt across the Latrobe Valley.

"We searched the areas in the immediate vicinity of the residential premises with no luck," Mr Rossiter said.

"Our intelligence suggests that O'Ryan isn't a bushman or a bush person, and whilst it's likely that he headed into that area, he's more known to frequent towns like Morwell and staying in abandoned houses and the like," he said.

Detective Inspector Mark Rossiter says Mr O'Ryan tends to frequent abandoned houses. (ABC News: Danielle Pope)

Authorities said Mr O'Ryan was a Tyers local and "very well known to police".

He said police had not found the assault weapon, and believed Mr O'Ryan could be armed.

Community remains vigilant

Police said there was nothing to suggest Mr O'Ryan posed a threat to the community.

"Whilst we urge people to be vigilant … there has been no intelligence to suggest that Peter O'Ryan would harm anybody else," Mr Rossiter said.

"This was an attack on people known to him, family members … early investigations have revealed that it probably resulted after an argument.

"Our intelligence isn't suggesting that there are any further threats to the community."

Mr O'Ryan was last seen wearing a mustard coloured jacket and carrying a black backpack.

Police are asking anyone who has CCTV or dash camera footage around the Tyers area to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Boys arrested over alleged assault at Adelaide youth detention facility
World.content:
Two teenagers have been arrested for allegedly assaulting a staff member at the Adelaide Youth Training Centre on Sunday night.

SA Police said STAR Group officers attended the centre and arrested the boys, aged 15 and 17, who had allegedly barricaded themselves in a room.

Police said the boys, who were allegedly armed with what were described as "makeshift weapons", assaulted a Youth Justice worker "and were causing extensive damage within a section of the centre".

The assaulted staff member at the Cavan facility sustained minor injuries, police said.

Police were initially called about 8pm and said that STAR Group officers entered the room where the boys were barricaded about 9:55pm.

The pair was arrested "without further incident" and charged with aggravated assault, property damage and aggravated affray.

They are expected to appear in the Adelaide Youth Court today.

World.title: Bathla stands down 213 staff, secures two-week funding extension
World.content:
The debt-ridden Bathla Group has reached a short-term funding agreement with five of its lenders which will continue its survival for another two weeks.

The property developer's administrator, Teneo, says this funding will allow construction to continue on those lenders' construction projects.

However, construction on other projects will be suspended today, resulting in approximately 213 employees being stood down.

The group has around 350 employees, many of whom are on working visas, who found out their fate on Monday morning at an all-staff meeting.

Administrators would not reveal which lenders had provided the temporary lifeline or which of Bathla's 45 projects were still going ahead.

Bathla's administrators have stood down 200 of its staff. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Administrator Stephen Longley said that although funding had been secured, they needed more if the group would be able to keep functioning in two weeks' time.

"The arrangements agreed today allow us to provide the central support required for construction to continue on projects associated with the lenders participating in the funding package," Mr Longley said in a statement.

"Significant work remains to secure the funding required to progress and ultimately complete all projects currently under construction.

"We will continue to work closely with lenders and other key stakeholders to pursue those arrangements."

Embattled developer

Bathla plunged into administration at the end of August after being unable to pay its $3.4 billion in debts.

The appointed administrators, Teneo, managed to reach an 11th-hour funding deal last Thursday to meet Bathla's payroll obligations that day, after revealing that some staff had not been paid for eight weeks.

Administrators estimate supporting construction would cost the business about $1 million to $1.3 million a week, depending on which projects continue.

Bathla is one of Sydney's biggest residential property developers, with a large pipeline of housing projects and land holdings across the region.

Its administration has left the fate of 200 projects across NSW in jeopardy, with roughly 2,000 homes under construction and another 13,000 in its development pipeline.

Administrators had tried tapping existing lenders for extra funds and in late August asked the New South Wales government for a $20 million lifeline to keep the business afloat.

However, the state government refused to offer any bailout money.

World.title: Man charged over alleged stabbing at Spotlight store
World.content:
One man has been charged and another remains in custody after a Spotlight staff member was allegedly stabbed at the rear of the store in Hobart's northern suburbs.

Police said they were called to the incident on Howard Road at Glenorchy about 1:35pm on Sunday.

They allege two men approached the rear of the store and stole an item.

An employee who approached the pair was assaulted, police said.

The employee was taken to the Royal Hobart Hospital and received medical assistance for a small knife wound. He has since been released.

Police arrested two men overnight, charging a 28-year-old man with wounding, common assault, stealing, and drug and bail-related offences.

He was detained in custody to appear in the Hobart Magistrates Court today.

Another man remains in custody assisting police with their enquiries.

Call for 'zero-tolerance' response

In response to violent crime in the city, the independent member for Elwick, Bec Thomas, has called for a "united, zero-tolerance response".

Tasmanian MLC Bec Thomas says urgent progress is needed on planned reforms aimed at reducing crime in her electorate. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"My thoughts are with the injured worker, his family and colleagues, and everyone who witnessed or was affected by this frightening incident," Ms Thomas said.

"No-one should go to work fearing they may be threatened, assaulted or stabbed. No customer should have to witness violence while simply going about their day.

"Whether a wound is small or serious, the act of violence and the fear and trauma it causes are not minor.

"Violence against workers and in public places must never be normalised."

Ms Thomas has long been calling for a range of measures to address crime in her electorate, including workplace protection orders, stronger powers and training for shopping centre security guards, as well as measures to limit access to knives and other sharp objects.

"I welcomed the government's June announcement that it would introduce workplace protection orders, but three months later the community is still waiting for draft legislation," Ms Thomas said.

She is also calling for the Police Offences Amendment (Knives and Prohibited Weapons) Bill 2026 to be progressed.

The draft bill proposes banning the sale or supply of knives to people under 18 and requiring secure storage and signage by retailers.

"Enough is enough. Glenorchy residents, workers and businesses deserve action, not another round of regret after someone has been hurt," she said.

Government minister Nick Duigan has described the alleged stabbing at Spotlight as unacceptable and said people should be able to go about their day safely.

In response to Ms Thomas's call for faster progression of laws relating to violent crime, he said: "We have got legislation coming; it has been out for consultation."

"That's important but it's also important to recognise we've giving police [knife] wanding powers so we've leant in there to give them the tools that they need to keep our community safe," he said.

"We take the issue very seriously, we want to be proactive on it and we are introducing a number of pieces of legislation to keep our community safe."

World.title: Labuschagne retained for South Africa Test series despite pressure
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne will travel to South Africa for next month's Test tour of South Africa after being named in a 16-man squad.

There have been calls for the number three to be dropped after more than three years without a Test century, but the 32-year-old has kept his spot for the tour despite being left out of the side for six ODIs leading up to the Test series.

Australia's men's team will play three ODIs against Zimbabwe in Harare followed by three more 50-over games against South Africa in Durban, Johannesburg and Potchefstroom before the Tests in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).

Chairman of selectors George Bailey said a pure focus on red-ball cricket "may be a benefit" for Labuschagne.

"Not shying away from the fact we'd like some more runs from Marn, that's clear," he said.

"But we're also confident he can still make a positive contribution to that squad."

Labuschagne has never played a Test in South Africa, where he was born and spent the first 10 years of his life.

Big-hitting Cooper Connolly, spinner Matthew Kuhnemann and seamer Michael Neser, another South Africa-born Australian, have been added to the group that contested the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay last month.

Bailey said Connolly, who bowls part-time spin, had been selected primarily for his batting, with Josh Inglis the only other batter in the squad outside the XI from the Bangladesh series.

Both players have traditionally batted in the middle order in first-class cricket.

It leaves the team without a huge number of options for change if the batting line-up continues to struggle.

"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," he admitted.

"But we've continued to win a lot of Test matches over that period and that ultimately is the key, scoring more runs than the opposition."

Australia Test squad: Pat Cummins (c), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Matthew Kuhnemann, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Michael Neser, Matthew Renshaw, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc, Beau Webster

World.title: Granddaughter snaps up historic fishing shack for $1.82 million
World.content:
PropertyNewsQueensland residential property Granddaughter snaps up historic fishing shack for $1.82 million Sarah Webb September 7, 2026 — 11:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An old fishing shack on one of Wynnum’s best streets has sold for $1.82 million, snapped up in a pre-auction deal by the deceased owner’s granddaughter. The rugged two-bedroom cottage features a cold room for the daily catch and a 923-square-metre block just metres from the waterfront at 11 Alkoomie Street. While it was built in the ’70s, the land has remained in the hands of pioneer fishing family the Castners for four generations. After her pre-auction offer was accepted last week, that legacy is set to live on for a fifth.



The Wynnum shack was one of 128 scheduled auctions across South East Queensland over the past week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary clearance rate of 17 per cent from 90 reported results, with five homes withdrawn. The “weak” auction figures follow fresh reports Brisbane dwelling values dipped in August. A two-bedroom cottage just metres from the Wynnum waterfront at 11 Alkoomie Street has sold for $1.82 million. McGrath Wynnum/Manly AMP chief economist Dr Shane Oliver said the Queensland capital had been “whacked” by poor affordability, predicting prices to fall as much as 15 per cent in the coming year. “Brisbane is getting hit hard because it’s coming off the top of a massive boom where prices surged dramatically and that has left the market vulnerable,” he said.



“And it’s gotten a bit worse because of the likelihood of more rate rises and the ongoing tax issues with investors.” Cotality figures for August revealed Brisbane dwelling prices fell 1 per cent to $1,080,142. The house was built in the 1970s, while the land has remained in the hands of the Castner family for generations. McGrath Wynnum/Manly Given Brisbane property prices doubled in the space of a few years during the pandemic-era boom, Oliver said the fall was far from disastrous and called the price correction inevitable. Gaby McEwan of McGrath Wynnum, who put away the historic Alkoomie Street deal, said about 28 groups inspected the home throughout the auction campaign.



“We didn’t get a huge amount of interest but that’s the market right now,” she said. “I think the bottom end of the market has taken a big smack because all the investors are dumping their properties and first-home buyers are stretched at a million dollars. “I’m seeing a 10 per cent drop in property prices now.” For the Castner family, however, the pre-auction sale delivered a fairytale ending. “This parcel has been in the family for well over 100 years - they’re a legendary fishing family in the area,” she said.



“Bert Castner built the home in the ’70s but he actually grew up in the house next door – at 15 Alkoomie - which also remains in the family. The home has long been held by the Castner family, with the late Bert (pictured at back), Darcy holding grandson River (back right), Shane (right) and the buyer’s brother, Reece in the foreground. “It’s a small but wonderfully tangible piece of Wynnum’s old fishing history … and now it’s beginning another chapter in Castner hands.” McEwan said the young family would restore the home. “That whole area is being gentrified and until a few weeks ago that street had the highest-recorded sale price in the suburb at $4,005,000,” she said.



In Indooroopilly, a 1920s Queenslander on a 1017-square-metre block at 11 Essex Road sold for $2.525 million to a young upsizing family bidding over the phone from Stradbroke Island. They were the sole bidders on the property, which features five bedrooms, a pool and character finishings. While it sold above reserve, auctioneer Sam Kelso, of Place, said just six months ago it would have fetched between $2.7 million and 2.8 million. “There were a lot of people interested in it because it’s a massive block and a beautiful Queenslander but at the end of the day it came down to people’s desire to renovate,” he said.



“Some buyers brought builders through to get an idea of the cost and they got scared away. I think if the house wasn’t there it would have been worth more. “But it’s character listed so it can’t be knocked down.” The property was a deceased estate that had remained in the same family for decades. “The other interesting trend I’ve noticed is with investors. I haven’t seen any for months, but this is the first weekend I saw some come back. “Rent prices are up and property prices are a bit down so I think there’s actually a huge opportunity in the residential sector.”



In Carindale, a five-bedroom home with a pool at 145 Cribb Road sold for $80,000 below reserve after a local couple outbid two others – paying $2.02 million. Perched on an 807-square-metre block in the Mansfield State High School catchment, the solid brick home has remained in the same family for almost three decades. Selling agent Will Torres, of Torres Property, said the buyers attempted to secure the home for $1.8 million ahead of the auction. “We definitely sold it for more than we would have if we’d tried to counter that pre-auction offer,” said Torres.



“I think they needed to see the competition.” Torres said 81 groups inspected the home with local buyers dominating the pool. “The reserve was set at $2.1 million, so we were $80,000 shy of that but if you look at the market there’s been a price change of up to 10 and 15 per cent,” he said. “I do think we’ll see our market drop a bit more.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Five killed as Amazon plane overruns runway, hitting vehicles and bursting into flames
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaAviation Five killed as Amazon plane overruns runway, hitting vehicles and bursting into flames Updated September 7, 2026 — 11:38am ,first published September 7, 2026 — 6:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Miami: An Amazon cargo plane has barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said. The aircraft overran the runway about 2pm on Sunday (4am Monday AEST) after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and ploughed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Loading Five people were killed, three critically injured, and two others hospitalised with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference. It wasn’t immediately clear whether the pilots survived or whether those killed were all in vehicles when the plane struck.



The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle. The crash halted flights at the airport, a busy travel hub, for most of Sunday afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. An Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport on Sunday (Florida time). Getty Images Firefighters used foam from specialised airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later. The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, according to images. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.



The cause had yet to be determined, and it was unclear if the weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 48 km/h were recorded in the area at the time, according to the US National Weather Service. The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24. More than 160 flights were cancelled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 320 kilometres north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there. The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami, led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy, to investigate.



Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation. Related Article Air accident Fatigue cracks found in US cargo plane that crashed on take-off killing 14 “We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.” Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said that a 767 cargo aircraft would typically be flown only by a pilot and copilot on domestic flights. A third pilot would be added for an international flight, and a long-haul international flight would require a fourth pilot.



Arroyo, a retired longtime United Airlines pilot, said he wants to know whether the Amazon plane landed in the touchdown zone of the runway, and if it was beyond that area, why it didn’t simply abort that landing and go around to line up for another attempt. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 914 metres of a runway. “Did the aircraft land within the required touchdown zone?” he asked. “If it did, what happened?” Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the Transportation Department, said that footage posted online of the landing showed the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground. View post on X “It didn’t touch down right away, and so it lost a lot of critical real estate by just continuing to float over the runway. It was literally still flying,” Schiavo said.



She noted that the Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems, which the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide, to safely stop planes that go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways. World.title: ‘We won’t cop it’: Police blast spate of bloody attacks across Sydney
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime ‘We won’t cop it’: Police blast spate of bloody attacks across Sydney Jack Gramenz Updated September 7, 2026 — 11:36am ,first published September 7, 2026 — 7:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police have blasted “unacceptable” violence on Sydney’s streets following a spate of unrelated attacks across the city that left several people in hospital. Three men filtered into Canterbury Hospital in the early hours of Monday morning with stab wounds following an alleged altercation outside a kebab shop on the corner of Canterbury Road and Fore Street at Canterbury. Loading Paramedics then transported the men to trauma hospitals. Two of the men, aged 23 and 24, were in a serious but stable condition, while a third man, 18, was stable. Detective Chief Superintendent Christine McDonald said the 24-year-old man and 18-year-old man were related, and arrived together at the location, before an alleged altercation with the 23-year-old.



“They are the three main people that we are looking at … we’ll continue looking into the reason why the altercation happened in the first place and whether anyone else is involved,” she said. “Their behaviour is completely unacceptable.” Forensic officers at the scene in Canterbury where three men were allegedly stabbed in an altercation. Nine It’s unclear what the men were doing in the area. “From the footage that I’ve seen, no one’s eating a kebab,” McDonald said.



In another incident on Sunday night, a 19-year-old was hospitalised after being stabbed during an alleged attempt to collect a debt. The teenager arrived at a home on Ingham Avenue in Five Dock along with his 63-year-old father, who McDonald said believed he was owed a debt by a 36-year-old man at the home. The 63-year-old’s wife and his father, aged in his 80s, also attended, McDonald said. The 36-year-old was allegedly beaten with a metal broom pole.



It’s not yet known whether the debt related to legitimate or criminal business, but the presence of children in the home at the time the group attended was concerning. “Four people turning up to someone’s house to get a debt back when there’s young children in the house is just completely unacceptable,” McDonald said. The 63-year-old man has been charged with affray while his teenage son remains under police guard in hospital. Separately, a 38-year-old man is fighting for life after he was found with a stab wound to the stomach in Sydney’s west. The man was found injured at Moreton Bay Square, Bidwill, about 8.10pm on Sunday.



A group of about 10 men and women who attended the scene allegedly attempted to interfere with the investigation but were dispersed without further incident, police say. Related Article Crime Shot man’s family say police need to do more to control gang violence Elsewhere, a 42-year-old man and a 38-year-old woman were taken to Westmead Hospital after what police believe to be a targeted home invasion at Guildford West. About eight men forced entry into a unit on Fairfield Road about 10pm, allegedly assaulting the pair before fleeing in a black 4WD and a white dual cab ute. Police have appealed for any CCTV or dashcam footage as part of investigations into the separate incidents.



McDonald said the incidents at Canterbury and Five Dock also appeared to be targeted attacks. “People in the community can be reassured that if you’re a law-abiding [person], going about your own day, generally you’re going to be safe in our community,” McDonald said. “These people target one another, unnecessary violence, and we won’t cop it.” The targeted attacks came days after two fatal shootings believed to be mistaken identity killings. Innocent men Marco Tapia, 23, and Joshua Macdonald were killed a day apart in what police say were cases of mistaken identity.

World.title: The inside story of the downfall of a Trump-loving host at Fox News
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing The inside story of the downfall of a Trump-loving host at Fox News Jim Rutenberg , Erik Wemple and Benjamin Mullin September 7, 2026 — 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In July, as US President Donald Trump was preparing a primetime speech on election security, word went out from executives at Fox News: the network would avoid covering his stock claims about a stolen election. Fox had landed in serious legal trouble in 2021 after amplifying false assertions by Trump’s allies about vote-stealing election machines, culminating in an extraordinary $US787 million defamation settlement. Fox News has taken Maria Bartiromo off the air. AP In 2020, Fox Business host Maria Bartiromo had made her show a central stop for proponents of the president’s election theories. And this northern summer, too, she was preparing to interview presidential adviser Peter Navarro the morning after Trump’s speech. But after she received a text message written by a Fox Business executive warning against post-speech coverage, she cancelled Navarro’s appearance.



Related Article Opinion

On Background ‘I was just weak’: How an avoidant Rupert Murdoch could have warded off family fight Calum Jaspan Media Writer As she did so, she shared the executive’s text with Navarro, who promptly sent it “up the chain” to the White House, he said in an interview on Friday. It was his duty, Navarro said, to relay “yet another example of Fox personnel censoring the Trump administration”. That sequence of events, described by Navarro and two other people with knowledge of the discussions, would bring an abrupt end to Bartiromo’s on-air career at the network. The White House complained to Fox, which considered the disclosure of the communication as a breach of company policy. Fox News did not provide a comment. A lawyer for Bartiromo, Bryan Freedman, called her “one of the hardest-working journalists throughout her award-winning career”. Bartiromo’s cancellation was a dramatic split between the nation’s most-watched cable news channel and one of cable’s earlier, defining stars.



But it also revealed an important shift at the network in the years since the 2020 election – one that could have real consequences for Trump as he seeks to again assert the US election system is rife with fraud before a midterm election that, polling shows, could be rough for his party. Where in 2020 he could count on hosts like Bartiromo to air his wildest election claims on Fox’s top-rated programs without much pushback, he cannot do so now. Fox’s most popular hosts remain overwhelmingly loyal to Donald Trump, but there has been a shift in tone. AP The changes are a consequence of the legal straits the network found itself in after the election, when two voting technology companies at the heart of the stolen election theories, Dominion Voting Systems and Smartmatic, sued Fox for $US1.6 billion and $US2.7 billion, respectively, for tarnishing their reputations. The $US787.5 million settlement stemmed from the Dominion case; Fox’s litigation with Smartmatic is ongoing, adding to the incentives to be careful about promoting conspiracies this election year.



Fox is in some ways a different network than it was in late 2020, in front of the camera and behind the scenes. Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing How Murdoch the Sun King sold out the planet Fox’s chief legal officer, Viet Dinh, whose handling of the Dominion case came under question, is no longer there. Neither is a Dinh deputy and former Trump aide, Raj Shah, who helped keep the network hyper-focused on right-wing criticism when it or its hosts were viewed as being insufficiently deferential to Trump’s fraud claims after the election. Early in 2021, Fox ended the program of host Lou Dobbs, who had been among the more enthusiastic promoters of claims the presidential election was rigged. After the Dominion settlement, it parted ways with host Tucker Carlson, who was mentioned in the case but also drew advertiser boycotts with his hard dive into right-wing conspiracies. Another figure in the two voting cases, Jeanine Pirro, is now working as Trump’s US attorney for the District of Columbia.



Fox’s most popular hosts remain overwhelmingly loyal to Trump, including its primetime stars, Sean Hannity, Laura Ingraham and Jesse Watters, and the network still tilts heavily in his favour. It was alone among the major news networks to run Trump’s July speech on election integrity in full, despite the guidance on coverage. But it has also shown a willingness to break from the administration on, for instance, its military campaign in Iran, which has been criticised by some on-air hosts, including Ingraham. Anchor Bret Baier delivered a rare, on-air defence of his colleague, Jonathan Hunt, when Trump blasted his coverage of Iran. A cancelled interview with Trump adviser Peter Navarro laid the groundwork for Bartiromo’s demise. Bloomberg In the interview on Friday, Navarro, who formally serves as Trump’s senior counsellor on trade, shared his displeasure with the shift. He said the network could not be trusted to “tell the truth about certain topics”. He had no such issues with Bartiromo, whose approach – at times permitting guest commentators to free-associate on live television – had not appeared to change much in the years since the Dominion settlement. News website Puck earlier reported on Bartiromo’s conversations with Navarro.



That was clear in July, when Fox was sued for defamation after investor Kevin O’Leary, of Shark Tank fame, used Bartiromo’s show to settle a score with his detractors. He baselessly claimed that two non-profit founders in Utah who were opposing his plans for a 40,000-acre data centre near the Great Salt Lake were Chinese agents. Related Article Murdoch family case ‘Making trouble’: Murdoch family’s bitter feud exposed in court documents According to the lawsuit, Bartiromo not only failed to challenge O’Leary, she “legitimised” his accusation. Fox’s response afterward was more reflective of the post-Dominion shift. Whereas the network stonewalled Dominion when it initially complained about its election-fraud coverage, it moved more quickly to apologise after O’Leary retracted his claims. Bartiromo still has considerable time left on her contract, according to two people familiar with the matter, meaning that Fox News is still obligated to pay her millions a year despite ending her on-air role. The contract could also keep her from appearing on other networks.



Trump, who called Bartiromo a “total professional, and a true warrior” in a Truth Social post, added that her “fans, of which there are many, will not be happy”. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Europeans can take their dogs everywhere on holidays. Why can’t we?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsPets Opinion Europeans can take their dogs everywhere on holidays. Why can’t we? Jo Pybus Writer September 7, 2026 — 11:31am

September 7, 2026 — 11:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Despite all the jaw-droppingly beautiful locations I hiked through Mont Blanc and the Dolomites in Italy last month, there is one sight I can’t seem to get out of my head. It was a man hiking with his companion. In my backpack, I carried litres of water, snacks and a first aid kit. In his, a dog. Don’t leave home without it. Getty Images This was no ordinary backpack, but a canine carrier with mesh windows on three sides. The occupant, a miniature schnauzer, looked quite pleased with his journey, hardly breaking into a sweat. I’m a sucker for dogs, so this image made me smile, and I soon became accustomed to seeing people who were holidaying with their pooches. These furry family members were allowed on trains, in cafes and restaurants, and even got to sleep with their humans across the hall in my Venice hotel, then accompany them to the breakfast buffet. There is nothing notable about seeing a small child being wheeled around in a shopping trolley while their parents buy the weekly groceries, but at a supermarket in Cortina, the home of the most recent Winter Olympics, I did need a second take. While I marvelled at the prosciutto at the deli counter, a dog was sitting in a trolley next to me, without excessively salivating – the dog, not me.



According to an article in Italian newspaper La Stampa, 60 per cent of Italians surveyed seek out pet-friendly destinations for their vacation. Italy is also marketed as the most dog-friendly holiday destination in Europe, as evident when I met Auguste at Lake Como, the long-haired Dachshund from France, and Luna, the playful 12-week-old golden retriever who was holidaying with her Austrian humans. Sitz, Luna! While I marvelled at the prosciutto, a dog was sitting in a trolley next to me. Seeing families wheeling their suitcases while appeasing their hot and tired kids and leading their dog through Milano Centrale railway station was fascinating. They were heading for accommodation that welcomed dogs, sat at restaurants that welcomed dogs, both inside and out, and took them shopping in multi-level department stores. Imagine the patience required for a dog to sit while you try on clothes. I’m hard-pushed to get my husband to tolerate that. And if you think the dog’s needs are not being considered, Lonely Planet has created a travel guide for pet-friendly Italy. You can visit Scooby Doo Beach in Campomarino Lido and hire a suite – picture a family-sized playpen on the sand – that includes shade, lounges and water mister for all occupants. Water bowls for dogs only. I can imagine the red flags this raises in your mind. Allergies. Fear of dogs. Hygiene. Trip hazard. Liability. Stepping in something warm and squishy. It is one thing having to collect your dog’s poop with an inverted plastic bag from the sidewalk, but another in the first-class carriage of a Trenitalia train.



Related Article Exclusive

Disability Uber stands by sacking of driver who refused guide dog Even a person like me, who wants to cuddle every dog I pass, was looking out for tripwires, but in six weeks I never once saw a dog misbehave or have an – ahem – accident. It became quite normal to have a dog sitting next to me while I tucked into my caprese salad. The La Stampa article cites that dogs and cats registered in Italy outnumber kids under 14 by 2.3 to 1. You may be surprised when I tell you that, remarkably, it is close to the same here in Australia. So, it raises the question, why can’t we take our dogs so easily on holidays? Should we be able to visit the Gold Coast and have Dougal the lab accompany us into every cafe, restaurant and shop we visit? Should our 15th-floor apartment be cool with a pooch sleeping in the living room? Should Coles at Pacific Fair be fine with Xena the red heeler strutting past the rotisserie chickens? It does sound like a stretch, I know, especially when we are still hearing cases of people with assistance dogs being denied transport despite it being illegal to refuse their fare. It was also apparent that these European pooches were raised with these freedoms so knew how to behave, at times better than their younger humans, I

might add.



This all got me thinking about an untapped tourism opportunity the Italians may have overlooked for those of us who can’t take our dog to Europe. If we can hire a car, a bike, skis and even travel clothes in Japan, then why not a pooch? I could be sitting in my Italian beach playpen, waiting for my gelato, while Bella the bulldog plays with her chew toy. Jo Pybus is a freelance writer. World.title: Garage doors to front doors: The unexpected spaces where Sydney could squeeze new homes
World.content:
From doors for cars to doors for people. That’s the change architect Peter McGregor says is needed to provide more housing in the overlooked rear lanes behind inner Sydney’s thousands of terraces. Faced with a shortage of affordable housing, the City of Sydney Council is considering ways to encourage “gentle density” – such as studio apartments built in the back of terraces and on top of their garages – to help deliver more homes in the dunny lanes where night soil was once collected. Peter McGregor on a Redfern laneway where many people have built studios or secondary dwellings over their garages. Sam Mooy McGregor likes the height and generosity of the home behind him, designed more than a decade ago by Raffaello Rosselli. Sam Mooy On Young Street in Redfern, McGregor designed a generous unit above the garage of his former family home with a roller door he decorated in the red and green of the Rabbitohs team colours.



It has little bunnies, as wall decorations, too. McGregor has been campaigning, though, for more generous back lane dwellings with windows that provide sun and privacy, unlike others that are too small, too high, cast shade on neighbours, have little privacy and are just big enough for a double bed. Deputy Mayor Jess Miller said planning reforms or land title structures enabling homes to be built fronting lanes had been used overseas to deliver housing in “what are generally quite protected heritage areas”. Related Article Architecture The tiny window problem creating two classes of home owners “In the UK, they came up with this idea of a ‘Torrens Terrace’, which basically enables people who have homes that are long and narrow, with a frontage to the street and a frontage to the rear laneway, to double the density of their property [by building a second dwelling],” Miller said. A Torrens title property is one where the purchaser owns the house and the land on which it is built, compared to a strata title where they own their private lot and share ownership of common spaces.



Miller said the council faced the dual challenges of increasing density and green space in the densely populated inner suburbs. The council has encouraged efforts to turn neglected laneways into green, public spaces, such as Cat Alley in Surry Hills, and Hayden Lane in Darlinghurst. But the City’s Housing for All discussion paper, which explored where and how more housing should be delivered, went a step further, suggesting the council consider tweaking planning rules to encourage more “small lot” homes, filling laneways with “front doors rather than roller doors”. Architect Peter McGregor of McGregor Westlake Architecture ouside the studio apartment he designed behind his former home, a terrace in Redfern. Sam Mooy Some of the bunnies on the back wall of the studio apartment McGregor designed. Sam Mooy The report suggested the standalone Torrens title dwellings could provide compact, liveable spaces up to two storeys high, with a rooftop terrace, along inner Sydney’s hundreds of back laneways.



The council said it had changed planning controls in Pyrmont to allow larger sites to be subdivided to create narrow lots for low-rise terraces facing laneways. The change showed how the council could introduce more small-lot housing into the area while maintaining local character. “As more small-lot homes are built, the laneways would become more attractive, walkable and safer. We already allow garages with upper levels on laneways. With adjustments, these types of buildings could become compact but high-amenity homes, providing more housing choice,” the paper said. Related Article City life First came the wedding, then the drag queens: Lane with ugly past transforms into an inner-city oasis Miller said the homes could ease housing pressures and encourage intergenerational living, providing homes for adult children or ageing parents. She noted some property owners had already built such dwellings, but said for the idea to be implemented at scale, the community would need to have a discussion about the potential trade-offs. “We’re asking people: Would you rather have rear-lane access for your car, or would you rather have two dwellings on your current title, which might effectively double the value of your property?



“There will be a range of views on that, but in areas where there is good access to public transport, it’s walkable, cycleable, and people have less need to own a car, there might be appetite for this.” Miller said Sydney had some of the world’s best architecture, landscape architecture, design minds and creative communities, and they were well-equipped to tackle design and practical challenges. Inside the Redfern tin shed: Everyone said the Young Street property’s former owner, Jane Smith, should have demolished the 80-year-old structure on her property, but Jane, pictured in 2012, loved it so much she kept it and turned it into an office. Quentin Jones “I think if there’s anywhere this can be done beautifully, it’s right here,” Miller said. For McGregor, the founder of McGregor Westlake Architecture, it feels “like Groundhog Day”. He has been urging the council to encourage more housing in back lanes for decades. (More eyes on the street made them safer too, he said.)



He said most cities around the world allowed terraces to be subdivided with Torrens titles, but McGregor’s application to subdivide his former home vertically was rejected. Related Article Exclusive

Architecture A loo with a view and no railings on ‘an impossible site’ in Sydney This works best, McGregor said, because the upstairs bedroom in a terrace is usually the largest room and makes an ideal living room for a second dwelling. His plan was rejected by council because of concerns about fire protection. This subdivision is encouraged across London, Dublin and the UK, and it is a technical issue that can be overcome. The McGregors sold the terrace and moved to an apartment. They know of two families whose larger terraces were not fit for purpose, but could be suitable for two groups, or families, to share. World.title: ‘Affordable for Coogee’: Local couple pays $2.5m for two-bedroom semi
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘Affordable for Coogee’: Local couple pays $2.5m for two-bedroom semi Carmen Forward September 7, 2026 — 11:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A local upsizing couple secured a semi in Coogee for $2.5 million at auction on Saturday, a price that the selling agent described as “affordable for Coogee”. The “half a house” at 5 Ritchard Avenue had a swimming pool, lower level with potential to improve and a lockup garage. The property was one of 709 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 57 per cent from 433 reported results throughout the week, while 125 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate Six parties registered on the two-bedroom property in the coastal postcode, with a guided range of $2.2 million to $2.4 million. Most were upsizing families, but some were builders looking to renovate.



Bidding opened at $2.3 million, instantly meeting the property’s reserve. Three parties were active, with rises of $50,000, $10,000 and $5000 to climb $200,000 above the reserve until the hammer fell at $2.5 million. Related Article Auctions Unrenovated inner west terrace sells for $355k over reserve at auction Sotheby’s Marnie Seinor said it was a “good opportunity for lots of young families to upgrade”. “People are just nervous about spending the money [on] marketing, and people are just holding for fear of not selling. But things are selling, and this is an example of that.” She said the property is a “semi … a half a house”.



“It’s affordable for Coogee, and it was livable and then lends itself to a lot of potential.” The buyers are upsizing from an apartment in Coogee. The vendor has moved to aged care. The home last traded for $390,000 in 1994, records show. In Cremorne, a clean and tidy three-bedroom apartment sold for $3.5 million to a downsizer from Riverview. The boutique unit with leafy water views at 7/45 Grasmere Road had a guide of $3 million and drew three registrations who all participated.



Bidding opened at $2.9 million and rose in $50,000 and $25,000 increments at a rapid pace before the apartment sold under the hammer for $300,000 above its $3.2 million reserve. Related Article Sydney house prices The prestige Sydney suburb where house prices fell most over a year There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Belle Property’s Matthew Smythe said: “It’s a good market for downsizers and upsizers. Upsizers, clearly financially; it’s a huge win for them because they can step up and save money on the changeover costs.” “But for downsizers as well. If you want to buy a lifestyle, it’s already cheaper than it was six months ago, and the smart ones understand that and want to get on with the next 10 years of their life.”



The vendor is moving to Queensland. The unit last traded for $1,815,000 in 2012, records show. In Lindfield, a well-maintained three-bedroom unit at 21/2B Havilah Road drew two registered bidders. The apartment on a quiet leafy street was guided at $2.58 million and had a reserve of $2.6 million. It sold below its guide, and $150,000 under its reserve, for $2.45 million. Only one bidder made an offer, opening the auction at $2.3 million, and then increased it to $2.4 million. Negotiations further lifted the price to $2.42 million before a final offer was made of $2.45 million. The vendor accepted, adjusting their reserve to sell.



Ray White’s Jessica Cao said: “A lot of my vendors at the moment, they’re downsizing. Yes, the market’s different. However, if they buy and sell in the same market, it doesn’t matter too much.” Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Retail boss lists $17m ‘interim’ home as he moves into Swans chairman’s $40m abode “What I do see is my downsizer vendors are pretty cautious. They want to sell first to know how much money they have before they commit [at] the other end.” The buyer is downsizing from a five-bedroom home in Lindfield. The vendor is relocating overseas. The flat last traded for $1,528,000 in 2014, records show.



AMP chief economist Dr Shane Oliver said that Domain’s clearance rate of 57 per cent for Sydney was “still a weak market”. “To me, it remains a perfect storm for the property market. We’ve got higher and rising interest rates. We’ve got big tax changes making it far less attractive for property investors, and we’ve got poor levels of confidence.” Oliver expected another rate hike and said debate centred on whether there would be two more hikes. “Because vendors are holding back, that’s limiting the supply, and consequently, the clearance rate has been able to rise because we’ve got less listings, so it’s not necessarily a sign of strength,” he said. “The only thing that’s helping the market is that vendors are holding off, possibly hoping for better prices.” Oliver said the real test will come once the spring selling season picks up in October.

World.title: The one thing I will use AI for when travelling
World.content:
If you’re at all familiar with my work, chances are you’ve heard me rant about the value of learning a language. It doesn’t take much. A few hours of study and you can revolutionise your experience in a country, opening doors that would have otherwise stayed closed to your typical tourist.

I know what you’re thinking. You’re thinking that study sounds like just the sort of thing a barely employed travel writer has time to do. It’s not something for someone with a job, a family and obligations that go beyond getting dressed in the morning.

Illustration: Greg Straight

The good news (or bad news, if you’re a rainforest) is that thanks to AI, learning a language has never been easier. And while it pains me to write this – given my general resentment for how much AI is being rammed down our throats these days – it has changed my approach to language learning.

AI can tailor lessons to you as an individual. Using voice mode on Gemini or ChatGPT, it can even respond to your questions and correct your pronunciation (although I’d still recommend YouTube for a more natural immersion). Most importantly, it can reveal things about a culture that would have otherwise been invisible to even the most seasoned travellers.

World.title: Granddaughter snaps up historic fishing shack for $1.82 million
World.content:
PropertyNewsQueensland residential property Granddaughter snaps up historic fishing shack for $1.82 million Sarah Webb September 7, 2026 — 11:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An old fishing shack on one of Wynnum’s best streets has sold for $1.82 million, snapped up in a pre-auction deal by the deceased owner’s granddaughter. The rugged two-bedroom cottage features a cold room for the daily catch and a 923-square-metre block just metres from the waterfront at 11 Alkoomie Street. While it was built in the ’70s, the land has remained in the hands of pioneer fishing family the Castners for four generations. After her pre-auction offer was accepted last week, that legacy is set to live on for a fifth.



The Wynnum shack was one of 128 scheduled auctions across South East Queensland over the past week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary clearance rate of 17 per cent from 90 reported results, with five homes withdrawn. The “weak” auction figures follow fresh reports Brisbane dwelling values dipped in August. A two-bedroom cottage just metres from the Wynnum waterfront at 11 Alkoomie Street has sold for $1.82 million. McGrath Wynnum/Manly AMP chief economist Dr Shane Oliver said the Queensland capital had been “whacked” by poor affordability, predicting prices to fall as much as 15 per cent in the coming year. “Brisbane is getting hit hard because it’s coming off the top of a massive boom where prices surged dramatically and that has left the market vulnerable,” he said.



“And it’s gotten a bit worse because of the likelihood of more rate rises and the ongoing tax issues with investors.” Cotality figures for August revealed Brisbane dwelling prices fell 1 per cent to $1,080,142. The house was built in the 1970s, while the land has remained in the hands of the Castner family for generations. McGrath Wynnum/Manly Given Brisbane property prices doubled in the space of a few years during the pandemic-era boom, Oliver said the fall was far from disastrous and called the price correction inevitable. Gaby McEwan of McGrath Wynnum, who put away the historic Alkoomie Street deal, said about 28 groups inspected the home throughout the auction campaign.



“We didn’t get a huge amount of interest but that’s the market right now,” she said. “I think the bottom end of the market has taken a big smack because all the investors are dumping their properties and first-home buyers are stretched at a million dollars. “I’m seeing a 10 per cent drop in property prices now.” For the Castner family, however, the pre-auction sale delivered a fairytale ending. “This parcel has been in the family for well over 100 years - they’re a legendary fishing family in the area,” she said.



“Bert Castner built the home in the ’70s but he actually grew up in the house next door – at 15 Alkoomie - which also remains in the family. The home has long been held by the Castner family, with the late Bert (pictured at back), Darcy holding grandson River (back right), Shane (right) and the buyer’s brother, Reece in the foreground. “It’s a small but wonderfully tangible piece of Wynnum’s old fishing history … and now it’s beginning another chapter in Castner hands.” McEwan said the young family would restore the home. “That whole area is being gentrified and until a few weeks ago that street had the highest-recorded sale price in the suburb at $4,005,000,” she said.



In Indooroopilly, a 1920s Queenslander on a 1017-square-metre block at 11 Essex Road sold for $2.525 million to a young upsizing family bidding over the phone from Stradbroke Island. They were the sole bidders on the property, which features five bedrooms, a pool and character finishings. While it sold above reserve, auctioneer Sam Kelso, of Place, said just six months ago it would have fetched between $2.7 million and 2.8 million. “There were a lot of people interested in it because it’s a massive block and a beautiful Queenslander but at the end of the day it came down to people’s desire to renovate,” he said.



“Some buyers brought builders through to get an idea of the cost and they got scared away. I think if the house wasn’t there it would have been worth more. “But it’s character listed so it can’t be knocked down.” The property was a deceased estate that had remained in the same family for decades. “The other interesting trend I’ve noticed is with investors. I haven’t seen any for months, but this is the first weekend I saw some come back. “Rent prices are up and property prices are a bit down so I think there’s actually a huge opportunity in the residential sector.”



In Carindale, a five-bedroom home with a pool at 145 Cribb Road sold for $80,000 below reserve after a local couple outbid two others – paying $2.02 million. Perched on an 807-square-metre block in the Mansfield State High School catchment, the solid brick home has remained in the same family for almost three decades. Selling agent Will Torres, of Torres Property, said the buyers attempted to secure the home for $1.8 million ahead of the auction. “We definitely sold it for more than we would have if we’d tried to counter that pre-auction offer,” said Torres.



“I think they needed to see the competition.” Torres said 81 groups inspected the home with local buyers dominating the pool. “The reserve was set at $2.1 million, so we were $80,000 shy of that but if you look at the market there’s been a price change of up to 10 and 15 per cent,” he said. “I do think we’ll see our market drop a bit more.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Five killed as Amazon plane overruns runway, hitting vehicles and bursting into flames
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaAviation Five killed as Amazon plane overruns runway, hitting vehicles and bursting into flames Updated September 7, 2026 — 11:38am ,first published September 7, 2026 — 6:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Miami: An Amazon cargo plane has barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said. The aircraft overran the runway about 2pm on Sunday (4am Monday AEST) after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and ploughed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Loading Five people were killed, three critically injured, and two others hospitalised with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference. It wasn’t immediately clear whether the pilots survived or whether those killed were all in vehicles when the plane struck.



The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle. The crash halted flights at the airport, a busy travel hub, for most of Sunday afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. An Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport on Sunday (Florida time). Getty Images Firefighters used foam from specialised airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later. The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, according to images. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.



The cause had yet to be determined, and it was unclear if the weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 48 km/h were recorded in the area at the time, according to the US National Weather Service. The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24. More than 160 flights were cancelled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 320 kilometres north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there. The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami, led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy, to investigate.



Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation. Related Article Air accident Fatigue cracks found in US cargo plane that crashed on take-off killing 14 “We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.” Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said that a 767 cargo aircraft would typically be flown only by a pilot and copilot on domestic flights. A third pilot would be added for an international flight, and a long-haul international flight would require a fourth pilot.



Arroyo, a retired longtime United Airlines pilot, said he wants to know whether the Amazon plane landed in the touchdown zone of the runway, and if it was beyond that area, why it didn’t simply abort that landing and go around to line up for another attempt. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 914 metres of a runway. “Did the aircraft land within the required touchdown zone?” he asked. “If it did, what happened?” Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the Transportation Department, said that footage posted online of the landing showed the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground. View post on X “It didn’t touch down right away, and so it lost a lot of critical real estate by just continuing to float over the runway. It was literally still flying,” Schiavo said.



She noted that the Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems, which the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide, to safely stop planes that go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.
