World.title: ‘We won’t cop it’: Police blast spate of bloody attacks across Sydney
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime ‘We won’t cop it’: Police blast spate of bloody attacks across Sydney Jack Gramenz Updated September 7, 2026 — 11:36am ,first published September 7, 2026 — 7:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police have blasted “unacceptable” violence on Sydney’s streets following a spate of unrelated attacks across the city that left several people in hospital. Three men filtered into Canterbury Hospital in the early hours of Monday morning with stab wounds following an alleged altercation outside a kebab shop on the corner of Canterbury Road and Fore Street at Canterbury. Loading Paramedics then transported the men to trauma hospitals. Two of the men, aged 23 and 24, were in a serious but stable condition, while a third man, 18, was stable. Detective Chief Superintendent Christine McDonald said the 24-year-old man and 18-year-old man were related, and arrived together at the location, before an alleged altercation with the 23-year-old.



“They are the three main people that we are looking at … we’ll continue looking into the reason why the altercation happened in the first place and whether anyone else is involved,” she said. “Their behaviour is completely unacceptable.” Forensic officers at the scene in Canterbury where three men were allegedly stabbed in an altercation. Nine It’s unclear what the men were doing in the area. “From the footage that I’ve seen, no one’s eating a kebab,” McDonald said.



In another incident on Sunday night, a 19-year-old was hospitalised after being stabbed during an alleged attempt to collect a debt. The teenager arrived at a home on Ingham Avenue in Five Dock along with his 63-year-old father, who McDonald said believed he was owed a debt by a 36-year-old man at the home. The 63-year-old’s wife and his father, aged in his 80s, also attended, McDonald said. The 36-year-old was allegedly beaten with a metal broom pole.



It’s not yet known whether the debt related to legitimate or criminal business, but the presence of children in the home at the time the group attended was concerning. “Four people turning up to someone’s house to get a debt back when there’s young children in the house is just completely unacceptable,” McDonald said. The 63-year-old man has been charged with affray while his teenage son remains under police guard in hospital. Separately, a 38-year-old man is fighting for life after he was found with a stab wound to the stomach in Sydney’s west. The man was found injured at Moreton Bay Square, Bidwill, about 8.10pm on Sunday.



A group of about 10 men and women who attended the scene allegedly attempted to interfere with the investigation but were dispersed without further incident, police say. Related Article Crime Shot man’s family say police need to do more to control gang violence Elsewhere, a 42-year-old man and a 38-year-old woman were taken to Westmead Hospital after what police believe to be a targeted home invasion at Guildford West. About eight men forced entry into a unit on Fairfield Road about 10pm, allegedly assaulting the pair before fleeing in a black 4WD and a white dual cab ute. Police have appealed for any CCTV or dashcam footage as part of investigations into the separate incidents.



McDonald said the incidents at Canterbury and Five Dock also appeared to be targeted attacks. “People in the community can be reassured that if you’re a law-abiding [person], going about your own day, generally you’re going to be safe in our community,” McDonald said. “These people target one another, unnecessary violence, and we won’t cop it.” The targeted attacks came days after two fatal shootings believed to be mistaken identity killings. Innocent men Marco Tapia, 23, and Joshua Macdonald were killed a day apart in what police say were cases of mistaken identity.

World.title: The inside story of the downfall of a Trump-loving host at Fox News
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing The inside story of the downfall of a Trump-loving host at Fox News Jim Rutenberg , Erik Wemple and Benjamin Mullin September 7, 2026 — 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In July, as US President Donald Trump was preparing a primetime speech on election security, word went out from executives at Fox News: the network would avoid covering his stock claims about a stolen election. Fox had landed in serious legal trouble in 2021 after amplifying false assertions by Trump’s allies about vote-stealing election machines, culminating in an extraordinary $US787 million defamation settlement. Fox News has taken Maria Bartiromo off the air. AP In 2020, Fox Business host Maria Bartiromo had made her show a central stop for proponents of the president’s election theories. And this northern summer, too, she was preparing to interview presidential adviser Peter Navarro the morning after Trump’s speech. But after she received a text message written by a Fox Business executive warning against post-speech coverage, she cancelled Navarro’s appearance.



Related Article Opinion

On Background ‘I was just weak’: How an avoidant Rupert Murdoch could have warded off family fight Calum Jaspan Media Writer As she did so, she shared the executive’s text with Navarro, who promptly sent it “up the chain” to the White House, he said in an interview on Friday. It was his duty, Navarro said, to relay “yet another example of Fox personnel censoring the Trump administration”. That sequence of events, described by Navarro and two other people with knowledge of the discussions, would bring an abrupt end to Bartiromo’s on-air career at the network. The White House complained to Fox, which considered the disclosure of the communication as a breach of company policy. Fox News did not provide a comment. A lawyer for Bartiromo, Bryan Freedman, called her “one of the hardest-working journalists throughout her award-winning career”. Bartiromo’s cancellation was a dramatic split between the nation’s most-watched cable news channel and one of cable’s earlier, defining stars.



But it also revealed an important shift at the network in the years since the 2020 election – one that could have real consequences for Trump as he seeks to again assert the US election system is rife with fraud before a midterm election that, polling shows, could be rough for his party. Where in 2020 he could count on hosts like Bartiromo to air his wildest election claims on Fox’s top-rated programs without much pushback, he cannot do so now. Fox’s most popular hosts remain overwhelmingly loyal to Donald Trump, but there has been a shift in tone. AP The changes are a consequence of the legal straits the network found itself in after the election, when two voting technology companies at the heart of the stolen election theories, Dominion Voting Systems and Smartmatic, sued Fox for $US1.6 billion and $US2.7 billion, respectively, for tarnishing their reputations. The $US787.5 million settlement stemmed from the Dominion case; Fox’s litigation with Smartmatic is ongoing, adding to the incentives to be careful about promoting conspiracies this election year.



Fox is in some ways a different network than it was in late 2020, in front of the camera and behind the scenes. Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing How Murdoch the Sun King sold out the planet Fox’s chief legal officer, Viet Dinh, whose handling of the Dominion case came under question, is no longer there. Neither is a Dinh deputy and former Trump aide, Raj Shah, who helped keep the network hyper-focused on right-wing criticism when it or its hosts were viewed as being insufficiently deferential to Trump’s fraud claims after the election. Early in 2021, Fox ended the program of host Lou Dobbs, who had been among the more enthusiastic promoters of claims the presidential election was rigged. After the Dominion settlement, it parted ways with host Tucker Carlson, who was mentioned in the case but also drew advertiser boycotts with his hard dive into right-wing conspiracies. Another figure in the two voting cases, Jeanine Pirro, is now working as Trump’s US attorney for the District of Columbia.



Fox’s most popular hosts remain overwhelmingly loyal to Trump, including its primetime stars, Sean Hannity, Laura Ingraham and Jesse Watters, and the network still tilts heavily in his favour. It was alone among the major news networks to run Trump’s July speech on election integrity in full, despite the guidance on coverage. But it has also shown a willingness to break from the administration on, for instance, its military campaign in Iran, which has been criticised by some on-air hosts, including Ingraham. Anchor Bret Baier delivered a rare, on-air defence of his colleague, Jonathan Hunt, when Trump blasted his coverage of Iran. A cancelled interview with Trump adviser Peter Navarro laid the groundwork for Bartiromo’s demise. Bloomberg In the interview on Friday, Navarro, who formally serves as Trump’s senior counsellor on trade, shared his displeasure with the shift. He said the network could not be trusted to “tell the truth about certain topics”. He had no such issues with Bartiromo, whose approach – at times permitting guest commentators to free-associate on live television – had not appeared to change much in the years since the Dominion settlement. News website Puck earlier reported on Bartiromo’s conversations with Navarro.



That was clear in July, when Fox was sued for defamation after investor Kevin O’Leary, of Shark Tank fame, used Bartiromo’s show to settle a score with his detractors. He baselessly claimed that two non-profit founders in Utah who were opposing his plans for a 40,000-acre data centre near the Great Salt Lake were Chinese agents. Related Article Murdoch family case ‘Making trouble’: Murdoch family’s bitter feud exposed in court documents According to the lawsuit, Bartiromo not only failed to challenge O’Leary, she “legitimised” his accusation. Fox’s response afterward was more reflective of the post-Dominion shift. Whereas the network stonewalled Dominion when it initially complained about its election-fraud coverage, it moved more quickly to apologise after O’Leary retracted his claims. Bartiromo still has considerable time left on her contract, according to two people familiar with the matter, meaning that Fox News is still obligated to pay her millions a year despite ending her on-air role. The contract could also keep her from appearing on other networks.



Trump, who called Bartiromo a “total professional, and a true warrior” in a Truth Social post, added that her “fans, of which there are many, will not be happy”. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Europeans can take their dogs everywhere on holidays. Why can’t we?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsPets Opinion Europeans can take their dogs everywhere on holidays. Why can’t we? Jo Pybus Writer September 7, 2026 — 11:31am

September 7, 2026 — 11:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Despite all the jaw-droppingly beautiful locations I hiked through Mont Blanc and the Dolomites in Italy last month, there is one sight I can’t seem to get out of my head. It was a man hiking with his companion. In my backpack, I carried litres of water, snacks and a first aid kit. In his, a dog. Don’t leave home without it. Getty Images This was no ordinary backpack, but a canine carrier with mesh windows on three sides. The occupant, a miniature schnauzer, looked quite pleased with his journey, hardly breaking into a sweat. I’m a sucker for dogs, so this image made me smile, and I soon became accustomed to seeing people who were holidaying with their pooches. These furry family members were allowed on trains, in cafes and restaurants, and even got to sleep with their humans across the hall in my Venice hotel, then accompany them to the breakfast buffet. There is nothing notable about seeing a small child being wheeled around in a shopping trolley while their parents buy the weekly groceries, but at a supermarket in Cortina, the home of the most recent Winter Olympics, I did need a second take. While I marvelled at the prosciutto at the deli counter, a dog was sitting in a trolley next to me, without excessively salivating – the dog, not me.



According to an article in Italian newspaper La Stampa, 60 per cent of Italians surveyed seek out pet-friendly destinations for their vacation. Italy is also marketed as the most dog-friendly holiday destination in Europe, as evident when I met Auguste at Lake Como, the long-haired Dachshund from France, and Luna, the playful 12-week-old golden retriever who was holidaying with her Austrian humans. Sitz, Luna! While I marvelled at the prosciutto, a dog was sitting in a trolley next to me. Seeing families wheeling their suitcases while appeasing their hot and tired kids and leading their dog through Milano Centrale railway station was fascinating. They were heading for accommodation that welcomed dogs, sat at restaurants that welcomed dogs, both inside and out, and took them shopping in multi-level department stores. Imagine the patience required for a dog to sit while you try on clothes. I’m hard-pushed to get my husband to tolerate that. And if you think the dog’s needs are not being considered, Lonely Planet has created a travel guide for pet-friendly Italy. You can visit Scooby Doo Beach in Campomarino Lido and hire a suite – picture a family-sized playpen on the sand – that includes shade, lounges and water mister for all occupants. Water bowls for dogs only. I can imagine the red flags this raises in your mind. Allergies. Fear of dogs. Hygiene. Trip hazard. Liability. Stepping in something warm and squishy. It is one thing having to collect your dog’s poop with an inverted plastic bag from the sidewalk, but another in the first-class carriage of a Trenitalia train.



Related Article Exclusive

Disability Uber stands by sacking of driver who refused guide dog Even a person like me, who wants to cuddle every dog I pass, was looking out for tripwires, but in six weeks I never once saw a dog misbehave or have an – ahem – accident. It became quite normal to have a dog sitting next to me while I tucked into my caprese salad. The La Stampa article cites that dogs and cats registered in Italy outnumber kids under 14 by 2.3 to 1. You may be surprised when I tell you that, remarkably, it is close to the same here in Australia. So, it raises the question, why can’t we take our dogs so easily on holidays? Should we be able to visit the Gold Coast and have Dougal the lab accompany us into every cafe, restaurant and shop we visit? Should our 15th-floor apartment be cool with a pooch sleeping in the living room? Should Coles at Pacific Fair be fine with Xena the red heeler strutting past the rotisserie chickens? It does sound like a stretch, I know, especially when we are still hearing cases of people with assistance dogs being denied transport despite it being illegal to refuse their fare. It was also apparent that these European pooches were raised with these freedoms so knew how to behave, at times better than their younger humans, I

might add.



This all got me thinking about an untapped tourism opportunity the Italians may have overlooked for those of us who can’t take our dog to Europe. If we can hire a car, a bike, skis and even travel clothes in Japan, then why not a pooch? I could be sitting in my Italian beach playpen, waiting for my gelato, while Bella the bulldog plays with her chew toy. Jo Pybus is a freelance writer. World.title: Garage doors to front doors: The unexpected spaces where Sydney could squeeze new homes
World.content:
From doors for cars to doors for people. That’s the change architect Peter McGregor says is needed to provide more housing in the overlooked rear lanes behind inner Sydney’s thousands of terraces. Faced with a shortage of affordable housing, the City of Sydney Council is considering ways to encourage “gentle density” – such as studio apartments built in the back of terraces and on top of their garages – to help deliver more homes in the dunny lanes where night soil was once collected. Peter McGregor on a Redfern laneway where many people have built studios or secondary dwellings over their garages. Sam Mooy McGregor likes the height and generosity of the home behind him, designed more than a decade ago by Raffaello Rosselli. Sam Mooy On Young Street in Redfern, McGregor designed a generous unit above the garage of his former family home with a roller door he decorated in the red and green of the Rabbitohs team colours.



It has little bunnies, as wall decorations, too. McGregor has been campaigning, though, for more generous back lane dwellings with windows that provide sun and privacy, unlike others that are too small, too high, cast shade on neighbours, have little privacy and are just big enough for a double bed. Deputy Mayor Jess Miller said planning reforms or land title structures enabling homes to be built fronting lanes had been used overseas to deliver housing in “what are generally quite protected heritage areas”. Related Article Architecture The tiny window problem creating two classes of home owners “In the UK, they came up with this idea of a ‘Torrens Terrace’, which basically enables people who have homes that are long and narrow, with a frontage to the street and a frontage to the rear laneway, to double the density of their property [by building a second dwelling],” Miller said. A Torrens title property is one where the purchaser owns the house and the land on which it is built, compared to a strata title where they own their private lot and share ownership of common spaces.



Miller said the council faced the dual challenges of increasing density and green space in the densely populated inner suburbs. The council has encouraged efforts to turn neglected laneways into green, public spaces, such as Cat Alley in Surry Hills, and Hayden Lane in Darlinghurst. But the City’s Housing for All discussion paper, which explored where and how more housing should be delivered, went a step further, suggesting the council consider tweaking planning rules to encourage more “small lot” homes, filling laneways with “front doors rather than roller doors”. Architect Peter McGregor of McGregor Westlake Architecture ouside the studio apartment he designed behind his former home, a terrace in Redfern. Sam Mooy Some of the bunnies on the back wall of the studio apartment McGregor designed. Sam Mooy The report suggested the standalone Torrens title dwellings could provide compact, liveable spaces up to two storeys high, with a rooftop terrace, along inner Sydney’s hundreds of back laneways.



The council said it had changed planning controls in Pyrmont to allow larger sites to be subdivided to create narrow lots for low-rise terraces facing laneways. The change showed how the council could introduce more small-lot housing into the area while maintaining local character. “As more small-lot homes are built, the laneways would become more attractive, walkable and safer. We already allow garages with upper levels on laneways. With adjustments, these types of buildings could become compact but high-amenity homes, providing more housing choice,” the paper said. Related Article City life First came the wedding, then the drag queens: Lane with ugly past transforms into an inner-city oasis Miller said the homes could ease housing pressures and encourage intergenerational living, providing homes for adult children or ageing parents. She noted some property owners had already built such dwellings, but said for the idea to be implemented at scale, the community would need to have a discussion about the potential trade-offs. “We’re asking people: Would you rather have rear-lane access for your car, or would you rather have two dwellings on your current title, which might effectively double the value of your property?



“There will be a range of views on that, but in areas where there is good access to public transport, it’s walkable, cycleable, and people have less need to own a car, there might be appetite for this.” Miller said Sydney had some of the world’s best architecture, landscape architecture, design minds and creative communities, and they were well-equipped to tackle design and practical challenges. Inside the Redfern tin shed: Everyone said the Young Street property’s former owner, Jane Smith, should have demolished the 80-year-old structure on her property, but Jane, pictured in 2012, loved it so much she kept it and turned it into an office. Quentin Jones “I think if there’s anywhere this can be done beautifully, it’s right here,” Miller said. For McGregor, the founder of McGregor Westlake Architecture, it feels “like Groundhog Day”. He has been urging the council to encourage more housing in back lanes for decades. (More eyes on the street made them safer too, he said.)



He said most cities around the world allowed terraces to be subdivided with Torrens titles, but McGregor’s application to subdivide his former home vertically was rejected. Related Article Exclusive

Architecture A loo with a view and no railings on ‘an impossible site’ in Sydney This works best, McGregor said, because the upstairs bedroom in a terrace is usually the largest room and makes an ideal living room for a second dwelling. His plan was rejected by council because of concerns about fire protection. This subdivision is encouraged across London, Dublin and the UK, and it is a technical issue that can be overcome. The McGregors sold the terrace and moved to an apartment. They know of two families whose larger terraces were not fit for purpose, but could be suitable for two groups, or families, to share. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Affordable for Coogee’: Local couple pays $2.5m for two-bedroom semi
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘Affordable for Coogee’: Local couple pays $2.5m for two-bedroom semi Carmen Forward September 7, 2026 — 11:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A local upsizing couple secured a semi in Coogee for $2.5 million at auction on Saturday, a price that the selling agent described as “affordable for Coogee”. The “half a house” at 5 Ritchard Avenue had a swimming pool, lower level with potential to improve and a lockup garage. The property was one of 709 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 57 per cent from 433 reported results throughout the week, while 125 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate Six parties registered on the two-bedroom property in the coastal postcode, with a guided range of $2.2 million to $2.4 million. Most were upsizing families, but some were builders looking to renovate.



Bidding opened at $2.3 million, instantly meeting the property’s reserve. Three parties were active, with rises of $50,000, $10,000 and $5000 to climb $200,000 above the reserve until the hammer fell at $2.5 million. Related Article Auctions Unrenovated inner west terrace sells for $355k over reserve at auction Sotheby’s Marnie Seinor said it was a “good opportunity for lots of young families to upgrade”. “People are just nervous about spending the money [on] marketing, and people are just holding for fear of not selling. But things are selling, and this is an example of that.” She said the property is a “semi … a half a house”.



“It’s affordable for Coogee, and it was livable and then lends itself to a lot of potential.” The buyers are upsizing from an apartment in Coogee. The vendor has moved to aged care. The home last traded for $390,000 in 1994, records show. In Cremorne, a clean and tidy three-bedroom apartment sold for $3.5 million to a downsizer from Riverview. The boutique unit with leafy water views at 7/45 Grasmere Road had a guide of $3 million and drew three registrations who all participated.



Bidding opened at $2.9 million and rose in $50,000 and $25,000 increments at a rapid pace before the apartment sold under the hammer for $300,000 above its $3.2 million reserve. Related Article Sydney house prices The prestige Sydney suburb where house prices fell most over a year There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Belle Property’s Matthew Smythe said: “It’s a good market for downsizers and upsizers. Upsizers, clearly financially; it’s a huge win for them because they can step up and save money on the changeover costs.” “But for downsizers as well. If you want to buy a lifestyle, it’s already cheaper than it was six months ago, and the smart ones understand that and want to get on with the next 10 years of their life.”



The vendor is moving to Queensland. The unit last traded for $1,815,000 in 2012, records show. In Lindfield, a well-maintained three-bedroom unit at 21/2B Havilah Road drew two registered bidders. The apartment on a quiet leafy street was guided at $2.58 million and had a reserve of $2.6 million. It sold below its guide, and $150,000 under its reserve, for $2.45 million. Only one bidder made an offer, opening the auction at $2.3 million, and then increased it to $2.4 million. Negotiations further lifted the price to $2.42 million before a final offer was made of $2.45 million. The vendor accepted, adjusting their reserve to sell.



Ray White’s Jessica Cao said: “A lot of my vendors at the moment, they’re downsizing. Yes, the market’s different. However, if they buy and sell in the same market, it doesn’t matter too much.” Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Retail boss lists $17m ‘interim’ home as he moves into Swans chairman’s $40m abode “What I do see is my downsizer vendors are pretty cautious. They want to sell first to know how much money they have before they commit [at] the other end.” The buyer is downsizing from a five-bedroom home in Lindfield. The vendor is relocating overseas. The flat last traded for $1,528,000 in 2014, records show.



AMP chief economist Dr Shane Oliver said that Domain’s clearance rate of 57 per cent for Sydney was “still a weak market”. “To me, it remains a perfect storm for the property market. We’ve got higher and rising interest rates. We’ve got big tax changes making it far less attractive for property investors, and we’ve got poor levels of confidence.” Oliver expected another rate hike and said debate centred on whether there would be two more hikes. “Because vendors are holding back, that’s limiting the supply, and consequently, the clearance rate has been able to rise because we’ve got less listings, so it’s not necessarily a sign of strength,” he said. “The only thing that’s helping the market is that vendors are holding off, possibly hoping for better prices.” Oliver said the real test will come once the spring selling season picks up in October.

World.title: The one thing I will use AI for when travelling
World.content:
If you’re at all familiar with my work, chances are you’ve heard me rant about the value of learning a language. It doesn’t take much. A few hours of study and you can revolutionise your experience in a country, opening doors that would have otherwise stayed closed to your typical tourist.

I know what you’re thinking. You’re thinking that study sounds like just the sort of thing a barely employed travel writer has time to do. It’s not something for someone with a job, a family and obligations that go beyond getting dressed in the morning.

Illustration: Greg Straight

The good news (or bad news, if you’re a rainforest) is that thanks to AI, learning a language has never been easier. And while it pains me to write this – given my general resentment for how much AI is being rammed down our throats these days – it has changed my approach to language learning.

AI can tailor lessons to you as an individual. Using voice mode on Gemini or ChatGPT, it can even respond to your questions and correct your pronunciation (although I’d still recommend YouTube for a more natural immersion). Most importantly, it can reveal things about a culture that would have otherwise been invisible to even the most seasoned travellers.

World.title: Man who raised thousands claiming to be dying of cancer wasn't ill, death ruled suicide - Coroner
World.content:
Warning: This story discusses suicide.

A coroner has found a man who raised thousands of dollars claiming to have terminal cancer did not have the disease when he died by suicide.

Douglas 'Doug' Ruch was a 56-year-old US National who arrived in New Zealand just days before his death.

He gained media attention claiming to have terminal prostate cancer and fundraising to travel and do volunteer work.

Ruch's campaign, 'DyingToServe', featured in a number of outlets including The Guardian, NBC, and The Washington Post.

He fundraised to travel to the US for volunteer work with different organisations, claiming to have the disease and wishing to 'spend his remaining time serving other,' Coroner Tracey Fitzgibbon said.

Ruch's campaigns raised significant amounts of money, with The Guardian reporting one of his GoFundMe's reached US$230,000 (NZ$391,386).

In September 2025, Ruch's ex-wife with whom he had four children and was estranged had contacted him over child support he had not been paying.

"Doug sent some money and mentioned that his health was declining, and he believed he would die within six months," Coroner Fitzgibbon said.

"On September 14 2025, Doug set up a new GoFundMe to fund travel to Australia."

A month later Ruch messaged his ex-wife again, saying that he only had "a few months" left to live.

In December 2025, Ruch's philanthropy and diagnosis came under scrutiny. He had deactivated his fundraisers and shut down his social media pages.

Days before his death, Ruch travelled to Auckland and checked into a central city hotel.

Local journalist David Farrier published an article on 17 December titled 'Beware of Doug'

"A GoFundMe conman tricked the USA. Now he's coming for NZ," the sub-heading read.

Ruch had phoned his hotel's reception raising concerns about his personal details being released after an unsaved number sent him a link to Farrier's article.

The receptionist assured him his details wouldn't be shared.

"Doug said this was 'good', as he had 'dangerous internet stalkers' who might be looking for him," Coroner Fitzgibbon said.

The next morning, Ruch was dead.

Details of his death cannot be reported, as the Coroner has ruled it a suicide.

A post mortem revealed no evidence of prostate cancer.

"Doug's ex-wife recalled that he had a history of anxiety, for which he was prescribed medication, and had an incident of suicidal intent in 2019 following their separation," the Coroner said.

World.title: Christopher Luxon defends hiking costs for low-deposit home buyers, saying it had no impact on uptake
World.content:
PM discusses supermarkets, superannuation, and housing Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Christopher Luxon has defended a move to make first-home buyers pay more under a government-assisted loan scheme, saying it hasn't impacted the number of applications.

At the weekend, National promised - if reelected - to help more people buy their first home by expanding access to the government's low-deposit scheme.

The existing First Home Loan scheme run by Kāinga Ora allows buyers to purchase their first home with a 5 percent deposit, rather than 20 percent which most banks require. National wants to increase the income threshold so anyone earning less than $300,000 combined could access it - whether that was a single or combined income.

The existing cap of $95,000 for single buyers with no dependents, or $150,000 for multiple buyers or single buyers with dependents was set in 2022.

"When you step back and think about the young people that we want to keep here in New Zealand, this is one way we can help support them," the National Party leader told Morning Report on Monday, saying it would allow people on slightly higher incomes such as "junior doctors and electricians and teachers and nurses and police" use it.

Last year the government scrapped its contribution towards the mortgage insurance premium, raising costs for low-deposit borrowers from 0.5 percent of the mortgage's total cost to 1.2 percent - nearly $4000 on average.

"We felt that was a better way to go, just making sure the mortgage lender insurance is a key component of it. But as you can see, it actually hasn't changed, people becoming eligible for it and people applying for it over the last nine months."

Kāinga Ora approved 7761 new First Home Loan applications between 1 July 2025, and 30 April 2026. Purchases using First Home Loans rose 31 percent in the year to June 2026, Infometrics statistics showed, to just over 4000.

Ministry figures show the share of purchases made by first-home buyers has crept up to just over 35 percent in the past year - down on 2023's peak at almost 40 percent, but well above 2017's 21 percent.

"The issue is now not so much about the serviceability of the mortgage because actual interest rates having come down, that's much more affordable for people. It's really about helping people get that deposit together."

While interest rates were creeping back up now, with two successive hikes to the official cash rate, two years ago they were as high as 5.5 percent.

Luxon said inflation had come down since the coalition took over, which would encourage Kiwis to stay here, or come back if they had already left.

Inflation's latest figure was 4.1 percent, a two-year high and well outside the Reserve Bank's target of 1-3 percent, hence the interest rate hikes.

Luxon said if you ignored the effects of the Middle East conflict, inflation was inside the target band, at 2.9 percent. He also pointed to food price inflation being at 1.9 percent.

Luxon said inflation was previously above 7 percent, without mentioning potential global causes such as the supply shock caused by Covid-19, or that it was just as high for most of our major trading partners.

"Having inflation in the band at a healthy level as it has been in New Zealand for a number of years is a good thing, because that means interest rates come down, interest rates lower inflation, lower interest rates means the economy starts growing and people get into jobs."

'Nudge' in favour of first-home buyers

Mortgage expert discusses National’s new first homebuyer policy Midday Report Download MP3 5m

Squirrel Mortgage Brokers chief David Cunningham told Midday Report the proportion of first home buyers entering the property market had been rising for five to seven years, but the National policy could act as a further "nudge" in that direction.

He said the policy was "using or a scheme that already exists and really extending it to a broader group of people, which basically means more young people can own their own homes and get into them faster".

The current settings for the scheme did not really make sense, he said, but with house prices falling the market was already opening up.

"It's been rising for about five, six, seven years now," he said. "I've described the last year or two as a 'Goldilocks time' for first-home buyers and it continues to be that way... it's about 30 percent of all house sales to first home buyers at the moment... this sort of gives it another little I suppose, nudge."

He said because it was a loan it was good fiscal policy because it was not a "giveaway", and borrowers would have to be able to afford to pay it back.

Buyers would also be at risk of falling into negative equity, where they owed more than the house was worth, but would not be forced to sell and the Reserve Bank would continue monitoring the system's stability.

"They've put in place loan-to-value ratios - in other words, how much you can borrow over that 80 percent level... and debt-to-income ratios which came in more recently, and those sort of control how much risk there is in the system.

World.title: Weather: Heavy rain falls on lower North, upper South Island
World.content:
State Highway 6 has reopened between Murchison and Kawatiri Junction in the South Island after being closed because of slips and flooding.

SH65 remains closed between O'Sullivans and Springs Junction because of a slip at Shenandoah.

The New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) says the highway might stay closed Monday night.

SH6 was still closed between Makarora and Lake Hawea because of a slip.

SH67 between Hector and Mokihinui on the West Coast has reopened to a single lane.

NZTA said road users were advised to delay their journeys if possible.

State Highway Six is still closed between Makarora and Lake Hāwea after recent slips. NZTA/Screenshot

The Tararua Ranges has had almost 100mm of rain over the past 12 hours and will remain under an orange level rain warning until Monday afternoon.

Rain watches also remained in place for parts of Wellington, Waiarapa, Manawatū and Taranaki.

Further south, highways around Nelson and Buller were also closed to flooding and slips.

"Snow is forecast to affect some of the higher-level roads and passes across the South Island," MetService said.

A snowfall warning was in place on the Lewis Pass till at least 9am.

MetService said by Tuesday, there would be minimal risk of severe weather.

"A complex low pressure system moves away to the east of New Zealand as a ridge of high pressure builds over the country. A weak front decays as it moves onto southern New Zealand."

World.title: Greens can't say how much cheaper KiwiMart would be, say government won't set prices
World.content:
Chloe Swarbrick discusses new publicly owned supermarket policy Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Chlöe Swarbrick says it won't be up to politicians to determine the price of eggs should the government set up its own supermarket chain.

The Greens at the weekend announced plans for KiwiMart - a government-owned alternative to the Foodstuffs and Woolworths duopoly. It would involve buying 120 existing stores and two distribution centres at a cost of $2.8 billion, immediately introducing a third player with a 15 percent market share.

"The red team formerly, and also now the blue team, has spent the last three years trying to beg an international third player to come to our shores. But I think with us being such a small market at the bottom of the world, that simply has not happened," she told Morning Report on Monday.

In March last year, Finance Minister Nicola Willis said all options were on the table to lower food prices. In the year following, food prices rose faster than inflation, and despite efforts to ease the process, big offshore supermarkets showed little to no interest in setting up in New Zealand.

The duopoly controls more than four-fifths of the market. RNZ

In 2022 the Commerce Commission said the duopoly was making $1 million in excess profit every day.

But little has changed. Just a month ago the commission took Foodstuffs South Island to court, alleging "far-reaching anti-competitive conduct that deprived customers of cheaper prices".

In June, it was reported the duopoly held 82 percent of the market, and more than 90 percent in some regions.

PM discusses supermarkets, superannuation, and housing Morning Report Download MP3 7m

"We've had successive governments now study this problem to death as New Zealanders continue to experience their grocery prices escalating," Swarbrick said.

"So what we've done is look at all of the best available evidence and propose that we do have the capacity to build a third competitor here."

Swarbrick said there were enough supermarkets, just not enough competition. But she would not say just how much cheaper goods could expect to be with a third, government-backed operator mandated to prioritise affordability.

"I think that any politician, I mean myself and Nicola Willis would probably have pretty different definitions of what constitutes excessive pricing. This is why we are powering up the Commerce Commission to be able to have some real economic calculus behind this."

Part of the Greens' plan is to spend more than $100 million on beefing up the commission's powers and introducing a mandatory pricing accuracy code with automatic compensation when shoppers are overcharged.

KiwiMart would not be a non-profit, she said, and after the initial cost outlay would be self-sustaining.

"Politicians are not economists. We leave monetary policy to the Reserve Bank. I think when it comes to defining excess profits, that is best left to the independent experts at the Commerce Commission,"

Swarbrick said.

"Otherwise perversely we end up with exactly all of the fearmongering that right-wing politicians have been throwing at us over this policy.

"I am not saying what the price of an egg should be. I am saying that there are independent experts who have spent their life studying the calculus as to what constitutes fairness when you look at all of the economic fundamentals, and that will look different on a case-by-case basis. So we should leave that to the experts."

Cameron Bagrie discusses Green’s KiwiMart announcement Midday Report Download MP3 6m

Independent economist Cameron Bagrie from Bagrie Economic told Midday Report a government-owned supermarket sounded good in theory, but he had a few "questions marks" around the costings.

"We've got a structural problem [and] when you've got a structural problem, you need a structural style solution.

"$1.3 billion to buy 120 supermarkets plus a couple of distribution centres ... I think you're way light in regard to how much the reality will be in regard to what that sort of cost is."

Bagrie said Kiwibank was an example of how the government was often poor managers of assets.

"If you look at the performance of Kiwibank relative to the big four, and Kiwibank's been around a long time, and the experience of Kiwibank is that the government doesn't tend to be very good at running these assets."

"I'm not necessarily convinced that state ownership is the right option. The route I'd be going down would be structural separation of retail versus wholesale division."

He said mistakes had been made over the past 20 years, leading to the duopoly being "pretty cosy".

"We don't have a huge population, so there's never going to be a huge number of firms in the industry."

World.title: Fire at Kerikeri café next to Kemp House was deliberately lit - FENZ
World.content:
A Far North fire investigator has confirmed a blaze close to New Zealand's oldest building was deliberately lit.

Police are now leading the investigation into Friday night's fire, which started in a storage shed next to Honey House Café, immediately behind Kemp House.

Built by English missionaries and Māori sawyers in 1821-22, Kemp House is the nation's oldest surviving building and a Category 1 historic place.

Fire and Emergency investigator Gary Beer said the fire had destroyed the storage shed and set the side of the Honey House alight.

It had damaged one wall, entered the top of the building, and destroyed water pipes and electrical cabling.

The Honey House Café and first-floor offices were likely to be out of action for some time, he said.

Firefighters dampen down the remains of Kerikeri’s Honey House Café. Supplied

Also destroyed were hundreds of historic shingles recently removed from the Kemp House roof and placed in the shed for future re-use.

Beer said he could not comment further on how the fire had started, given that it was now a police investigation.

A spokesperson for Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga said the Stone Store had reopened on Sunday but had no Eftpos due to cable damage.

World.title: Family seek judicial review of police shooting of unarmed Taranaki man Kaoss Price
World.content:
The family of Kaoss Price is seeking a judicial review of the Independent Police Conduct Authority's (IPCA) investigation into his fatal shooting in April 2022.

The unarmed 22-year-old died on State Highway 3, between New Plymouth and Waitara, after ramming a police car and attempting to steal cars from passers-by.

The IPCA's investigation found the officer who fired the fatal shot used excessive force, but did not recommend prosecuting the officer.

The family is now asking for that recommendation to be ignored, and for prosecution to go ahead.

At the High Court in Wellington on Monday, the family's lawyer Christopher Stevenson KC said when the officer shot Price point blank, the young man was running for his life.

Previously, his lawyers argued police had not provided adequate information to support the decision not to prosecute.

"Given the alarming rate of fatal police shootings, particularly of young Māori men, it is critical that more information is provided so that what happened can be properly understood," they said.

Monday's hearing was attended more than a dozen members of Price's family and friends - including his grandmother, mother, sister and aunt.

Stevenson told the court Officer A - whose name has been suppressed - shot Price "point blank in the chest" while he attempted to car jack another vehicle after fleeing a routine traffic stop, driving dangerously and ramming a police car.

He said the ICPA's investigation acknowledged, contrary to the officer's testimony, it was unlikely that the officer saw a high risk of harm from Price as her fled police while under fire.

Stevenson pointed out police fired on Price's vehicle and continued to fire at him as ran, with his back to officers, before he attempted to hijack another vehicle.

Stevenson said a witness in the second vehicle described Price offering $500 if they would drive him away from the scene and quoted the witness's testimony as saying: "He was just scared and wanted to get away. He was terrified."

"Officer A arrives at the driver's side of the vehicle and it's at this point that he shoots the unarmed Mr Price point blank in the chest," Stevenson said.

Stevenson told the court the IPCA investigation into the shooting found Officer A's contention that he believed Price was going for a weapon at that point was "implausible and improbable".

"The essential facts are not in dispute. By the time he was in the vehicle he was not a threat to officer or to the passengers in the vehicle - who described him as 'terrified' - the only conceivable threat was driving away," Stevenson said.

Another lawyer for Price's family, Max Harris, said the IPCA's investigation had failed in it's obligations under the Bill of Rights to be independent, impartial, prompt, thorough and transparent - and the process had undermined the effectiveness and the credibility of the investigation.

Stevenson noted it took two weeks before Officer A was interviewed about the shooting and during the process the officer was allowed to refer to pre-written notes.

He said interview transcripts revealed a troubling familiarity with how the officer was treated - including being referred to as "mate" 14 times during the process.

"[Officer A] was never appropriately pressed on his account and never appropriately challenged," Stevenson said.

He said it was concerning the officer was treated primarily as "a witness rather than a suspect" in their testimony regarding the incident.

He cited concerns over the independence of interviewing officers, noting that interviewers came from the same region and one had been trained on interviewing procedures by Officer A's lawyer.

"There can be inadvertent and unconscious bias which we know from decades of social sciences," Stevenson said.

He said there was also a lack of transparency regarding the explanation for the IPCA's decision not to prosecute Officer A and the family had been further traumatised by the 15-month delay in publishing the IPCA's decision which was "provided in a conclusory form - absent of reasons".

Stevenson described the treatment of Price's family in the investigation as "egregious" and said the disregard was further emphasised by the lack of information in support of the decision.

Harris told the court the lapse of time before a decision was published should not impact the conclusions of the investigation of the case of "a profound failing by police".

He said the lack of reasoning to reinforce the investigation's decision not to prosecute contradicted police and the authority's obligations under the Bill of Rights.

"The police should be aware they are subject to the Bill of Rights," he said.

World.title: Port of Tauranga will almost double its handling capacity following fast-track approval
World.content:
Port of Tauranga has been granted fast-track approval by the government to enable a major port expansion known as the Stella Passage development.

The project will involve extending the Sulphur Point container berth by 385 metres and the Mount Maunganui wharf by 315 metres, almost doubling its handling capacity.

The port said the project will see it convert existing cargo storage land within the port's current footprint, as well as reclaim land behind the new wharves and dredge the passage.

An application for fast-tracking the project was lodged in January 2026, with approval taking around five months from the appointment of an independent expert panel.

It follows an earlier application in 2021 for fast-tracking through the Covid-19 fast-track system, which was declined.

Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop said the project has a lengthy history under the Resource Management Act, spending roughly seven years navigating standard RMA processes and Environment Court hearings.

Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Mark Papalii

"The Port of Tauranga is New Zealand's largest port by volume, handling roughly a third of all cargo in New Zealand. Current activities at the wharves are constrained by limited container capacity, vessel congestion and the age of the existing infrastructure.

"The Stella Passage development will address these constraints by enabling larger ships and almost doubling the handling capacity at the port."

Port of Tauranga chief financial officer Simon Kebbell said the approval was very welcome news.

World.title: Patients left waiting weeks for lifesaving procedures amid bed shortage
World.content:
Shortage of cardiac beds leaving patients waiting weeks Nine To Noon Download MP3 14m

A shortage of cardiac beds and staff in Wellington and Christchurch hospitals is leaving patients at risk and waiting weeks for treatment instead of the recommended days - a situation one doctor describes as a "shambles".

The shortage also means that cardiac cath labs - used for procedures such as placing stents - are left unused for parts of the day due to a lack of staff.

The newly upgraded cath lab in Wellington needs radiologists and physiologists along with nurses to care for patients in the cardiac wards after treatment.

In its pre-election manifesto, the Heart and Lung Foundation is calling for better staffing and more cardiac beds to help tackle the country's single biggest killer.

Anna Haarkman has been waiting in Palmerston North Hospital for more than two weeks for a pacemaker after being admitted with chest pains.

Palmerston North Hospital. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

She is needing to go to Wellington Hospital to have the procedure done but they are "snowed under" and has had no update on when it'll be her turn.

Haarkman told Nine to Noon there weren't enough beds or surgeons for her to be transferred.

"Mainly I'm totally bored out of my skull. I'm not ill. I walk the corridors here to keep my legs going, that's about all I can do."

Haarkman said she had spoken to doctors about leaving but would need to sign a waiver and would end up having to start the process all over again.

She was also told there could be "another situation and that would be the end of me".

Dr Andrew Chatfield, the Heart and Lung Foundation's cardiac medical director and a practising cardiologist in Wellington, said Haarkman's situation was unfortunate and not for lack of staff wanting to help - but that there just wasn't enough beds for patients.

Chatfield said the shortage of available beds meant they were "missing out" on guidelines for helping people who had suffered a heart attack, for example.

He said people should have a procedure or angiogram within 48 hours but he knew of people waiting weeks.

The lack of beds meant they continued having influxes of "really acute patients" or "outliers" in their beds who had come from the emergency department and meant they weren't able to bring their specialist cardiac patients in from the regions.

"It all has a big flow on effect."

Chatfield said it wasn't a new problem and while there had been improvements in the past six months, it wasn't enough.

There was still parts of the day where the new cath lab - used to perform lifesaving procedures - sat idle because there wasn't anyone to staff it.

"The team comes in overnight, deals with the life-threatening situation and then we're unable to staff the lab the following day."

As well as highly specialised doctors and nurses, Chatfield said the centre also needed cardiac physiologists, medical radiation technologists and sonographers.

Without them, they couldn't do the procedures - and he was hearing that they weren't getting enough staff in these positions.

Chatfield said there was risk of harm - and death - to patients waiting in local hospitals to be transferred for their procedure.

They were in constant communication with regional hospitals and made every attempt to transfer them quicker if there was a sudden change in their health.

But he said there needed to be a "shake-up" - and care towards cardiac centres needed to be prioritised.

In a statement, Health New Zealand interim group director of operations for Capital, Coast and Hutt Valley, Robert Blaikie, said demand varied and there were times when bed availability and wider hospital capacity affected how quickly patients could be transferred to Wellington for specialist treatment.

Additional beds are expected to come online across Wellington Hospital over the coming years, he said.

"Wellington Hospital has three cardiac catheter laboratories operating 27 weekday sessions. The medical, nursing, cardiac physiology and anaesthetic workforce doing this work is highly specialised and recruitment for additional staff is ongoing.

World.title: Kids sport costing families more than $4,500 a year for each child
World.content:
For Rockhampton parents Aaron and Paula Harmsworth, keeping three children involved in multiple sports comes with a growing price tag.

"It's something we talk about regularly because we do look at the bank balance and go, 'Geez, we're spending a lot of money here,'" Mr Harmsworth said.

"But we counteract that pretty quickly with: 'There is no price tag on what the kids learn through sport.'

"The people they meet, the places they go, and the different traits they learn … respect and resilience, they're probably two of the biggest key components."

Siblings Sienna, Indy and Jace Harmsworth are all competing at representative level in a range of sports. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

New research has found the average annual total cost for a child to play in a community sport competition is $4,567 a year, considerably higher than previously reported numbers.

The Cost of Sport study, commissioned by the Australian Sports Commission and undertaken by researchers from Federation University, also found adults were forking out $2,894 per year for themselves to play.

Researchers investigated a wide range of expenses, including registration, equipment, uniforms, coaching, travel, accommodation and lost parental income due to sport commitments.

Sienna Harmsworth has earned selection in Queensland teams in three sports this year. (Supplied: The Cathedral College)

For the Harmsworth family, those costs quickly add up.

Their children, Jace, 17, Sienna, 15, and Indy, 13, have represented their city, region and state in various sports, with Sienna making Queensland teams in hockey, netball and touch football in 2026.

Already this year, sport has taken the central Queensland family from Hobart to Darwin and plenty of places in between.

"We have to map out our year and generally we have to be pretty organised," Mr Harmsworth said.

"This year alone we've done Goulburn, Gold Coast, Mackay, Brisbane, and then back to Brisbane, Hobart, Mackay, Cairns, Melbourne, Gold Coast again, Mackay again, Brisbane, Coffs Harbour, Darwin, back to Brisbane, back to Mackay, Cairns and Hervey Bay."

This year alone Sienna Harmsworth has pulled on the maroon jersey in hockey, netball and touch football. (Supplied: Paula Harmsworth)

It all adds up for families

The study's lead researcher, Rochelle Eime, said previous research had tended to focus on registration fees, while her team captured the broader financial commitment families made to sport.

"It seems like a really high number, but when you start looking at all the different categories, it all stacks up," Professor Eime said.

" You've got $1,400 for coaching for an individual sport on average, $1,000 lost to parent income to travel, another $700 for tournament or competition accommodation fees, $500 for travel. "

Rochelle Eime says travel, coaching and other costs can quickly add up for families involved in community sport. (Supplied: Rochelle Eime)

Mr Harmsworth said the sacrifices for his family were not just monetary.

"You accrue leave and, all of a sudden, you're using your leave on a sporting trip," he said.

" You certainly look at what the word family holiday means now and that generally means a sporting holiday. "

New research has found the average annual cost of community sport for a child is more than $4,500. (ABC News: Jonathon Gul)

The study surveyed about 5,500 sport participants across Australia, including children and adults.

It found the overall cost for children to play sport was similar in regional and remote areas compared with metropolitan areas.

But regional children faced higher travel and accommodation costs, while metropolitan families paid more for coaching and registration fees.

Equipment such as headgear and boots can add to the cost of playing community sport. (ABC News: Jen Browning)

Entry-level participation was much cheaper, averaging $1,161 a year for children, while the average cost for adults was $1,200.

Individual sports were also found to be more expensive than team sports.

"What we're seeing is most people and families aren't just entry-level sport participants," Professor Eime said.

"As soon as you get into that later childhood, you do need to travel to play in competitions and that all adds up."

Researchers say the cost of community sport rises as children progress into competitive and representative sport. (AAP: Joe Castro)

Keeping kids in the game

Professor Eime said sporting clubs and organisations were already finding ways to ensure cost did not become a barrier to participation.

Some were repurposing equipment and uniforms, while many supported state government voucher programs, which in Queensland can reduce the cost of sport by up to $200 per child.

"The value of community sport is so great for our children in terms of their youth development and social connectedness, a whole range of different life skills they get from playing sport," Professor Eime said.

A shot at goal can come with a growing price tag for sporting families. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"If we highlight what the true costs are, and they are much higher than what previous research has shown, we need to actually do something about it because everyone should have the chance to play community sport."

Danya Hodgetts, a senior researcher at CQUniversity and an expert in community sport, who was not involved in the study, said the findings reflected what many regional parents already knew: that the cost of getting their children off screens and involved in sport extended well beyond registration fees.

Danya Hodgetts says community sport provides benefits that extend well beyond the playing field. (Supplied: CQUniversity)

"It's a really tricky situation because it is important that, while we talk about the cost of sport, we also talk about the value of sport because we know sport is valuable," Dr Hodgetts said.

"It builds good humans, keeps kids out of trouble, it keeps them occupied, it keeps them healthy and it also, particularly in regional areas, it's our village.

"Sporting clubs are the networks that parents and kids rely on to help get through daily life, not just inside sport, but outside of sport as well."

More sporting road trips are ahead for the Harmsworth family, with the September school holidays bringing another round of travel. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

For the Harmsworth family, finding ways to keep those costs under control has become part of playing the sporting game.

Mr Harmsworth said their caravan had become one of their biggest money savers.

"One of our saving graces is the caravan and we take it everywhere we go," he said.

"You also need to book early and in advance in a lot of cases, particularly your bigger sporting carnivals."

World.title: Mary Fowler kicks off Manchester City season with opening goal
World.content:
Matildas star Mary Fowler has kicked off her 2026/27 Women's Super League season by scoring Manchester City's opening goal in a 3-1 win over Birmingham City.

Bunny Shaw was player of the match for her double, but Fowler started the day with a brilliant first-time strike to set the tone for the reigning champions.

After a goalless first half, Fowler worked down the right wing, where her cross was deflected and Neve Herron's hack ended at the feet of Laura Blindkilde Brown.

She then tried a second cross and, after another failed clearance by Geum-min Lee, the ball returned to Fowler, who fired a first-time strike into the bottom right corner.

Her 49th-minute goal was quickly followed by Shaw's first, nodding home a well-directed corner from Kerstin Casparij.

Shaw, last season's leading scorer and Professional Footballers' Association player of the year, repeated the feat in the shadows of full-time before newly promoted Birmingham got a consolation goal through Oceane Hurtre in the 90th minute.

"The most important thing was to get the ​win ‌and start off on the right foot. I think we did that today … we have to keep on going," Shaw told ⁠Sky Sports.

Fellow newcomer Charlton Athletic was ‌also given a tough ‌introduction to the top flight as Grace Fisk scored twice in Liverpool's commanding ‌4-0 victory.

Crystal Palace, who finished second behind Birmingham in WSL 2 last season, enjoyed a happier return to the ‌top ​division, beating Everton ⁠1-0 through Lexi Lloyd-Smith's 34th-minute winner.

Last season's runners-up Arsenal secured a 1-0 win at Brighton & Hove Albion earlier on Sunday, with 19-year-old winger Lisa Baum marking her club debut by surging forward ⁠from midfield and finishing left-footed from a tight angle in the 10th minute.

Arsenal's north London ‌rival Tottenham Hotspur ‌eased to a 3-1 win over West Ham ​United, with Scotland forward Kirsty Hanson scoring twice on her Spurs debut.

The WSL season will pause after its first month for a brief international window from October 5-13, during which Germany will host the Matildas for a friendly.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Forehand rocket shows Carlos Alcaraz back to 'full power' in US Open win
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz has beaten American 20th seed Tommy Paul 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 to reach the quarterfinals of the US Open and remain ​firmly on track for back-to-back titles at Flushing Meadows.

The seven-time grand slam champion has hit top form in New York after nearly five months out with a right wrist injury and extended his major match-winning streak to 18 with a stunning display of shot-making.

It included a blistering 164km/h forehand winner down the line as he established an advantage early in the second set on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

For a man who missed the past two slams and has been out since April due to a wrist injury, an ailment that had ended or stunted multiple tennis careers, it was an indicator that he is back to "full power".

It was one of 33 winners for Alcaraz, including another rocket of a forehand to bring up match point at a venue where he has thrived ever since his maiden major triumph four years ago.

"I think so," ⁠Alcaraz said when asked about being back to his best in New York, where he has reached the quarterfinals in five of his six ‌appearances now.

"It shows ‌how special this place is to me. I'm just trying to enjoy my time on the court, so it probably doesn't matter that I was out for four and a half months.

"Every time I come here, I play my best."

Despite the scoreline, Alcaraz was pushed by the speed demon on the other side of the net, with Paul pulling out his second around-the-post winner of the tournament.

The Spaniard was unfazed.

"I think I ‌just played my game," Alcaraz said.

"I tried to play to my style. Tommy's such a talented player and his shots are pretty dangerous and it's difficult to ‌control the ball when it comes to you. I was ready for a battle.

"I was trying to ⁠be aggressive all the time … I did well to put pressure on his ‌return, which helped me stay calm and to ​think clearly. I was really ‌happy with the performance."

Even with much of the showcourt crowd yearning for ‌a home winner, second seed Alcaraz ‌continued to steal the show with his audacious play and moved to the brink of improving his win-loss record against ‌American players at the grand slams to 13-0.

After shifting down to cruise mode, Alcaraz briefly flinched at the finish line, but he regrouped to deliver the knockout blow and set ‌up a ​meeting with American Ben Shelton, who swept aside Greece's Stefanos Tsitsipas 6-2, 6-3, 6-4.

On the other side of the draw, Frances Tiafoe beat Daniil Medvedev 7-6(7/1), 6-4, 7-6(8/6) to set up an all-American quarterfinal with Alex Michelsen.

The 22-year-old beat 27th-seeded Argentinian Tomas Martin Etcheverry 7-6(8/6), 6-4, 6-4 in their fourth-round clash.

World.title: Sabalenka powers back to US Open quarters in search for first 2026 slam
World.content:
Defending champion Aryna Sabalenka will take on Wimbledon winner Linda Noskova in the US Open quarterfinals, after the two battled their way ​into the final eight with confident wins.

World number one Sabalenka broke down the defences of 96th-ranked American Taylor Townsend to win 6-4, 6-3 in a competitive contest that belied the gulf in their ​rankings, neutralising the inventive ‌left-hander with a largely pristine display.

"It was really challenging, and going through tough challenges and overcoming those challenges, it definitely gives you strength and really strong belief that you can do ‌it," Sabalenka said of facing the unconventional doubles star.

"These kind of matches are really, really, really like a boost ⁠of confidence."

Sixth seed Noskova showed her mettle in a 7-5, ‌5-7, 6-4 victory over Marta Kostyuk, ​collapsing to the court ‌in relief after sealing the contest with an unreturnable serve on her sixth match point.

Linda Noskova beat Marta Kostyuk for the second-straight major. (Getty Images: Pete Staples/USTA)

The Czech's run is her deepest at Flushing Meadows and continues a remarkable season in which she claimed her maiden grand slam title at the All England ​Club.

The victory over Kostyuk was her second straight at the slams after Noskova came out on top in their Wimbledon semifinal, and it was almost another straight-sets affair as Noskova had two match points on serve at 5-4 in the second set, but Kostyuk rattled off four straight games to force a decider.

Noskova got another chance to serve for the match at 5-4 in the third set and missed three more match points before closing it out after two hours and 27 minutes.

American third ⁠seed Jessica Pegula closed the schedule at Louis Armstrong Stadium against a familiar foe, beating Romanian Sorana ‌Cirstea for the fourth straight time 6-3, 6-4.

Pegula's ​compatriot Emma Navarro plays Anna Kalinskaya in the final match of the night on Ashe.
